evidence.snippet: The individuals in our cohort carried 2 deletions, 8 likely gene-disruptive, 2 splice-site, and 20 different missense variants, most of them de novo.
evidence.explanation: Comprehensive description of the mutation spectrum in the largest reported cohort.

evidence.snippet: we now identified two de novo frameshift mutations and one de novo missense mutation in CTCF
evidence.explanation: Original discovery of pathogenic CTCF variants.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous de novo loss-of-function mutations (frameshift, nonsense, splice site) and missense variants (predominantly in zinc finger domains) cause this disorder. CTCF encodes an 11-zinc finger transcription factor essential for chromatin organization. Approximately 80%-85% of informative cases are de novo, with rare familial cases showing variable expressivity. Recurrent variants include p.Arg339Gln, p.Arg368Cys, and p.Arg567Trp.

evidence.snippet: monitor developmental progress and educational needs;
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports tracking developmental progress and educational needs as a routine management domain.

treatments/0.description: Early intervention services, speech therapy, occupational therapy, physical therapy, and individualized educational supports address developmental delays, intellectual disability, speech delay, and motor delay.

evidence.snippet: Feeding therapy with a low threshold for clinical feeding evaluation and/or radiographic swallowing study for those with clinical signs or symptoms of dysphagia; gastrostomy tube placement may be required for persistent feeding issues.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly supports feeding therapy, swallowing evaluation, and gastrostomy escalation for persistent feeding problems.

treatments/1.description: Nutritional support, feeding therapy, clinical feeding evaluation, swallowing studies, and gastrostomy tube placement when needed address feeding difficulty, dysphagia, aspiration risk, and persistent growth compromise.

treatments/2.description: Treat constipation and related gastrointestinal symptoms with standard symptom-directed agents while monitoring for reflux and bowel symptoms.

evidence.snippet: If a parent of the proband is known to have the pathogenic variant identified in the proband, the risk to the sibs of inheriting the pathogenic variant is 50%.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports recurrence-risk counseling based on parental testing and autosomal dominant inheritance.

treatments/3.description: Genetic counseling for families regarding recurrence risk, inheritance patterns, and implications of diagnosis. Most cases are de novo, but rare familial cases have been reported and an affected parent's recurrence risk is 50%.

open_questions/0.rationale: The entry models CTCF haploinsufficiency → weakened TAD boundaries → PCDH cluster misregulation as a core causal path, supported by R567W mouse model and human cell-line Hi-C data (PMID:38951485) and RNA-seq in five patients (PMID:31239556). However, no published dataset maps 3D chromatin architecture specifically at the PCDH locus in patient-derived iPSC cortical NPCs carrying confirmed truncating or diverse zinc-finger-domain missense variants. Three unresolved questions limit the mechanistic generalization: (A) whether PCDH TAD disruption is a universal consequence of CTCF haploinsufficiency regardless of variant type; (B) whether the disruption is differentiation-stage dependent (NPC vs. postmitotic neuron); and (C) whether the extent of inter-domain contact gain correlates with clinical severity. Without this data the entry's chromatin architecture claim rests on R567W-anchored evidence rather than disorder-level generalization across the full mutation spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Here we identify mutations in one such element, a regulatory alternative exon of SNRPB as the cause of cerebro-costo-mandibular syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The discovery paper localises the causal variants to the regulatory alternative exon rather than to the coding sequence.

evidence.snippet: All variants were located in the premature termination codon (PTC)-introducing alternative exon of transcript 3.
evidence.explanation: An independent cohort places every variant in the same PTC-introducing alternative exon.

steps/1.description: The CCMS variants cluster in a highly conserved alternative exon of SNRPB that contains a premature termination codon. Rather than changing the SmB/B' protein sequence, they shift splicing so that this exon is included more often.

evidence.snippet: Quantitative RT-PCR analysis revealed a significant increase in transcript 3 levels in leukocytes of CCMS individuals compared to controls.
evidence.explanation: Patient leukocytes show the predicted shift toward the decay-targeted transcript, measured directly.

steps/2.description: Less SmB/B' core Sm protein is available for assembly of the small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles of the major spliceosome. The transcript that is degraded is measurable in patients: quantitative RT-PCR shows the PTC-containing transcript raised in patient leukocytes.

evidence.snippet: We also found a small but significant increase in exon skipping of several transcripts required for head and midface development, including Smad2 and Rere.
evidence.explanation: The affected transcripts are developmental regulators of the same structures that are malformed in CCMS.

evidence.snippet: SNRPB knockdown altered splicing of TCF7L2 which impacts Wnt/β-catenin pathway activities.
evidence.explanation: A specific mis-spliced transcript is identified and tied to a named signalling pathway.

steps/3.description: Reduced core Sm protein produces increased exon skipping and intron retention. Affected transcripts include negative regulators of the P53 pathway, head and midface regulators such as Smad2 and Rere, and the Wnt effector TCF7L2.

evidence.snippet: However, removing Trp53 in Snrpb heterozygous mutant neural crest cells did not completely rescue craniofacial development.
evidence.explanation: The rescue experiment bounds how much of the phenotype the P53 arm accounts for, which is why this node is not drawn as the sole cause.

steps/4.description: Nuclear P53 and its target genes rise in the developing head. Removing Trp53 from Snrpb-heterozygous neural crest cells does not fully rescue craniofacial development, so P53 activation is one contributing arm rather than the whole mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Suppressed osteogenic markers by SNRPB knockdown were partly rescued by Wnt/β-catenin pathway activation.
evidence.explanation: A rescue experiment establishes the direction of the link between the pathway shift and the differentiation defect.

steps/5.description: Loss of SmB/B' shifts the balance of two skeletal patterning pathways. The source reports "attenuated Wnt pathway and/or enhanced BMP pathway activities", so the two directions are not established as always co-occurring and the modifiers below record each arm as reported rather than as a fixed pair. Suppressed osteogenic markers are partly rescued by activating Wnt/beta-catenin, which places the Wnt arm upstream of the differentiation defect rather than beside it.

evidence.snippet: We found that low levels of SmB/B' by knockdown or mutations of SNRPB led to suppressed osteodifferentiation in Saos-2 osteoprogenitor-like cells, which was accompanied by affected splicing of Dlx5.
evidence.explanation: The osteogenic arm of the differentiation defect is measured directly and linked to a specific mis-spliced transcription factor.

evidence.snippet: On the other hand, low SmB/B' led to promoted chondrogenesis in HEPM mesenchymal stem cells.
evidence.explanation: The chondrogenic arm runs in the opposite direction, which is why the node is written as an altered balance rather than a uniform loss.

steps/6.description: Low SmB/B' suppresses osteodifferentiation in osteoprogenitor-like cells and promotes chondrogenesis in mesenchymal cells, with altered splicing of the osteogenic transcription factor Dlx5. The chondrogenic direction here is the opposite of what the in-vivo rib model shows, so this node is deliberately not routed to the costal lesion; see the ccms_chondrogenesis_direction discussion.

evidence.snippet: Cerebro-Costo-Mandibular syndrome (CCMS) is a rare autosomal dominant condition comprising branchial arch-derivative malformations with striking rib-gaps.
evidence.explanation: The series characterises the craniofacial component explicitly as branchial arch-derivative malformation.

steps/7.description: Hypoplasia of first pharyngeal arch derivatives, above all the mandible. This is the branchial arch component of the syndrome and the immediate cause of the Pierre Robin sequence.

evidence.snippet: Key radiological findings are of a narrow thorax, multiple posterior rib gaps and abnormal costo-transverse articulation.
evidence.explanation: The three components of the costal lesion are stated together as the key radiological findings.

steps/8.description: Posterior rib gaps, reduced rib number, shortened ribs and abnormal costovertebral articulation. The rib gaps are the visually striking and near-specific radiographic sign.

evidence.snippet: Rather, the increase in chest wall compliance due to the rib gaps and the decrease in compliance at the costovertebral complex was considered to result in an equilibrium, minimizing the impact of these abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: This review supports the thorax being mechanically abnormal, but argues against the rib gaps being the dominant driver of neonatal distress. It is cited here as the qualification on this node rather than as support for a simple gap-to-distress link, and the inference from the compliance argument to the clinical outcome is the review's, not a measurement.

steps/9.description: A narrow thorax with reduced capacity. How much of the neonatal respiratory distress the rib gaps themselves contribute is contested: an anatomical review argues that increased chest wall compliance from the gaps and reduced compliance at the costovertebral complex partly offset each other.

evidence.snippet: A tracheostomy was formed on day of life 9 given the immediate risk to the baby's airway.
evidence.explanation: The airway risk is severe enough to require tracheostomy in the first days of life.

steps/10.description: Obstruction at the level of the tongue base and small oral cavity, the Pierre Robin mechanism. It is the component that makes intubation difficult and that tracheostomy addresses.

evidence.snippet: He was born limp and apnoeic and required multiple attempts at intubation before a definitive airway was eventually sited.
evidence.explanation: A case documents the neonatal respiratory failure and the difficulty of securing an airway.

steps/11.description: The convergence point of the airway and thoracic lesions, and the dominant cause of early mortality.

evidence.snippet: This exon contains a premature termination codon that triggers nonsense-mediated mRNA decay when included in the transcript. These mutations cause increased inclusion of the alternative exon and decreased overall expression of SNRPB.
evidence.explanation: This sentence states the causal step from raised exon inclusion to lower SNRPB expression, via nonsense-mediated decay.

edges/2.description: Inclusion of the PTC-containing exon routes the transcript to nonsense-mediated decay, so increased inclusion lowers the amount of SNRPB message that survives to be translated.

evidence.snippet: RNAseq analysis of mutant heads prior to morphological defects revealed increased exon skipping and intron retention in association with increased 5' splice site strength.
evidence.explanation: In the mouse model, reduced Snrpb produces a measurable, genome-wide splicing shift, and it precedes the morphological defect.

edges/3.description: Lower core Sm protein alters the splicing of many transcripts, with increased exon skipping and intron retention.

evidence.snippet: We found increased exon skipping in negative regulators of the P53 pathway, along with increased levels of nuclear P53 and P53 target genes.
evidence.explanation: The paper connects the splicing change in P53 regulators to a measured rise in nuclear P53 in the same tissue.

edges/4.description: Exon skipping in negative regulators of P53 raises nuclear P53 and its target genes in the developing head.

evidence.snippet: Reporter analysis revealed that suppression of SNRPB results in attenuated Wnt pathway and/or enhanced BMP pathway activities.
evidence.explanation: Reporter output is measured directly in cells with suppressed SNRPB.

edges/5.description: Reporter assays in SNRPB-knockdown cells show reduced Wnt pathway output and increased BMP pathway output.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, heterozygous deletion of Snrpb in the developing brain and neural crest cells models craniofacial malformations found in CCMS, and results in death shortly after birth.
evidence.explanation: Tissue-restricted deletion in neural crest reproduces the human craniofacial phenotype, placing the lesion in that lineage.

edges/6.description: P53 activation together with disturbed patterning signals in the same embryos produces the craniofacial malformation.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with other reports, osteogenesis was promoted by the Wnt/β-catenin pathway activator and suppressed by Wnt and BMP blockers, whereas chondrogenesis was promoted by Wnt inhibitors.
evidence.explanation: The pathway dependence of osteogenesis and chondrogenesis is established in the same experimental system.

edges/7.description: The pathway shift changes how skeletal precursors differentiate.

evidence.snippet: Wnt/β-catenin inhibition manifested characteristic rib phenotypes seen in CCMS, including rib gaps (P < 0.05) and missing ribs
evidence.explanation: Beads delivering a Wnt inhibitor to chick somites reproduce the rib gaps, making this a sufficiency test for the edge rather than a correlation.

evidence.snippet: Reduced expression of Sox9 was detected with Wnt/β-catenin inhibition, indicating that inhibition of chondrogenesis precipitated the rib defects in the presence of Wnt/β-catenin inhibitors.
evidence.explanation: Names the cellular step between the pathway shift and the rib defect, and gives its direction at the rib: chondrogenesis is inhibited there. Note this runs opposite to the promoted chondrogenesis seen in HEPM cells; see the ccms_chondrogenesis_direction discussion.

edges/8.description: Local Wnt/beta-catenin inhibition during somitogenesis is sufficient to produce rib gaps in vivo.

edges/9.description: Defective osteogenic differentiation in first-arch derivatives is the proposed route to mandibular hypoplasia. The differentiation data are from cell lines, not from patient mandible, so the step to the tissue is inferred.

evidence.snippet: Affected patients often have respiratory difficulties, associated with upper airway obstruction, reduced thoracic capacity, and scoliosis.
evidence.explanation: The series names upper airway obstruction as one of the two respiratory mechanisms.

edges/10.description: A hypoplastic mandible displaces the tongue base and obstructs the airway.

evidence.snippet: Affected patients often have respiratory difficulties, associated with upper airway obstruction, reduced thoracic capacity, and scoliosis.
evidence.explanation: Reduced thoracic capacity is named as a mechanism of the respiratory difficulty.

edges/11.description: The rib defects give a narrow thorax with reduced capacity. On the compliance argument, the absence of ribs rather than the gaps is the part that carries the respiratory consequence.

evidence.snippet: Cerebro-costo-mandibular syndrome (CCMS) is a congenital condition with skeletal and orofacial abnormalities that often results in respiratory distress in neonates.
evidence.explanation: The review states the link from the skeletal abnormality to neonatal respiratory distress.

evidence.snippet: Affected patients often have respiratory difficulties, associated with upper airway obstruction, reduced thoracic capacity, and scoliosis.
evidence.explanation: Upper airway obstruction is named as a direct contributor to the respiratory difficulty.

evidence.snippet: Here we identify mutations in one such element, a regulatory alternative exon of SNRPB as the cause of cerebro-costo-mandibular syndrome.
evidence.explanation: This is the gene-disease discovery statement.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that CCMS is due to heterozygous mutations in SNRPB, enhancing inclusion of a SNRPB PTC-introducing alternative exon, and show that this developmental disease is caused by defects in the splicing machinery.
evidence.explanation: An independent group replicates the gene-disease relationship and the mechanism.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous variants in the PTC-introducing alternative exon of SNRPB transcript 3. Because the variants act by shifting an autoregulatory splicing decision rather than by changing SmB/B' protein sequence, they are easy to miss on a coding-only analysis; SNRPB is a worked example in the poison-exon annotation literature.

evidence.snippet: A tracheostomy was formed on day of life 9 given the immediate risk to the baby's airway.
evidence.explanation: A case report documents tracheostomy as the definitive airway intervention.

treatments/0.description: Securing the airway is the first intervention. Intubation may be difficult and tracheostomy is often needed early.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Tracheostomy bypasses the obstruction at the tongue base created by the hypoplastic mandible.

evidence.snippet: A boy, having a mother with Pierre-Robin sequence and a sister with CCMS, was diagnosed prenatally with CCMS and successfully treated with ex utero intrapartum treatment (EXIT) at 36 weeks 6 days of gestation.
evidence.explanation: A single successfully treated case. The NCIT binding is the delivery procedure, because NCIT has no ex-utero-intrapartum-treatment term; the preferred_term carries the specificity.

treatments/1.description: Where CCMS is diagnosed prenatally, the airway can be secured on placental circulation before the cord is clamped, avoiding the emergency intubation that the postnatal presentation otherwise forces.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Secures the airway before the neonate depends on it, so it pre-empts the obstruction rather than relieving it.

evidence.snippet: Cleft palate, feeding difficulties, respiratory distress, tracheostomy requirement, and scoliosis are common.
evidence.explanation: The quote establishes that cleft palate is common in this population. It does not report repair or its outcome, so the step from the phenotype to the standard operation is the curator's inference, which is what directness INDIRECT records here.

treatments/2.description: Cleft palate is common in CCMS and is repaired surgically as it would be in isolated cleft palate.

evidence.snippet: Cleft palate, feeding difficulties, respiratory distress, tracheostomy requirement, and scoliosis are common.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that feeding difficulty is common. No CCMS series reports gastrostomy rates or outcomes, so the management step is inferred.

treatments/3.description: Feeding difficulties are common, and a gastrostomy is the usual route when oral feeding cannot be sustained alongside a tracheostomy and cleft palate.

evidence.snippet: Affected patients often have respiratory difficulties, associated with upper airway obstruction, reduced thoracic capacity, and scoliosis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes scoliosis as part of the respiratory problem, which is the argument for treating it. No CCMS-specific surgical series exists, so the operation itself is inferred from general practice.

treatments/4.description: Scoliosis is common and, in a thorax already restricted by rib defects, compounds the respiratory restriction. Surveillance is the mainstay, with spinal fusion where curve progression demands it.

evidence.snippet: Cleft palate, feeding difficulties, respiratory distress, tracheostomy requirement, and scoliosis are common.
evidence.explanation: The problems that supportive care addresses are enumerated in the series.

treatments/5.description: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Management is respiratory support, feeding support, and monitoring for scoliosis.

evidence.snippet: Although gene splicing occurs throughout the body, the phenotype of spliceosomal defects is largely limited to specific tissues.
evidence.explanation: The paper opens by stating the paradox, which is what this gap records.

open_questions/0.rationale: This is the central unexplained feature of every spliceosomopathy, and it is stated as an open question in the field rather than answered. The candidate answers on offer -- P53 sensitivity of neural crest, Wnt/BMP dose sensitivity of rib patterning -- each explain one half of the phenotype and neither explains why other tissues are spared.

evidence.snippet: anatomical consideration, and meta-analyses suggested that they might not be the significant factor in causing respiratory distress in neonates
evidence.explanation: The review states the counterintuitive conclusion that this gap records.

evidence.snippet: a further absence of ribs or vestigial rib formation is associated with respiratory distress and increased lethality.
evidence.explanation: Names the fourth contributor that the gap statement would otherwise omit, and the one the review argues is prognostically relevant.

evidence.snippet: priority indicator to develop a personalized treatment plan based on the phenotypes exhibited.
evidence.explanation: The review proposes an actionable measurement, which is what makes this an answerable gap rather than an open-ended one.

open_questions/1.rationale: The rib gaps are the sign everyone reaches for, but an anatomical review argues they may be close to mechanically neutral because increased chest wall compliance from the gaps is offset by decreased compliance at the costovertebral complex. The same review nominates a fourth contributor the gaps get credited for: absent or vestigial rib formation, which it links to respiratory distress and increased lethality and proposes counting as a priority indicator for treatment planning. So the question is not only "how much do the gaps contribute" but "which of the four thoracic features should be measured", and no prospective respiratory-mechanics study exists to settle either.

evidence.snippet: On the other hand, low SmB/B' led to promoted chondrogenesis in HEPM mesenchymal stem cells.
evidence.explanation: One direction, in craniofacial mesenchymal cells with SNRPB knocked down.

evidence.snippet: Reduced expression of Sox9 was detected with Wnt/β-catenin inhibition, indicating that inhibition of chondrogenesis precipitated the rib defects in the presence of Wnt/β-catenin inhibitors.
evidence.explanation: The opposite direction, in the in-vivo model of the rib phenotype. Cited as REFUTE against a uniform "chondrogenesis is promoted" reading, which is what makes the tension explicit rather than leaving it for a reader to notice.

open_questions/2.rationale: SNRPB knockdown promotes chondrogenesis in HEPM craniofacial mesenchymal cells, while in the chick rib model Wnt inhibition reduces Sox9 and the authors conclude that inhibited chondrogenesis precipitates the rib defects. Both may be right if the direction is tissue-specific -- craniofacial mesenchyme and somite-derived costal cartilage are different lineages -- but nothing published tests that, and the two systems also differ in species and in whether SNRPB itself is perturbed. Until it is resolved, this entry does not route the in-vitro chondrogenic finding to the costal lesion.

evidence.snippet: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare, bilateral, granulomatous, panuveitis following penetrating trauma or surgery to one eye.
evidence.explanation: Ocular penetrating injury is the required environmental trigger of sympathetic ophthalmia.

evidence.snippet: Eleven of the 13 states with the highest POHS rates bordered the Mississippi and Ohio rivers.
evidence.explanation: Geographic clustering along the Mississippi/Ohio river valleys ties POHS risk to Histoplasma-endemic residence.

evidence.snippet: Immunocompromised patients showed a significantly larger size of retinitis than immunocompetent patients.
evidence.explanation: Impaired host immunity worsens infectious choroiditis, the biological basis of the immunosuppression hazard.

evidence.snippet: The spectrum of etiologies for uveitis is very broad and includes infectious and auto-immune diseases.
evidence.explanation: States the infectious/autoimmune aetiologic dichotomy that structures this entry.

evidence.snippet: Out of 6191 cases with uveitis, 1925 were infectious, 4125 were non-infectious
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the infectious/non-infectious split in a 30-year tertiary uveitis cohort, showing both arms are numerically substantial.

steps/4.description: The root branch point of the entry. Choroidal inflammation may be driven by a replicating pathogen within ocular tissue or by an antigen-driven autoimmune/autoinflammatory process against ocular self-antigen. Both arms produce clinically overlapping choroiditis, and both converge on the same downstream tissue-injury cascade, but they diverge completely at the level of management: the infectious arm requires antimicrobial eradication and is made worse by unopposed immunosuppression, whereas the non-infectious arm requires exactly that immunosuppression. Distinguishing the arms is therefore the single most consequential diagnostic act in choroiditis.

evidence.snippet: the association with HLA-A29 suggests that it is directly involved in the presentation of peptide antigens to T cells
evidence.explanation: Frames the non-infectious arm as MHC-restricted peptide presentation to T cells.

evidence.snippet: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare, bilateral, granulomatous, panuveitis following penetrating trauma or surgery to one eye.
evidence.explanation: Sympathetic ophthalmia is the clearest human demonstration that breach of ocular antigen sequestration triggers bilateral autoimmune uveitis.

steps/5.description: In the non-infectious arm, T cells recognise peptide derived from ocular self-antigen presented on MHC molecules, breaking the eye's immune privilege. Loss of sequestration is explicit in sympathetic ophthalmia, where penetrating trauma exposes previously sequestered uveal antigen and provokes bilateral granulomatous disease. In birdshot chorioretinopathy the presenting molecule itself is the dominant genetic risk factor.

evidence.snippet: BSCR is the strongest documented association between HLA and disease in humans
evidence.explanation: Direct statement that birdshot-HLA-A29 is the strongest known human HLA-disease association.

evidence.snippet: Of these 49 patients, 47 (95.9%) had the HLA-A29 antigen.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies HLA-A29 carriage at 95.9% in a birdshot series.

evidence.snippet: The HLA-B12 (B44) antigen was also significantly associated with the disease, but this antigen is known to be in linkage disequilibrium with the antigen HLA-A29.
evidence.explanation: Supports the statement that the secondary HLA-B12(B44) signal reflects linkage disequilibrium rather than independent effect.

evidence.snippet: We also confirm that ERAP1 and ERAP2 haplotypes modulate disease risk.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the antigen-processing genes as risk modifiers within HLA-A29 carriers.

evidence.snippet: Homozygosity for HLA-A29 increased the risk of developing BSCR without affecting disease severity.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates an allele-dosage effect of HLA-A29 on susceptibility.

steps/6.description: Birdshot chorioretinopathy carries one of the strongest HLA-disease associations documented in human medicine: essentially all patients are HLA-A29 positive. In a classic series 47 of 49 birdshot patients (95.9%) carried HLA-A29, and the linked HLA-B12(B44) association is explained by linkage disequilibrium with HLA-A29 rather than by independent effect. Mechanistically the association is not merely a marker - genetic modifiers act on the peptide-loading pathway that supplies HLA-A29. ERAP1 and ERAP2 haplotypes that increase ERAP2 expression and decrease ERAP1 expression raise risk in HLA-A29 carriers, while a haplotype disrupting ERAP2 expression is protective, and homozygosity for HLA-A29 further increases susceptibility. Together these implicate a peptide-presentation threshold model in which excess presentation of ERAP2-shaped peptides on HLA-A29 activates the immune response in the choroid.

evidence.snippet: Ocular toxoplasmosis is the leading cause of posterior uveitis worldwide
evidence.explanation: Establishes an infectious organism as the single commonest driver of posterior uveitis/choroiditis.

evidence.snippet: Ocular involvement can occur at any stage of syphilis and any part of the eye can be affected.
evidence.explanation: Documents haematogenous ocular seeding by Treponema pallidum at any disease stage.

evidence.snippet: evidence of tuberculosis, including histologically or microbiologically confirmed infection, positive interferon-γ release assay test, or positive tuberculin skin test
evidence.explanation: Consensus criteria require demonstrable mycobacterial infection, supporting organism presence as the driver of the tubercular arm.

steps/7.description: In the infectious arm, an organism reaches and persists in the choroid, RPE or outer retina: Toxoplasma gondii as encysted bradyzoites in retinal scars, Mycobacterium tuberculosis within choroidal macrophages, Treponema pallidum disseminated haematogenously to the highly vascular choroid, or Histoplasma capsulatum presumed to have seeded the choroid during earlier fungaemia. The choroid's exceptionally high blood flow makes it a preferential site of haematogenous seeding. Organism persistence, not merely acute invasion, is what makes the infectious arm relapsing and what makes unopposed immunosuppression dangerous.

evidence.snippet: The cumulative incidence of recurrent OT at three years was 33.9%
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the recurrent nature of ocular toxoplasmosis in a treated tertiary cohort.

evidence.snippet: OT reactivation, owing to the persistence of tissue cysts in retinal tissues, can increase the probability of VA loss.
evidence.explanation: Directly states the tissue-cyst-persistence mechanism of reactivation and its link to cumulative visual loss.

evidence.snippet: Immunocompromised patients showed a significantly larger size of retinitis than immunocompetent patients.
evidence.explanation: Shows host immune control constrains lesion size, consistent with reactivation being restrained by immunity.

steps/8.description: The signature relapsing behaviour of ocular toxoplasmosis. Bradyzoites encysted in the retina at the edge of an old pigmented chorioretinal scar convert back to proliferating tachyzoites, producing a new satellite focus of necrotising retinochoroiditis at the scar border. Each reactivation enlarges the area of destroyed outer retina, so cumulative visual loss is driven by recurrence count and lesion location rather than by any single episode. Immunocompromise markedly worsens lesion size and visual outcome.

evidence.snippet: moderate diffuse lymphocytic infiltrates throughout the choroid
evidence.explanation: Histologic confirmation of diffuse lymphocytic infiltration of the choroid in serpiginous choroiditis.

evidence.snippet: Posterior involvement includes vitritis, vasculitis and choroidal lesions.
evidence.explanation: Documents the co-occurrence of choroidal inflammation with vitritis and retinal vasculitis.

steps/9.description: The convergence node of both aetiologic arms. Leukocytes - lymphocytes, macrophages and, in granulomatous forms, epithelioid and giant cells - are recruited across the choroidal vasculature into the choroidal stroma, with spillover into the vitreous (vitritis) and retinal vessels (retinal vasculitis). Histologically, serpiginous lesions show moderate diffuse lymphocytic infiltrates throughout the choroid. Because both an infectious and an autoimmune trigger produce a broadly similar infiltrate, the pattern of inflammation narrows but does not settle aetiology - some morphologies are informative (caseation favours tuberculosis; a serpiginous-like or tuberculoma pattern is a SUN criterion for tubercular uveitis) but microbiologic and serologic confirmation is what actually decides treatment.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis is based on histology with the presence of non-caseating epithelioid granulomas.
evidence.explanation: Defines the sarcoid granuloma as the histologic substrate.

evidence.snippet: Tuberculosis is a classic differential diagnosis to be wary of, especially in people who have spent time in endemic areas.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that infectious (TB) and sterile (sarcoid) granulomatous choroiditis are not separable on morphology alone.

evidence.snippet: It manifests as acute/chronic granulomatous uveitis with yellowish-white choroidal lesions or Dalen-Fuchs nodules.
evidence.explanation: Documents Dalen-Fuchs nodules as the granulomatous choroidal lesion of sympathetic ophthalmia.

steps/10.description: In sarcoidosis, tuberculosis and sympathetic ophthalmia the choroidal infiltrate organises into granulomas. Sarcoid granulomas are non-caseating epithelioid granulomas; tubercular disease produces choroidal tubercles and tuberculoma; sympathetic ophthalmia produces Dalen-Fuchs nodules, focal aggregates of epithelioid cells between Bruch's membrane and the RPE. That both an infectious (TB) and a sterile (sarcoid) trigger yield broadly overlapping granulomatous choroiditis is a second, tissue-level restatement of why the aetiologic fork is not reliably settled on morphology alone - tuberculosis is the standing differential for ocular sarcoidosis, and caseation, while suggestive of tuberculosis, is often unavailable because ocular biopsy is rarely performed.

evidence.snippet: PICCPs are resulting from one common clinicopathological mechanism, inflammatory choriocapillaris hypo- or non-perfusion.
evidence.explanation: States choriocapillaris non-perfusion as the single shared mechanism of this disease group.

evidence.snippet: ICGA shows the typical pattern of patchy lobular hypofluorescence reflecting hypo- or non-perfusion of the choriocapillaris
evidence.explanation: Links the mechanism to its imaging signature on indocyanine green angiography.

evidence.snippet: Choriocapillaris non-perfusion can affect the end-choriocappilaries, at the benign end of the PICCP spectrum (MEWDS), to larger choriocapillaris vessels or precapillary vessels at the origin of more severe forms such as acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE), idiopathic multifocal choroiditis (MFC) and Serpiginous Choroiditis (SC).
evidence.explanation: Supports the vessel-calibre severity gradient asserted in this node. (The spelling "end-choriocappilaries" is as printed in the source.)

steps/11.description: The shared final common pathway of several white-dot entities. Inflammation of the choriocapillaris and its precapillary supply produces hypo- or non-perfusion of choroidal lobules, which is the defining clinicopathological mechanism of the primary inflammatory choriocapillaropathies. The calibre of vessel affected grades disease severity: involvement of only terminal choriocapillaries gives the benign end of the spectrum (MEWDS), whereas involvement of larger choriocapillaris or precapillary vessels gives the severe forms - APMPPE, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis and serpiginous choroiditis. Because the choriocapillaris is the sole blood supply of the outer retina and RPE, its non-perfusion is directly ischaemic to the photoreceptor/RPE complex, and it is imaged as patchy lobular hypofluorescence on indocyanine green angiography.

evidence.snippet: Choroidal tuberculosis (TB) infection may present itself as a diffuse choroiditis that resembles serpiginous choroiditis, usually treated with immunossupressants.
evidence.explanation: States the misclassification hazard directly - a TB choroiditis that phenocopies an entity conventionally treated with immunosuppressants. Marked PARTIAL because the source documents the risk of misdirected treatment rather than measuring harm from immunosuppression. (The spelling "immunossupressants" is as printed in the source.)

evidence.snippet: Recent studies have demonstrated that patients with serpiginous-like choroiditis and evidence of systemic or latent TB are best treated with antituberculosis treatment (ATT) in addition to the corticosteroid therapy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that corticosteroid is appropriate in the infectious arm only when combined with antimicrobial therapy - the operational content of the management fork.

evidence.snippet: ocular syphilis should always be a part of the differential diagnosis of most, if not all, ocular infectious and inflammatory presentations
evidence.explanation: Supports mandatory syphilis exclusion in any inflammatory ocular presentation before immunosuppression.

steps/12.description: The harm arm of the aetiologic fork, and the reason the fork must be modelled mechanistically rather than as a list. When infectious choroiditis is misclassified as an idiopathic non-infectious entity, it receives the correct treatment for the wrong diagnosis — corticosteroid and/or steroid-sparing immunosuppression without antimicrobial cover. The expected consequence is loss of host immune restraint on a replicating organism; note that the documented evidence here is for the misclassification hazard and for the superiority of adding antimicrobial therapy, rather than a trial measuring harm from unopposed immunosuppression directly. Tubercular serpiginous-like choroiditis is the canonical case, because its idiopathic phenocopy is conventionally immunosuppressed; syphilis is the second, because it can imitate essentially any uveitic phenotype. This is why serologic and mycobacterial exclusion precede immunosuppression in all choroiditis.

evidence.snippet: The histological findings of the lesions are atrophy of the choriocapillaris, retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptor cells
evidence.explanation: Direct histologic evidence that choroiditis destroys the RPE/photoreceptor complex, not just the choroid.

evidence.snippet: Visual outcome is directly related to the involvement of the para-fovea and fovea by the lesions or secondary choroidal neovascularization.
evidence.explanation: Links outer-retinal lesion location to the visual outcome.

steps/13.description: The route from choroidal inflammation to actual vision loss. Because the choroid supplies the avascular outer retina, choroidal inflammation and choriocapillaris non-perfusion injure the photoreceptor/RPE complex rather than the choroid alone. Histology of serpiginous lesions shows atrophy of the choriocapillaris, RPE and photoreceptor cells together, and on OCT active lesions show disruption of the ellipsoid zone and RPE. Photoreceptor loss is irreversible, which is why choroiditis causes permanent scotomata and why the therapeutic goal is preventing new lesions rather than recovering old ones.

evidence.snippet: Inflammatory CNV develops when inflammation or infection directly involves the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)-Bruch's membrane complex.
evidence.explanation: Identifies RPE-Bruch's membrane involvement as the precondition for inflammatory CNV.

evidence.snippet: circumscribed areas of chorioretinal atrophy and subretinal pigmented fibrotic scars
evidence.explanation: Documents atrophic and fibrotic chorioretinal scarring as the healed end-state of multifocal choroiditis.

steps/14.description: Healed choroiditis lesions become punched-out atrophic, often pigmented, chorioretinal scars with disruption of the RPE-Bruch's membrane complex. The scar is not inert: a breached RPE-Bruch's membrane barrier is the anatomical precondition for ingrowth of new choroidal vessels into the subretinal space, and in ocular toxoplasmosis the scar border is the reservoir from which recurrent disease arises. Scars are therefore simultaneously the record of past disease and the substrate of future sight-threatening complications.

evidence.snippet: Inflammation itself can compromise perfusion, generating a gradient of retinal-choroidal hypoxia that additionally promotes the formation of choroidal neovascularization in the course of uveitis.
evidence.explanation: States the hypoxia-driven mechanism connecting choroidal inflammation to neovascularization.

evidence.snippet: The development of choroidal neovascularization may be a complication, especially in conditions such as punctate inner choroidopathy, multifocal choroiditis, serpiginous choroiditis, and presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the choroiditis subtypes in which inflammatory CNV is most frequent.

evidence.snippet: A number of uveitic entities may be complicated by the development of choroidal neovascularization leading to a decrease in central visual acuity.
evidence.explanation: Confirms inflammatory CNV as a cause of central acuity loss across uveitic entities.

steps/15.description: A major sight-threatening complication of inflammatory chorioretinal scars, and in some entities the dominant cause of vision loss rather than the inflammation itself. Inflammation compromises choroidal perfusion, generating a retinal-choroidal hypoxia gradient; VEGF, SDF-1-alpha and other mediators are released; and with the RPE-Bruch's membrane barrier already breached, new choroidal vessels grow into the subretinal space, the majority appearing as a classic type 2 lesion. It is especially common in punctate inner choroidopathy, multifocal choroiditis, serpiginous choroiditis and presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome. Clinically it is hard to distinguish from an active inflammatory lesion, which matters because the treatments differ: anti-VEGF for the neovascular membrane versus anti-inflammatory therapy for active choroiditis.

evidence.snippet: Posterior uveitis is a common chorioretinal pathology affecting all ages worldwide and is a frequent reason for referral to the retina clinic.
evidence.explanation: Establishes posterior uveitis as the clinical presentation class of chorioretinal inflammation.

steps/16.description: Inflammation localised to the posterior segment involving the choroid and retina, the defining anatomic class of choroiditis.

evidence.snippet: patients may complain of a temporal scotoma, metamorphopsia, floaters, photopsias, photophobia, and decreased vision
evidence.explanation: Lists decreased vision among the presenting symptoms of multifocal choroiditis.

evidence.snippet: At the final visit, 21% of all affected eyes suffered VA ≤ 20/200.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies severe residual acuity loss after treated ocular toxoplasmosis.

steps/17.description: Loss of central visual acuity, the principal functional consequence of choroiditis. In a treated ocular toxoplasmosis cohort one-fifth of affected eyes ended with acuity of 20/200 or worse.

evidence.snippet: circumscribed areas of chorioretinal atrophy and subretinal pigmented fibrotic scars
evidence.explanation: Documents chorioretinal atrophy as a defining structural outcome of idiopathic multifocal choroiditis.

steps/18.description: Confluent loss of choriocapillaris, RPE and outer retina producing well-demarcated atrophic chorioretinal zones, the structural end-state of repeated or extensive choroiditis.

evidence.snippet: Affected eyes typically show multiple punched-out chorioretinal lesions ranging from 50 to 350 μm in size
evidence.explanation: Documents punched-out chorioretinal lesions as the characteristic healed lesion morphology.

evidence.snippet: Patients mainly presented with primary retinitis without previous scar (62%)
evidence.explanation: Marked PARTIAL because this is an argument from the complement: 62% had no previous scar, so the remaining ~38% presented in eyes carrying a pre-existing chorioretinal scar. The source reports the former directly, not the latter.

steps/19.description: Punched-out, often pigmented healed chorioretinal lesions. In ocular toxoplasmosis a pre-existing scar marks the site from which recurrent retinochoroiditis characteristically arises at the lesion border.

evidence.snippet: Choroidal neovascularization (CNV) secondary to OHS is considered one of the principal causes of central vision loss among young adults in endemic areas.
evidence.explanation: Documents CNV as the dominant vision-threatening complication in POHS.

evidence.snippet: New or worsening PIC lesions suggest active inflammation, while new neovascular membranes may indicate secondary neovascular processes.
evidence.explanation: Confirms neovascular membranes as a distinct, treatment-relevant complication of PIC.

steps/20.description: Ingrowth of new choroidal vessels through a breached RPE-Bruch's membrane complex into the subretinal space. A major sight-threatening complication and in POHS and PIC the dominant cause of vision loss.

evidence.snippet: Posterior involvement includes vitritis, vasculitis and choroidal lesions.
evidence.explanation: Documents vitritis accompanying choroidal involvement in posterior uveitis.

evidence.snippet: BSCR is characterized by distinctive multiple choroidal hypopigmented lesions in combination with retinal vasculitis and vitritis
evidence.explanation: Documents vitritis as a defining feature of birdshot chorioretinopathy.

steps/21.description: Inflammatory cells in the vitreous cavity, reflecting spillover from choroidal and retinal inflammation. Characteristically present in ocular toxoplasmosis, birdshot chorioretinopathy and MFCPU, and characteristically absent in punctate inner choroidopathy - a discriminating sign.

evidence.snippet: BSCR is characterized by distinctive multiple choroidal hypopigmented lesions in combination with retinal vasculitis and vitritis
evidence.explanation: Documents retinal vasculitis as a defining feature of birdshot chorioretinopathy.

evidence.snippet: (4) occlusive retinal vasculitis, and (5) in hosts with evidence of active systemic tuberculosis, multifocal choroiditis
evidence.explanation: Lists occlusive retinal vasculitis among the SUN-defining presentations of tubercular uveitis.

steps/22.description: Inflammation of retinal vessels accompanying choroidal inflammation. A defining component of birdshot chorioretinopathy and a recognised feature of sarcoid and tubercular posterior uveitis (where it may be occlusive).

evidence.snippet: higher frequency of structural complications such as cataract, cystoid macular edema (CME), and epiretinal membrane (ERM) related to intraocular inflammation
evidence.explanation: Documents cystoid macular edema as an inflammation-related structural complication of MFCPU.

steps/23.description: Accumulation of intraretinal fluid at the macula from inflammatory breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier. A leading reversible cause of vision loss in choroiditis and the primary endpoint of several uveitis trials.

evidence.snippet: patients may complain of a temporal scotoma, metamorphopsia, floaters, photopsias, photophobia, and decreased vision
evidence.explanation: Lists scotoma among the presenting symptoms of multifocal choroiditis.

steps/24.description: A localised blind spot in the visual field corresponding to a zone of destroyed outer retina. Because photoreceptor loss is irreversible, scotomata from healed choroiditis lesions are permanent.

evidence.snippet: patients may complain of a temporal scotoma, metamorphopsia, floaters, photopsias, photophobia, and decreased vision
evidence.explanation: Lists metamorphopsia among the presenting symptoms of multifocal choroiditis.

steps/25.description: Distortion of straight lines, typically signalling macular involvement by subretinal fluid or a choroidal neovascular membrane.

evidence.snippet: patients may complain of a temporal scotoma, metamorphopsia, floaters, photopsias, photophobia, and decreased vision
evidence.explanation: Lists photopsia among the presenting symptoms of multifocal choroiditis.

steps/26.description: Perceived flashes or shimmering of light arising from dysfunctional or irritated photoreceptors overlying active outer-retinal inflammation.

evidence.snippet: Ocular toxoplasmosis (OT), a severe manifestation of T. gondii infection, can lead to potentially blinding complications.
evidence.explanation: Documents blindness as a potential outcome of the commonest infectious choroiditis.

steps/27.description: Severe irreversible visual loss, the feared endpoint of macula-involving or repeatedly recurrent choroiditis.

evidence.snippet: patients may complain of a temporal scotoma, metamorphopsia, floaters, photopsias, photophobia, and decreased vision
evidence.explanation: Lists floaters among the presenting symptoms of multifocal choroiditis.

steps/28.description: Perceived mobile opacities from inflammatory cells and debris in the vitreous, a common presenting symptom of active choroiditis.

evidence.snippet: Macular scar 24 (24.7)
evidence.explanation: Complications table reports macular scar in 24 of 97 patients (24.7%), supporting the OCCASIONAL (5-29%) frequency band.

steps/29.description: A healed, often pigmented chorioretinal scar involving the macula. The commonest structural complication in an ocular toxoplasmosis cohort, present in 24.7% of patients, and a direct cause of permanent central visual loss.

evidence.snippet: Ocular hypertension (IOP >21 mmHg) 20 (20.6)
evidence.explanation: Complications table reports ocular hypertension in 20 of 97 patients (20.6%), supporting the OCCASIONAL (5-29%) frequency band.

steps/30.description: Raised intraocular pressure (above 21 mmHg) complicating intraocular inflammation and its corticosteroid treatment, recorded in 20.6% of an ocular toxoplasmosis cohort.

evidence.snippet: higher frequency of structural complications such as cataract, cystoid macular edema (CME), and epiretinal membrane (ERM) related to intraocular inflammation
evidence.explanation: Documents epiretinal membrane as an inflammation-related structural complication of MFCPU.

steps/31.description: A fibrocellular membrane on the inner retinal surface, a structural complication of chronic intraocular inflammation that can distort the macula and reduce acuity. Reported in 12.6% of an ocular toxoplasmosis cohort.

evidence.snippet: higher frequency of structural complications such as cataract, cystoid macular edema (CME), and epiretinal membrane (ERM) related to intraocular inflammation
evidence.explanation: Documents cataract as an inflammation-related structural complication of MFCPU.

steps/32.description: Lens opacification arising from chronic intraocular inflammation and from the corticosteroid therapy used to treat it - a complication of both the disease and its management.

edges/37.description: Sympathetic ophthalmia is the worked example this node already names for loss of antigen sequestration, and penetrating injury to one eye is what breaches it. The intervening step is therefore a known one. evidence.snippet: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare, bilateral, granulomatous, panuveitis following penetrating trauma or surgery to one eye.

edges/38.description: The same sentence read one step further along: it describes the post-traumatic entity as granulomatous, which is this node rather than the generic infiltrate node upstream of it. Both edges are drawn because the autoimmune recognition and the granulomatous character of the resulting inflammation are separate claims and this entry models them as separate nodes.

evidence.snippet: Eleven of the 13 states with the highest POHS rates bordered the Mississippi and Ohio rivers.

edges/39.description: Endemic residence is an ecological proxy for exposure to the organism, and the organism reaching and persisting in the choroid is this node. Graded low because the evidence is geographic clustering of a syndrome across states, which is several steps removed from any observation of the fungus in ocular tissue, and the syndrome itself is named presumed for that reason.

evidence.snippet: Immunocompromised patients showed a significantly larger size of retinitis than immunocompetent patients.
evidence.explanation: Immunocompromised patients had significantly larger retinitis than immunocompetent patients. Lesion size is a proxy for unrestrained organism growth rather than a measure of persistence itself.

edges/40.description: Impaired host immunity permits the organism to grow and persist rather than causing it to arrive, which is why this is recorded as exacerbating. Pointed at pathogen persistence and not at this entry's unopposed-immunosuppression node, which is a distinct claim: that node models iatrogenic immunosuppression given for a misdiagnosed infection, whereas this exposure is host immunocompromise however arising.

evidence.snippet: BSCR is the strongest documented association between HLA and disease in humans
evidence.explanation: Establishes the exceptional strength of the HLA-A29 association.

evidence.snippet: Homozygosity for HLA-A29 increased the risk of developing BSCR without affecting disease severity.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the allele-dosage effect on susceptibility.

genes/0.notes: The dominant genetic risk factor for birdshot chorioretinopathy and the strongest documented HLA-disease association in humans. Virtually all patients carry HLA-A29, and homozygosity increases susceptibility further without altering severity. This is a susceptibility allele in an HLA-restricted autoimmune disease, not a Mendelian causal gene.

evidence.snippet: an expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) decreasing ERAP1 expression
evidence.explanation: Identifies the ERAP1 risk variant as an expression-lowering eQTL.

genes/1.notes: Endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 1 trims peptides for MHC class I loading. An expression quantitative trait locus decreasing ERAP1 expression (rs27432) raises birdshot risk within HLA-A29 carriers, consistent with a model in which altered peptide processing changes the HLA-A29 peptidome.

evidence.snippet: an eQTL increasing ERAP2 expression. Furthermore, ERAP2-rs2248374 that disrupts ERAP2 expression is protective
evidence.explanation: Documents both the risk-increasing and the protective ERAP2 expression variants.

genes/2.notes: Endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 2, whose increased expression raises birdshot risk while a haplotype disrupting its expression is protective. The opposing directions of the two ERAP2 variants make the antigen-processing mechanism unusually well supported.

evidence.snippet: The current mainstay for the treatment, if necessary, is the use of oral antibiotic with systemic corticosteroids.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the combined antimicrobial-plus-corticosteroid regimen - the infectious arm's version of anti-inflammatory therapy, always paired with antimicrobial cover.

evidence.snippet: the combination of pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and corticosteroids
evidence.explanation: Names the conventional antiparasitic-plus-corticosteroid regimen for ocular toxoplasmosis.

treatments/0.description: Antimicrobial eradication of the active Toxoplasma focus, historically pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine with corticosteroid ("classic therapy"), with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole a well-supported alternative in immunocompetent patients. Corticosteroid is added only under antiparasitic cover; it must never be given alone.

evidence.snippet: Based on our network meta-analysis, therapy with TMP-SMX seems to be an alternative treatment of OT in immunocompetent patients.
evidence.explanation: Network meta-analysis supporting antiparasitic therapy directed at the organism.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Antiparasitic drugs suppress replicating tachyzoites in the retina and choroid.

evidence.snippet: The use of ATT in these patients is likely to reduce active inflammation and eliminate future recurrences.
evidence.explanation: States the dual benefit of antitubercular therapy in serpiginous-like choroiditis.

treatments/1.description: Multi-drug antitubercular therapy (ATT) added to corticosteroid in serpiginous-like choroiditis with evidence of systemic or latent tuberculosis. ATT reduces active inflammation and, critically, eliminates the recurrences that immunosuppression alone would not prevent. Trials are ongoing on optimal duration.

evidence.snippet: patients with serpiginous-like choroiditis and evidence of systemic or latent TB are best treated with antituberculosis treatment (ATT) in addition to the corticosteroid therapy

evidence.snippet: With the timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment, ocular syphilis is curable. However, delayed diagnosis of ocular syphilis may result in long-term visual impairment.
evidence.explanation: Documents curability with timely antibiotic therapy and the cost of delay.

treatments/2.description: Ocular syphilis is managed as neurosyphilis, with parenteral aqueous crystalline penicillin G the drug of choice. Timely treatment is curative; delay produces long-term visual impairment. This is the clearest case in which the correct diagnosis converts an untreatable-looking uveitis into a curable infection.

evidence.snippet: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommend that ocular syphilis be managed according to its treatment guidelines for neurosyphilis, with parenteral aqueous crystalline penicillin G the drug of choice.
evidence.explanation: Guideline-level support for penicillin G as the eradicating therapy.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Penicillin eradicates Treponema pallidum from ocular and CNS compartments.

evidence.snippet: Local and systemic corticosteroids can be used for short periods, but immunosuppressive or biological therapies are usually needed for the long-term management of the disease.

evidence.snippet: Choroidal tuberculosis (TB) infection may present itself as a diffuse choroiditis that resembles serpiginous choroiditis, usually treated with immunossupressants.
evidence.explanation: Supports the safety caveat by documenting a TB choroiditis that phenocopies an entity conventionally treated with immunosuppression. Marked PARTIAL because the source states the misclassification risk rather than measuring corticosteroid harm directly.

treatments/3.description: First-line anti-inflammatory therapy for non-infectious choroiditis, given locally or systemically. It is the mainstay of the non-infectious arm and remains first-line in ocular sarcoidosis. In the infectious arm it is permissible only in combination with antimicrobial therapy; given alone to an unrecognised infectious choroiditis it removes immune restraint on the organism. Up to 30% of sarcoidosis patients require high doses, which is what drives the move to steroid-sparing agents.

evidence.snippet: Corticosteroids remain the first-line treatment for sarcoidosis, but up to 30% of patients require high doses, justifying the use of corticosteroid-sparing treatments.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Corticosteroid suppresses the choroidal inflammatory infiltrate.

evidence.snippet: immunosuppressive or biological therapies are usually needed for the long-term management of the disease

evidence.explanation: Supports immunosuppression in serpiginous choroiditis, marked PARTIAL because the evidence base is small uncontrolled case series.

treatments/4.description: Corticosteroid-sparing immunomodulation - methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, and anti-TNF biologics - for chronic non-infectious choroiditis, especially birdshot chorioretinopathy, serpiginous choroiditis, MFCPU and sarcoid uveitis. This is the arm of the treatment fork that is actively dangerous if the aetiology is in fact infectious and untreated. Spans two platforms (small-molecule antimetabolites and monoclonal-antibody biologics), hence therapeutic_modality OTHER.

evidence.snippet: immunosuppressive treatments such as methotrexate may be introduced. More recent biotherapies such as anti-TNF are also very effective (as they are in other non-infectious uveitis etiologies)
evidence.explanation: Supports methotrexate and anti-TNF for non-infectious uveitis broadly.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Immunomodulatory therapy suppresses the autoreactive T-cell response driving non-infectious choroiditis.

treatments/5.description: Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection for inflammatory choroidal neovascular membranes, with or without concomitant anti-inflammatory therapy. In POHS and PIC, where CNV rather than inflammation dominates vision loss, this is the principal sight-preserving intervention.

evidence.snippet: Management of these neovascular membranes consists of anti-vascular growth factor agents, with or without concomitant anti-inflammatory and/or corticosteroid therapy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes anti-VEGF as the management of inflammatory CNV.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: VEGF blockade causes regression of the inflammatory neovascular membrane.

evidence.snippet: Extrafoveal CNVs are successfully treated with laser photocoagulation.
evidence.explanation: Documents laser photocoagulation as effective for extrafoveal neovascular membranes.

treatments/6.description: Thermal laser ablation of extrafoveal inflammatory choroidal neovascular membranes, where the membrane is far enough from the fovea that the resulting scotoma is acceptable. Largely superseded by anti-VEGF for subfoveal and juxtafoveal lesions.

evidence.snippet: Extrafoveal CNVs are successfully treated with laser photocoagulation.
evidence.explanation: Supports laser photocoagulation for extrafoveal CNV.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: Photocoagulation ablates the extrafoveal neovascular membrane.

evidence.snippet: RESULTS: We observed hemizygous mutations in the moesin (MSN) gene (located on the X chromosome and coding for MSN) in all 7 patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes MSN as the causative locus across the founding series.

evidence.snippet: METHOD: Whole genome microarray copy number variant (CNV) analysis was performed on the proband followed by whole exome sequencing (WES) and trio analysis of the proband and family members.
evidence.explanation: An independent diagnosis of the same entity by exome sequencing, confirming the gene outside the founding cohort.

steps/1.description: Hemizygous variants in MSN on the X chromosome, identified in all seven males of the founding series drawn from five different families.

steps/2.description: Moesin is an ERM protein whose job is to link filamentous actin at the cell cortex to membrane proteins. Losing it degrades the lymphocyte's ability to remodel its cortex, which is the shared requirement behind migration, adhesion, receptor surface display and the cytoskeletal reorganisation that proliferation depends on.

evidence.snippet: MSN-deficient T cells also displayed poor chemokine receptor expression, increased adhesion molecule expression, and altered migration and adhesion capacities.
evidence.explanation: Measures all four of the defects this node asserts, in patient-derived T cells.

steps/3.description: Patient T cells show poor chemokine receptor expression, increased adhesion molecule expression, and altered migration and adhesion. The combination is characteristic: the cells are not simply less adhesive or less mobile but dysregulated in both directions, which is what a scaffolding defect rather than a receptor defect predicts.

evidence.snippet: This phenotype was associated with impaired T-cell proliferation, which was rescued by expression of wild-type MSN.
evidence.explanation: Both the defect and its rescue by wild-type MSN. The rescue is what makes this a demonstrated dependency rather than an association, and it is why this node carries more weight than the others.

steps/4.description: Reduced T-cell proliferative capacity. This is the node with the strongest causal evidence in the entry, because re-expressing wild-type MSN in patient cells restores it.

evidence.snippet: BACKGROUND: We investigated 7 male patients (from 5 different families) presenting with profound lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, fluctuating monocytopenia and neutropenia, a poor immune response to vaccine antigens, and increased susceptibility to bacterial and varicella zoster virus infections.
evidence.explanation: The full clinical and haematological picture across the founding series, and the source for the phenotype records below.

evidence.snippet: X-linked moesin-associated immunodeficiency (X-MAID) is a recently described form of primary immunodeficiency, characterized by severe leukopenia affecting T and B cells as well as neutrophils (1).
evidence.explanation: An independent statement of the multi-lineage leukopenia that defines this node.

steps/5.description: Severe leukopenia affecting T and B cells and neutrophils, with fluctuating monocytopenia. The breadth across lineages is what makes this a combined immunodeficiency rather than a T-cell-selective one.

evidence.snippet: presenting with profound lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, fluctuating monocytopenia and neutropenia
evidence.explanation: Documents the lymphopenia at presentation.

steps/6.description: Profound lymphopenia, the cardinal laboratory abnormality.

evidence.snippet: BACKGROUND: We investigated 7 male patients (from 5 different families) presenting with profound lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, fluctuating monocytopenia and neutropenia, a poor immune response to vaccine antigens, and increased susceptibility to bacterial and varicella zoster virus infections.
evidence.explanation: Documents the neutropenia and that it fluctuates.

steps/7.description: Neutropenia, described as fluctuating rather than persistent.

evidence.snippet: BACKGROUND: We investigated 7 male patients (from 5 different families) presenting with profound lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, fluctuating monocytopenia and neutropenia, a poor immune response to vaccine antigens, and increased susceptibility to bacterial and varicella zoster virus infections.
evidence.explanation: Documents the monocytopenia and that it fluctuates.

steps/8.description: Monocytopenia, likewise fluctuating.

evidence.snippet: profound lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, fluctuating monocytopenia and neutropenia, a poor immune response to vaccine antigens
evidence.explanation: Documents the hypogammaglobulinemia together with the impaired vaccine response described in this record.

steps/9.description: Hypogammaglobulinemia, accompanied by a poor antibody response to vaccine antigens - which is the functional counterpart of the low immunoglobulin level and a stronger indicator of B-cell failure than the level alone.

evidence.snippet: increased susceptibility to bacterial and varicella zoster virus infections
evidence.explanation: Documents the bacterial infection susceptibility.

steps/10.description: Increased susceptibility to bacterial infection, the clinical consequence of the combined cellular and humoral defect.

evidence.snippet: increased susceptibility to bacterial and varicella zoster virus infections
evidence.explanation: Documents the varicella zoster susceptibility. Note the bound term is the general HPO concept for recurrent viral infection; preferred_term carries the specific organism, since HPO's general term is the closest accurate fit and manufacturing a narrower match would misstate the binding.

steps/11.description: Susceptibility to varicella zoster virus specifically, which is the characteristic viral vulnerability in this disorder. The record is named for what the source states. The bound HPO term's label says "Recurrent", but the source claims only increased susceptibility, so the recurrence is the ontology's wording rather than a claim this entry makes.

edges/1.description: Loss of moesin removes one of the ERM cross-linkers that tether cortical actin to the plasma membrane in lymphocytes.

edges/2.description: Chemotaxis and adhesion both require regulated cortical actin remodelling.

edges/3.description: Proliferation is impaired in patient cells and is restored by wild-type MSN, establishing the dependency rather than merely the association.

edges/4.description: Defective migration and adhesion contribute to the failure to maintain normal circulating lymphocyte numbers and distribution.

edges/5.description: Failure to expand contributes directly to the depleted lymphocyte compartment.

evidence.snippet: hemizygous mutations in the moesin (MSN) gene (located on the X chromosome and coding for MSN) in all 7 patients
evidence.explanation: Establishes the gene, its chromosomal location and the hemizygous state.

genes/0.notes:
MSN encodes moesin, one of the three ERM (ezrin-radixin-moesin) proteins that cross-link cortical actin to the plasma membrane. The gene is on the X chromosome, which is why the disorder is X-linked and all reported patients are male.
The binding here is hgnc:7373. Note that a substring search for "MSN" in HGNC also returns SAMSN1 (hgnc:10528) and MSNP1 (hgnc:7374), the moesin pseudogene; the CURIE bound here was resolved with an exact-label lookup for that reason.

evidence.snippet: X-linked moesin-associated immunodeficiency (X-MAID) is a recently described form of primary immunodeficiency, characterized by severe leukopenia affecting T and B cells as well as neutrophils (1).
evidence.explanation: Establishes that this case report concerns the disease in question. The report's title states its subject is transplantation for X-MAID.

evidence.snippet: Several studies have highlighted better outcomes for SCID patients diagnosed and transplanted early in life, a key element of justifying implementation of newborn SCID screening in the US and other countries (6, 7).
evidence.explanation: Marked INDIRECT deliberately, and worth reading as such. This sentence is about SCID, not X-MAID. It is cited for the timing principle the case report invokes, and the explanation says so rather than letting a quote about a different disease read as evidence about this one.

treatments/0.description: Replacement of the affected haematopoietic compartment. Moesin acts in lymphocytes and other leukocytes, all haematopoietic, so transplantation addresses the lesion in the lineages where it matters.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replaces MSN-deficient haematopoietic cells with donor cells carrying functional MSN, removing the lesion from the affected lineages.

evidence.snippet: We investigated 7 male patients (from 5 different families)
evidence.explanation: Establishes the size of the founding series, which is the basis for the claim that the evidence base is narrow.

evidence.snippet: These findings underscore the importance of moesin in IL-15-dependent CD8+ Treg cell homeostasis and, thus, the control of self-tolerance.
evidence.explanation: The mouse self-tolerance finding that the human series does not report, which is the specific discrepancy named in this gap.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Nearly all the clinical content of this entry comes from one 2016 series of seven males from five families, with an independent exome diagnosis confirming the gene in one further patient. The only curated treatment evidence is a single transplant case report.
That is enough to establish the disease and its mechanism, and not enough to say how it behaves over time or how well transplantation works. Specifically unaddressed: whether the fluctuating cytopenias fluctuate predictably or progress, whether the varicella susceptibility persists after immune reconstitution, what proportion of patients need transplantation rather than immunoglobulin replacement and prophylaxis, and whether the autoimmune arm predicted by the mouse CD8+ Treg finding appears in patients followed long enough.
The last of these is the sharpest, because the mouse and the human series currently point in different directions: the mouse loses self-tolerance, the patients present with infection.

evidence.snippet: All cases reported an antecedent event and fracture was the most common trigger (46%).
evidence.explanation: The exposure-frequency evidence for this environmental entry.

evidence.snippet: All cases reported an antecedent event and fracture was the most common trigger (46%).
evidence.explanation: Population-based evidence that an antecedent injury is universal and that fracture dominates it.

steps/1.description: The initiating event, and almost always a common one — distal limb fracture above all, with sprain, crush, surgery, and immobilization also recognized. In the Olmsted County population study every identified case reported an antecedent event and fracture was the trigger in 46%. Because the trigger is ubiquitous and the syndrome is rare, this node is necessary but far from sufficient, which is the premise of the whole entry.

evidence.snippet: Compelling evidence implicates biological pathways that underlie aberrant inflammation, vasomotor dysfunction, and maladaptive neuroplasticity in the clinical features of CRPS.
evidence.explanation: Names aberrant inflammation and vasomotor dysfunction as evidenced pathways underlying the clinical features this node produces.

steps/2.description: Activated C-fibre nociceptors release substance P and CGRP into the injured limb, producing vasodilation, plasma extravasation, oedema, erythema, and increased sweating, and recruiting local immune cells. This node is the direct substrate of three of the four Budapest domains — vasomotor, sudomotor/oedema, and part of the trophic — and it is what makes early CRPS a warm, swollen limb rather than a purely sensory complaint.

evidence.snippet: We identified these autoantibodies as immunoglobulin G directed against peptide sequences from the second extracellular loop of these receptors.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the molecular target epitopes that define this node.

evidence.snippet: The identification of functionally active autoantibodies in serum samples from CRPS patients supports an autoimmune pathogenesis of CRPS.
evidence.explanation: States the functional activity, which is what separates these from incidental autoreactivity.

evidence.snippet: Twenty seven (33%) of the 82 CRPS patients of whom serum was available showed a positive ANA test. This prevalence is significantly higher than in the general population.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the autoreactive subset this node applies to, using a general autoimmunity screen rather than the receptor-specific assay — which is why it is PARTIAL: it bounds the size of the subset without confirming the specific antibodies.

steps/3.description: Functionally active IgG directed at the second extracellular loop of the beta-2 adrenergic and muscarinic-2 receptors, with agonist-like properties in a cardiomyocyte bioassay. These are not bystander antibodies: they act on the receptors, they are found in a defined subset of patients, and their transfer into injured mice reproduces the syndrome. The node is the hinge of the entry — it converts a post-traumatic inflammatory response into a self-sustaining one.

evidence.snippet: After a short-lasting paw inflammatory response in all groups, CRPS IgG-injected mice displayed sustained, profound microglia and astrocyte activation in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and pain-related brain regions, indicating central sensitization.
evidence.explanation: Reports exactly the cellular state and location this node describes, and its persistence beyond the peripheral response.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, with the generation of an IL-1β floxed(fl/fl) mouse line, we demonstrated that CRPS IgG-induced changes are in part mediated by microglia-derived IL-1β, suggesting that both peripheral and central inflammatory mechanisms contribute to the transferred disease phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the cellular source of the mediating cytokine, which is what makes this a mechanism rather than a description.

steps/4.description: Microglia and astrocytes in the dorsal horn and in pain-related brain regions become and remain activated. The passive transfer experiment shows this state persisting long after the peripheral inflammatory response has resolved, and identifies microglia-derived IL-1beta as the mediator — with IL-1 receptor blockade both preventing it and reversing an already established phenotype. It is curated separately from the sensitization it produces because the two have different drug targets: IL-1 blockade acts here, NMDA antagonism acts downstream.

evidence.snippet: The primary pathology of both types of CRPS (Type I, also known as reflex sympathetic dystrophy, RSD; Type II, also known as causalgia) is featured by allodynia, edema, changes in skin color and temperature, and dystrophy, predominantly affecting extremities.
evidence.explanation: Places dystrophic change of the extremity among the primary pathology, the regional expression of which this node records.

steps/5.description: Patchy periarticular demineralization of the affected region — the finding Sudeck originally described as acute inflammatory bone atrophy, and the structural correlate of the intense periarticular uptake on the delayed phase of three-phase bone scintigraphy. It is curated as a distinct node because it is the target of the treatment with the strongest randomized evidence in this disease: intravenous bisphosphonate.

evidence.snippet: Key mechanisms underlying clinical manifestations include peripheral and central sensitization, sympathetic dysregulation, and alterations in somatosensory processing.
evidence.explanation: Names central sensitization among the key mechanisms underlying the clinical picture.

evidence.snippet: The pathophysiology of CRPS is not known but both clinical and experimental evidence demonstrate the important of the NMDA receptor and glial activation in its induction and maintenance.
evidence.explanation: States the NMDA-receptor dependence that defines this node and motivates the ketamine trial curated under treatments.

steps/6.description: An NMDA-receptor-dependent lowering of the threshold for nociceptive transmission, so that innocuous input is experienced as painful and painful input as more so, over a territory well beyond the original injury. It is the state that allodynia and hyperalgesia report, and the node ketamine targets: the NMDA receptor is the reason a dissociative anaesthetic has an analgesic role in this disease at all.

evidence.snippet: The center of the hand was shifted toward the cortical representation of the lip.
evidence.explanation: The spatial distortion component of the reorganization this node describes.

evidence.snippet: Using multiple regression analysis, the best predictor for the plastic changes was found to be mechanical hyperalgesia.
evidence.explanation: Identifies which clinical feature the cortical change tracks most closely.

steps/7.description: The cortical representation of the affected hand in primary somatosensory cortex shrinks and its centre shifts toward the lip representation, while tactile-evoked S1 responses on the affected side are increased. The extent of reorganization correlates with pain and, more strongly, with mechanical hyperalgesia, and mechanical hyperalgesia is its best single predictor. This node is the target of the rehabilitative treatments — graded motor imagery and mirror therapy — that work by restoring coherent sensorimotor representation rather than by any pharmacological action.
