evidence.snippet: Key mechanisms underlying clinical manifestations include peripheral and central sensitization, sympathetic dysregulation, and alterations in somatosensory processing.
evidence.explanation: Names sympathetic dysregulation among the key mechanisms underlying the clinical manifestations, which is what this node records.

steps/8.description: Disturbed sympathetic vasomotor control of the affected limb, producing the temperature and colour asymmetry of the vasomotor Budapest domain: an early warm, vasodilated phase and a later cold, cyanotic one. Importantly, not all CRPS pain is sympathetically maintained — a subset is sympathetically independent — which is the clearest explanation for why sympathetic blockade helps some patients and not others, and why this entry does not curate sympathetic block as a general treatment.

edges/0.description: Mechanical and chemical activation of nociceptor terminals in the injured tissue releases the neuropeptides that produce the local inflammatory response.

edges/1.description: How local neuro-immune activation breaks tolerance to autonomic receptor epitopes is not established; the edge is recorded at that strength.

edges/2.description: Sustained nociceptive input from the inflamed limb drives the spinal changes curated downstream.

edges/3.description: The transition from the early vasodilated limb to the later cold, cyanotic one accompanies the inflammatory response, but the mechanism of the switch is not resolved.

edges/4.description: Local inflammatory cytokines are the proposed route to the periarticular bone loss that three-phase scintigraphy detects.

edges/5.description: Patient IgG transferred to incised mice produces sustained microglial and astrocyte activation in the dorsal horn and pain-related brain regions, with microglia-derived IL-1beta as a demonstrated intermediate.

edges/6.description: The antibodies are agonist-like at receptors on autonomic neurons, so their action on vasomotor control is direct rather than mediated.

edges/7.description: Activated glia release IL-1beta and other mediators into the dorsal horn, lowering the threshold for nociceptive transmission — the step the IL-1 rescue experiment isolates.

edges/8.description: Persistent altered afferent input is the presumed driver of the cortical map change; the intermediates are not established, and the direction of causation between the two is itself an open question.

evidence.snippet: All cases reported an antecedent event and fracture was the most common trigger (46%).
evidence.explanation: Establishes fracture as the dominant trigger in a population-based ascertainment.

edges/9.description: The fracture is the tissue trauma node; the link makes the disease-level exposure explicit in the pathograph rather than leaving it implied.

genes/0.notes: HLA-DQ8, encoded at HLA-DQB1, is the most consistently reported MHC association with CRPS, particularly with the dystonic presentation, and several other class II alleles have been reported less consistently. The gene is recorded here as a susceptibility locus without an evidence item: the deep-research report cited the association only to a journal URL, and no citable primary source with a verifiable quote was established during curation. Treat as a curation lead — see the corresponding `discussions` entry. CRPS is not Mendelian and no causal gene exists.

evidence.snippet: In patients with acute CRPS-I, four i.v. infusions of neridronate 100 mg are associated with clinically relevant and persistent benefits.
evidence.explanation: The randomized efficacy result underpinning this treatment entry.

evidence.snippet: During the open-extension phase in the formerly placebo group the results of treatment were superimposable on those seen during the blind phase in the active group.
evidence.explanation: The internal replication that strengthens the result beyond a single between-group comparison.

treatments/0.description: An amino-bisphosphonate, and the intervention with the strongest randomized evidence in CRPS-I. In a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 82 patients, four 100 mg infusions over ten days produced a substantially greater fall in visual analogue pain score than placebo, with the effect sustained, replicated in the open-label crossover of the former placebo group, and with no patient reporting CRPS-related symptoms a year later.

evidence.snippet: These results provide conclusive evidence that the use of bisphosphonates, at appropriate doses, is the treatment of choice for CRPS-I.
evidence.explanation: The trial's own conclusion, linking the bisphosphonate drug class this node's biology predicts to clinical benefit.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Bisphosphonates act on osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, which is the process this node describes; whether the analgesic benefit is entirely explained by that action or also involves an anti-inflammatory effect is not established by the trial.

evidence.snippet: This study showed that intravenous ketamine administered in an outpatient setting resulted in statistically significant (p<0.05) reductions in many pain parameters. It also showed that subjects in our placebo group demonstrated no treatment effect in any parameter.
evidence.explanation: The randomized result with its negative-control arm, which is what makes this more than an open-label impression.

evidence.snippet: Intravenous ketamine demonstrated strong short-term analgesia, though findings were limited by small samples, variable protocols, and lack of long-term data.
evidence.explanation: Bounds the claim across the whole RCT literature rather than resting on the single trial above.

treatments/1.description: An NMDA-receptor antagonist, and the treatment that targets the central sensitization node directly. In a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial, four-hour daily outpatient infusions for ten days produced statistically significant reductions in many pain parameters, with the placebo group showing no treatment effect in any parameter. The trial is small and its authors call explicitly for a larger one with higher doses and longer follow-up, and a 2025 systematic review characterizes the analgesia as strong but short-term with no long-term data — so this is curated as an evidenced treatment with an explicitly bounded claim.

evidence.snippet: Ketamine is the most potent clinically available safe NMDA antagonist that has a well established role in the treatment of acute and chronic pain.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the drug's molecular target as the receptor this node's mechanism turns on.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Ketamine antagonizes the NMDA receptor on which this node's sensitization depends. Unusually for this disease, the drug's molecular target and the node's defining mechanism are the same object.

evidence.snippet: GMI and MT can improve pain in patients with CRPS type 1; however, there is not sufficient evidence to recommend these therapies over other treatments given the small size and heterogeneity of the studied population.
evidence.explanation: The systematic-review conclusion, quoted with its own qualifier.

treatments/2.description: A sequenced rehabilitative program — limb laterality recognition, then explicit motor imagery, then mirror therapy — aimed at the cortical representation rather than at any peripheral target. It is curated with its evidence caveat: a systematic review supports an effect on pain and function, but the trial base is small and heterogeneous.

evidence.snippet: GMI and MT can improve pain in patients with CRPS type 1; however, there is not sufficient evidence to recommend these therapies over other treatments given the small size and heterogeneity of the studied population.
evidence.explanation: Supports the effect on pain while stating the evidential limitation this entry preserves rather than overselling.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: The intervention is designed to re-establish a coherent sensorimotor representation of the affected limb, which is the node it targets; the inference that clinical benefit occurs through reversing reorganization is mechanistically motivated rather than directly demonstrated by the review.

evidence.snippet: The prevalence of complex regional pain syndrome was 2.4% (eight of 328) in the vitamin C group and 10.1% (ten of ninety-nine) in the placebo group (p=0.002); all of the affected patients were elderly women.
evidence.explanation: The randomized effect size on CRPS prevalence that this prevention entry rests on.

treatments/3.description: The prevention arm, and the reason CRPS is unusual among chronic pain syndromes: a cheap supplement given after the commonest inciting injury lowers incidence. In a randomized multicentre dose-response trial of 416 patients with 427 wrist fractures, vitamin C reduced CRPS-I compared with placebo (2.4% vs 10.1%), with no further benefit at 1500 mg.

evidence.snippet: Vitamin C reduces the prevalence of complex regional pain syndrome after wrist fractures.
evidence.explanation: The clinical prevention effect; the mechanism attributed to this node is stated as inference in the link description.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: The proposed mechanism is antioxidant limitation of the exaggerated inflammatory response to the fracture. The trial establishes the clinical effect; the mechanistic attribution to this node is inference and is recorded as such rather than as a demonstrated action.

evidence.snippet: Collectively, the evidence points to CRPS being a multifactorial disorder that is associated with an aberrant host response to tissue injury.
evidence.explanation: States the framing this hypothesis group is named for.

evidence.snippet: Variation in susceptibility to perturbed regulation of any of the underlying biological pathways probably accounts for the clinical heterogeneity of CRPS.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the corollary the pathograph is built on — parallel pathways with variable activation, rather than one obligatory chain.

hypotheses/0.description: The organizing framework. The inciting trauma is often trivial and is always common; CRPS is rare. What distinguishes patients is therefore the response, not the injury — an exaggerated and self-sustaining inflammatory, vasomotor, and neuroplastic reaction whose three pathways are activated to different degrees in different people. This is what the entry's branching pathograph encodes, and it is also why the clinical picture is so heterogeneous that a four-domain criteria set was needed to capture it.

evidence.snippet: Herein, we demonstrate the presence of autoantibodies in a subset of CRPS patients with agonistic-like properties on the β(2) adrenergic receptor and/or the muscarinic-2 receptor.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the autoantibodies and their targets in patients, with the "subset" qualifier this entry preserves.

evidence.snippet: CRPS IgG significantly increased and prolonged swelling and induced stable hyperalgesia of the incised paw compared with IgG from healthy controls.
evidence.explanation: The transfer result that converts the autoantibody finding from an association into a causal claim.

evidence.snippet: Genetic deletion of interleukin-1 (IL-1) using IL-1αβ knockout (KO) mice and perioperative IL-1 receptor type 1 (IL-1R1) blockade with the drug anakinra, but not treatment with the glucocorticoid prednisolone, prevented these changes.
evidence.explanation: The mechanistic rescue that identifies IL-1 as the mediator, with a negative control arm (prednisolone) that rules out generic anti-inflammatory action.

hypotheses/1.description: The strongest mechanistic result in the modern CRPS literature, and the reason this is not merely an inflammation story. Functionally active IgG against the beta-2 adrenergic and muscarinic-2 receptors is present in a subset of patients; transferring patient IgG into mice with a plantar incision produces prolonged swelling and stable hyperalgesia together with sustained microglial and astrocyte activation. Crucially the experiment includes its own mechanistic rescue: IL-1 knockout or IL-1 receptor blockade prevents the transferred phenotype, and blockade started eight days after incision reverses it. Curated as CANONICAL for that causal structure, with the caveat that the autoantibodies define a subset rather than all patients.

evidence.snippet: The authors found a significant shrinkage of the extension of the cortical hand representation for the CRPS affected side.
evidence.explanation: The primary magnetoencephalography finding this hypothesis rests on.

evidence.snippet: The cortical reorganization correlated with the amount of CRPS pain (r = 0.792), as measured by the McGill questionnaire, and the extent of mechanical hyperalgesia (r = 0.860).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the coupling to symptom severity that distinguishes this from an incidental imaging difference.

evidence.snippet: Despite this acuity deficit, CRPS was not associated with altered GABA or glutamate concentrations within the sensorimotor cortex on either the side that represents the affected or unaffected hand.
evidence.explanation: Refutes the specific disinhibition account of cortical reorganization — reduced total cortical GABA — while leaving the reorganization finding itself standing. The model is retained as CANONICAL for the map change and explicitly not for a GABA mechanism.

evidence.snippet: We found that individuals with upper limb CRPS displayed reduced tactile acuity in the painful hand, compared with the nonpainful hand and pain-free control subjects.
evidence.explanation: Independently replicates the sensory-cortical deficit this hypothesis predicts, in the same study that refutes the GABA explanation for it.

hypotheses/2.description: Above the spinal cord, the somatosensory representation of the affected hand shrinks and shifts toward the lip representation. What makes this more than an epiphenomenon is that the magnitude of reorganization correlates with CRPS pain and, most strongly, with mechanical hyperalgesia — and that the rehabilitative treatments aimed at this level (graded motor imagery, mirror therapy) have a real effect on pain. The direction of causation between reorganization and symptom is not settled by the correlational imaging alone, which is why the treatment evidence is curated alongside it.

open_questions/0.rationale: Pathological studies of amputated chronic CRPS-I limbs and skin biopsies show degeneration of small C and A-delta fibres, so the "no nerve lesion" criterion cannot mean an intact peripheral nervous system. Whether that degeneration is causal or consequent is undetermined, and loss of C-fibre terminals is not specific to CRPS since it accompanies other neuropathic pain states. The entry keeps the operational distinction because the criteria and the epidemiology use it, while recording that it does not cleanly separate mechanisms.

open_questions/1.rationale: The autoantibodies are described in a subset of patients, and the transfer experiments used IgG from patients with longstanding severe disease. Whether seronegative patients have a different mechanism, a lower antibody titre, or antibodies against untested targets is unresolved — and it matters therapeutically, because IL-1 blockade prevented and reversed the transferred phenotype in mice and would be expected to help only the antibody-driven group. No CRPS trial of IL-1 blockade stratified by antibody status was identified during curation.

open_questions/2.rationale: The tibia fracture model reproduces early CRPS well — pain behaviour, oedema, warmth, trophic change, spinal glial activation — which is why it carries this entry's links. But most post-fracture changes resolve within about five months, whereas the human disease that matters clinically is the one that does not resolve. Evidence therefore exists in the model for the initiating and early-maintenance mechanisms and is absent for the chronicity mechanism, which is a translational-validity limit rather than a knowledge gap. The IgG transfer model partly fills it — its donors are patients with longstanding disease — but it supplies the antibodies rather than generating them, so neither model contains the whole chronic disease.

open_questions/3.rationale: The deep-research report cited the HLA association only to a journal article URL and the candidate SNPs to a review, without an identifier whose abstract contains a quotable statement of the association. The HLA-DQB1 entry is therefore curated with `relationship_type: SUSCEPTIBILITY`, an explanatory note, and no evidence item; the SNP candidates are not curated at all.

evidence.snippet: Coronary artery anomalies (CAAs) are a group of congenital conditions characterized by abnormal origin or course of any of the 3 main epicardial coronary arteries.
evidence.explanation: Defines coronary artery anomalies as congenital abnormalities of origin or course of the epicardial coronary arteries.

steps/0.description: Coronary arteries form during embryogenesis through coordinated contributions of the proepicardium, epicardial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), endothelial progenitor migration into the developing myocardium, and connection of the nascent coronary plexus to the aortic root at the sinuses of Valsalva. Aberrations in coronary vasculogenesis, coronary stem formation, or septation of the outflow tract can produce anomalous origin from the aorta or pulmonary trunk, ostial atresia or stenosis, single coronary artery, or fistulous persistence of intramural sinusoidal connections. Cardiac neural crest cells and second heart field derivatives shape the outflow-tract anatomy that determines the final position of coronary ostia.

evidence.snippet: Anomalous left coronary artery from the right aortic sinus (L-AAOCA) with interarterial course carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD); therefore, current guidelines recommend exercise restriction and surgical intervention.
evidence.explanation: Links interarterial AAOCA course to high SCD risk and supports the mechanical-interference mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Although rare, congenital CAAs confer a high risk of myocardial ischemia and SCD, especially in young, previously "healthy" athletes during or immediately after vigorous exertion.
evidence.explanation: Documents exertional ischemia and SCD as the dominant clinical consequence of CAA anatomy in young patients.

steps/1.description: Subtype-specific mechanism for AAOCA. The anomalous proximal segment may be compressed between the aorta and pulmonary trunk (interarterial course), tunnel through the aortic wall as an intramural segment with a slit-like ostium, kink at an acute take-off angle, or stretch on exertion when aortopulmonary distention increases. These mechanisms reduce coronary luminal area and flow reserve during exercise, producing dynamic ischemia that can trigger lethal ventricular arrhythmias.

evidence.snippet: Overall, 114 (82.6%) patients received coronary reimplantation, 21 (15.2%) underwent Takeuchi repair, and three (2.1%) were treated by closure of the ALCAPA plus coronary artery bypass graft.
evidence.explanation: Large ALCAPA cohort shows that re-establishing dual-coronary perfusion is the dominant therapeutic strategy, consistent with the perfusion-mismatch / coronary-steal pathophysiology.

steps/2.description: Subtype-specific mechanism for ALCAPA. The postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance leaves the left coronary territory perfused at low pressure from the pulmonary trunk. Once intercoronary collaterals develop, blood is shunted retrograde from the right coronary into the pulmonary trunk (coronary steal), producing chronic subendocardial ischemia of the left ventricle and the classic infantile dilated cardiomyopathy with mitral regurgitation.

evidence.snippet: Congenital coronary ostial abnormalities can lead to severe heart failure and unexpected neonatal death.
evidence.explanation: Conclusion of a neonatal case series — congenital ostial obstruction produces refractory heart failure and unexpected neonatal death, supporting fixed-obstruction physiology as a distinct mechanism.

steps/3.description: Subtype-specific mechanism for congenital coronary atresia/ostial stenosis. There is fixed structural obstruction to antegrade coronary flow from the aortic root. Unlike AAOCA (dynamic interference) and ALCAPA (perfusion mismatch), obstruction is anatomic and constant, producing neonatal/infantile ischemia, cardiomyopathy, and often early death.

evidence.snippet: Coronary artery anomalies (CAAs) are a heterogeneous group of rare congenital diseases whose features and pathophysiological mechanisms are extremely variable, ranging from silent anomalies to sudden cardiac death (SCD) in the most severe cases.
evidence.explanation: Anchors the clinical range from silent disease to sudden cardiac death as the downstream consequence of CAA mechanisms.

evidence.snippet: In patients with decreased preoperative left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) (<50%), the LVEF significantly improved from 25% to 33% at discharge (p = 0.001).
evidence.explanation: ALCAPA patients present with markedly depressed LVEF that is reversible after restoration of dual coronary perfusion, supporting the ischemia-driven LV dysfunction mechanism.

steps/4.description: Demand-induced myocardial ischemia produced by AAOCA mechanical interference, ALCAPA coronary steal, or fixed ostial stenosis creates regional electrophysiological heterogeneity, fibrosis, and ventricular arrhythmias that can culminate in sudden cardiac death. In infants with ALCAPA and severe ostial obstruction, sustained ischemia leads to left ventricular dysfunction, mitral regurgitation, and dilated cardiomyopathy.

evidence.snippet: Coronary artery anomalies (CAAs) are a group of congenital conditions characterized by abnormal origin or course of any of the 3 main epicardial coronary arteries.
evidence.explanation: Establishes abnormal coronary artery origin as the defining feature of CAAs.

steps/5.description: The defining structural abnormality across AAOCA, ALCAPA, and several other subtypes is an abnormal origin of one or more coronary arteries from the aorta, the pulmonary artery, or with malposed ostia.

evidence.snippet: Coronary artery anomalies (CAAs) are a group of congenital conditions characterized by abnormal origin or course of any of the 3 main epicardial coronary arteries.
evidence.explanation: Supports abnormal course as part of the defining anatomic spectrum.

steps/6.description: Many subtypes feature an abnormal coronary course — interarterial, intramural, intraseptal, prepulmonic, or retroaortic — which contributes to ischemic risk independent of the ostial origin.

evidence.snippet: Anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery (AAOCA) from the inappropriate sinus of Valsalva is increasingly recognized by cardiac imaging.
evidence.explanation: Defines AAOCA in terms of anomalous origin from the opposite (inappropriate) sinus of Valsalva.

steps/7.description: Anomalous origin from the contralateral aortic sinus of Valsalva is the AAOCA-defining anatomic finding most associated with sudden death risk when accompanied by an interarterial course.

evidence.snippet: This study aims to assess the clinical presentation and the outcomes of a surgical correction of an anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA).
evidence.explanation: Defines ALCAPA as the anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery.

steps/8.description: The defining structural lesion of ALCAPA / Bland-White-Garland syndrome: origin of the left main coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk rather than the aorta.

evidence.snippet: The median normalisation time of left ventricular function was 6 months.
evidence.explanation: Supports the reversibility of ALCAPA-induced left ventricular dysfunction after surgical correction.

steps/9.description: Sustained ischemia from ALCAPA produces dilated cardiomyopathy in infants. Left ventricular function typically normalises within 6 months of restoring dual coronary perfusion.

evidence.snippet: The three infants with coronary stenosis died within minutes to days after birth because of cardiac failure refractory to intensive care treatment
evidence.explanation: Supports refractory congestive heart failure as a presentation of congenital coronary ostial stenosis in neonates.

steps/10.description: Infants with ALCAPA classically present with congestive heart failure once pulmonary vascular resistance falls; congenital coronary ostial atresia and ostial stenosis can also present with refractory neonatal heart failure.

evidence.snippet: Dyspnoea, palpitation, poor feeding, fatiguability, pallor and a murmur of mitral regurgitation were the main presenting features.
evidence.explanation: Documents mitral regurgitation among the main presenting features of ALCAPA.

steps/11.description: Ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction and left ventricular dilatation in ALCAPA commonly produce mitral regurgitation, which may require concomitant repair at the time of coronary re-implantation.

evidence.snippet: These fistulas are congenital or acquired coronary artery abnormalities in which blood is shunted into a cardiac chamber, great vessel, or other structure, bypassing the myocardial capillary network.
evidence.explanation: Defines the fistula phenotype as a shunt bypassing the myocardial capillary network.

steps/12.description: Coronary artery fistula is the defining anatomic abnormality of the fistula subtype: an abnormal communication between a coronary artery and a cardiac chamber, the coronary sinus, the pulmonary trunk, or another vessel, bypassing the myocardial capillary network.

evidence.snippet: Congenital left coronary artery abnormalities such as ostial stenosis or atresia are extremely rare.
evidence.explanation: Establishes congenital coronary ostial stenosis as a distinct rare malformation.

steps/13.description: Congenital narrowing of a coronary artery — particularly at the ostium — constitutes the defining lesion of the ostial stenosis/atresia subtype.

steps/14.description: Chest pain (angina equivalent) with or without exertion can be a presenting symptom of AAOCA, severe ostial stenosis, or coronary fistula with steal physiology. Listed as a clinical presentation per disease-overview literature; no cited PMID in this entry quotes "chest pain" verbatim, so no evidence block is attached (per dismech SOP for unverifiable snippets).

evidence.snippet: We also summarized the predominant mechanisms for interference with normal coronary artery function, which might contribute to the onset of life-threatening arrhythmias and SCD.
evidence.explanation: Connects CAA-mediated coronary interference to life-threatening arrhythmias.

steps/15.description: Ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias are common across the subtypes and can be the proximate cause of sudden cardiac death.

evidence.snippet: Although rare, congenital CAAs confer a high risk of myocardial ischemia and SCD, especially in young, previously "healthy" athletes during or immediately after vigorous exertion.
evidence.explanation: Identifies sudden cardiac death — particularly exertional — as a hallmark consequence of congenital CAAs.

steps/16.description: Sudden cardiac death, frequently exertional, is the most feared presentation of high-risk AAOCA (especially interarterial L-AAOCA) and can be a presenting event in undiagnosed ALCAPA or congenital ostial obstruction.

steps/17.description: Exertional syncope is a warning symptom in AAOCA that should prompt coronary imaging because it may herald sudden cardiac death. Listed as a clinical presentation per disease-overview literature; no cited PMID in this entry quotes "syncope" verbatim, so no evidence block is attached (per dismech SOP for unverifiable snippets).

edges/0.description: Anomalous aortic origin with interarterial or intramural course sets the anatomic stage for dynamic, exercise-triggered compression and kinking of the proximal coronary segment.

edges/1.description: Anomalous origin of the left coronary from the pulmonary trunk establishes the low-pressure perfusion bed that, once postnatal pulmonary vascular resistance falls, drives coronary steal.

edges/2.description: Failed coronary ostial formation or septation of the outflow tract produces fixed structural obstruction to antegrade coronary flow from the aortic root.

edges/3.description: Misplacement of the connection between the nascent coronary plexus and the aortic root, or its connection to the pulmonary trunk instead, is what is seen on imaging as an abnormal coronary ostial origin.

edges/4.description: Where the coronary stem attaches determines the path the proximal segment must take to reach its territory, so the same developmental error produces the interarterial, intramural, intraseptal, prepulmonic, and retroaortic courses.

edges/5.description: Connection of a coronary stem to the inappropriate sinus of Valsalva is the specific AAOCA form of the aberrant ostial connection.

edges/6.description: Failure of the left coronary stem to connect to the aortic root, leaving it attached to the pulmonary trunk, is the defining anatomic lesion of ALCAPA.

edges/7.description: Persistence of intramural sinusoidal connections that should regress during coronary vasculogenesis leaves a fistulous communication between a coronary artery and a chamber or vessel.

edges/8.description: Exercise-induced reduction in coronary luminal area drives myocardial ischemia and ventricular arrhythmia; SCD risk concentrates in young athletes during or just after vigorous exertion.

edges/9.description: Sustained low-pressure perfusion and coronary steal produce chronic subendocardial ischemia, infantile dilated cardiomyopathy, mitral regurgitation, and heart failure.

edges/10.description: Fixed obstruction to coronary inflow drives neonatal ischemia and infantile cardiomyopathy, often presenting as early heart failure or sudden death.

edges/11.description: The fixed anatomic narrowing or atresia at the coronary ostium is what is recorded as congenital coronary artery stenosis.

evidence.snippet: We also summarized the predominant mechanisms for interference with normal coronary artery function, which might contribute to the onset of life-threatening arrhythmias and SCD.
evidence.explanation: Connects CAA-mediated coronary interference to life-threatening arrhythmias.

edges/12.description: Regional ischemia and the fibrosis it leaves behind create the electrophysiological heterogeneity on which ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias arise.

edges/13.description: Demand-induced myocardial ischemia is felt as chest pain or an anginal equivalent, typically on exertion in AAOCA and ostial stenosis.

edges/14.description: Sustained subendocardial ischemia in infants with ALCAPA or severe ostial obstruction causes chronic left ventricular dysfunction and chamber dilation, the dilated cardiomyopathy characteristic of these subtypes; chronic hypoperfusion and infarction of viable myocardium are the omitted intermediate steps.

edges/15.description: Once the ischemic left ventricle dilates and its systolic function falls, filling pressures rise and the infant presents in congestive heart failure.

edges/16.description: Ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction together with left ventricular dilatation tethers the mitral leaflets and prevents coaptation, producing regurgitation.

edges/17.description: A malignant ventricular arrhythmia arising on the ischemic substrate is the proximate cause of the exertional sudden death that dominates the risk picture in high-risk AAOCA.

edges/18.description: A non-sustained arrhythmia that terminates before becoming fatal presents as exertional syncope, the warning symptom that should prompt coronary imaging.

genes/0.notes: Growth differentiation factor 1, a TGF-β superfamily member with established roles in cardiogenesis and left-right axis patterning. Identified as a candidate AAOCA susceptibility variant in paediatric whole-exome-sequencing cohorts.

genes/1.notes: Wnt-signalling co-receptor (LDL receptor-related protein 6). Mutations described in coronary artery disease type 2 (reduced/absent coronary blood flow) and identified in AAOCA WES cohorts.

genes/2.notes: Myocyte enhancer factor 2A. Loss-of-function mutations cause autosomal-dominant coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction (CAD/MI estimated up to ~2% of affected patients in some populations). Highly expressed in endothelium.

genes/3.notes: Kalirin, a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor regulating cytoskeletal dynamics. Associated with coronary heart disease susceptibility type 5 and identified in AAOCA WES cohorts.

genes/4.notes: Cardiac ryanodine receptor; canonical CPVT gene. Identification of RYR2 variants in AAOCA cohorts suggests potential concomitant arrhythmia susceptibility on top of structural anomaly.

genes/5.notes: PDZ-LIM domain-containing protein involved in muscle gene expression and Z-disc / cytoskeletal organisation; established association with dilated cardiomyopathy. Identified as candidate in AAOCA WES cohorts.

evidence.snippet: Overall, 114 (82.6%) patients received coronary reimplantation, 21 (15.2%) underwent Takeuchi repair, and three (2.1%) were treated by closure of the ALCAPA plus coronary artery bypass graft.
evidence.explanation: Documents coronary re-implantation as the dominant surgical strategy for ALCAPA repair in a large cohort.

treatments/0.description: Coronary re-implantation transfers the anomalous left coronary back to the aortic root and restores a dual-coronary supply. It is the mainstay of ALCAPA management and produces normalization of LV function within months in most infants.

evidence.snippet: Overall, 114 (82.6%) patients received coronary reimplantation, 21 (15.2%) underwent Takeuchi repair, and three (2.1%) were treated by closure of the ALCAPA plus coronary artery bypass graft.
evidence.explanation: Documents coronary re-implantation as the dominant surgical strategy for ALCAPA repair in a large cohort.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Transferring the anomalous left coronary back to the aortic root re-establishes dual-coronary, systemic-pressure perfusion and abolishes the retrograde steal into the pulmonary trunk.

evidence.snippet: Anomalous left coronary artery from the right aortic sinus (L-AAOCA) with interarterial course carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD); therefore, current guidelines recommend exercise restriction and surgical intervention.
evidence.explanation: Supports surgical intervention as guideline-recommended therapy for high-risk AAOCA.

treatments/1.description: For high-risk AAOCA (notably interarterial L-AAOCA, and selected R-AAOCA with inducible ischemia), surgical unroofing of the intramural segment, coronary re-implantation, or pulmonary artery translocation is indicated to relieve mechanical interference and abolish exertional ischemia.

evidence.snippet: Anomalous left coronary artery from the right aortic sinus (L-AAOCA) with interarterial course carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD); therefore, current guidelines recommend exercise restriction and surgical intervention.
evidence.explanation: Supports surgical intervention as guideline-recommended therapy for high-risk AAOCA.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Unroofing the intramural segment, re-implanting the coronary into the correct sinus, or translocating the pulmonary artery removes the anatomic basis for dynamic compression of the proximal coronary segment.

evidence.snippet: Anomalous left coronary artery from the right aortic sinus (L-AAOCA) with interarterial course carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD); therefore, current guidelines recommend exercise restriction and surgical intervention.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports exercise restriction as recommended management for high-risk AAOCA.

treatments/2.description: Pending or instead of surgery, restriction from competitive and vigorous exercise is recommended for high-risk AAOCA anatomies to reduce the risk of exertional sudden cardiac death.

evidence.snippet: Anomalous left coronary artery from the right aortic sinus (L-AAOCA) with interarterial course carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD); therefore, current guidelines recommend exercise restriction and surgical intervention.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports exercise restriction as recommended management for high-risk AAOCA.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Exercise restriction leaves the anomalous anatomy untouched and instead withholds the exertional trigger, so the demand ischemia and the arrhythmias it provokes do not arise.

evidence.snippet: With the advancement of transcatheter equipment and techniques, CAFs have been increasingly closed using a percutaneous approach.
evidence.explanation: Supports transcatheter closure as contemporary CAF management; the dedicated dismech fistula entry covers further detail.

treatments/3.description: Significant coronary artery fistulas with hemodynamic or ischemic sequelae are managed by transcatheter (percutaneous) closure or by surgical correction. Detailed treatment patterns are curated in the dismech entry for coronary arterial fistulas.

evidence.snippet: With the advancement of transcatheter equipment and techniques, CAFs have been increasingly closed using a percutaneous approach.
evidence.explanation: Supports transcatheter closure as contemporary CAF management; the dedicated dismech fistula entry covers further detail.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Percutaneous or surgical closure obliterates the fistulous communication itself. The target is the anatomic phenotype rather than a mechanism node because the fistula's downstream steal physiology is curated in the dedicated coronary arterial fistulas entry.

evidence.snippet: Revascularization surgery seems indicated in symptomatic children based on small patient series.
evidence.explanation: Supports revascularization as indicated treatment for symptomatic congenital coronary ostial obstruction.

treatments/4.description: Revascularization — typically by surgical patch angioplasty, re-implantation, or coronary bypass — is indicated for symptomatic congenital coronary ostial stenosis or atresia, although outcomes remain limited by small case series.

evidence.snippet: Revascularization surgery seems indicated in symptomatic children based on small patient series.
evidence.explanation: Supports revascularization as indicated treatment for symptomatic congenital coronary ostial obstruction.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Patch angioplasty, re-implantation, or bypass re-establishes antegrade coronary inflow past the atretic or stenotic ostium, removing the fixed obstruction.

evidence.snippet: BAP31 also serves as a cargo receptor for the export of transmembrane proteins.
evidence.explanation: States the molecular activity lost with BAP31, the basis for the cargo receptor activity binding. It is the paper's summary of prior cell-biology work, hence BACKGROUND and IN_VITRO.

evidence.snippet: The three mutations identified in BCAP31 are probable loss-of-function alleles that abolish the production of normal BAP31
evidence.explanation: Immunoblot of patient fibroblasts shows absence of normal BAP31.

evidence.snippet: It is a chaperone protein involved in several pathways, including ER-associated degradation, export of ER proteins to the Golgi apparatus, and programmed cell death.
evidence.explanation: The normal functions of BAP31 that loss of function removes.

steps/1.description: Hemizygous splice, nonsense, frameshift or exonic-deletion variants abolish normal BAP31. In the founding family the splice variant reduced BCAP31 transcript to 7% of normal, consistent with nonsense-mediated decay.

evidence.snippet: We found that the Golgi apparatus was disorganized in up to 29.5% of BAP31-deficient fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the Golgi defect in patient fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: Contrary to what has been described with transient-RNA-interference experiments, we demonstrate that constitutive BCAP31 deficiency does not activate the unfolded protein response or cell-death effectors.
evidence.explanation: Excludes UPR activation and apoptosis as the cellular lesion in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: our data demonstrate that the lack of BAP31 disturbs ER metabolism and impacts the Golgi apparatus, highlighting an important role for BAP31 in ER-to-Golgi crosstalk
evidence.explanation: The authors' interpretation of the fibroblast findings as an ER-to-Golgi defect.

steps/2.description: BAP31-deficient patient fibroblasts are enlarged, with a swollen ER and a Golgi apparatus fragmented into scattered patches in up to about 30% of cells, and contain large vesicles with electron-dense inclusions. Constitutive BAP31 loss does not cause measurable accumulation of an ERAD substrate, activate the unfolded protein response, or trigger apoptosis, unlike transient knockdown, so the defect is placed in ER-to-Golgi exchange rather than in ER stress.

evidence.snippet: Mitochondrial dysfunction was suspected by respiratory chain enzyme assay on his cultured skin fibroblasts which showed significantly decreased complex I enzyme activity.
evidence.explanation: Complex I deficiency in one patient's fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: Within this complex, BAP31 interacts with mitochondria-localized proteins, including Tom40, to stimulate the translocation of NDUFS4, the component of complex I from the cytosol to the mitochondria.
evidence.explanation: Mechanism by which BAP31 loss could lower complex I, shown in cell lines.

evidence.snippet: His muscle biopsy revealed pleomorphic subsarcolemmal mitochondria collection in electron microscopy.
evidence.explanation: Abnormal mitochondrial morphology in a patient's muscle. Morphology is not a complex I measurement, so this is indirect support at most.

evidence.snippet: Respiratory chain enzyme activities were normal in muscle.
evidence.explanation: Normal respiratory-chain activity in the same patient's muscle.

evidence.snippet: The mitochondrial-respiratory-chain activities in the muscle of person F3-III.1 were normal (data not shown), and the mitochondrial network displayed a normal morphology in all affected fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Normal respiratory chain and mitochondrial network in the founding patients.

evidence.snippet: Mitochondrial complex activities were normal in the fibroblast of two brothers (P2 and P3).
evidence.explanation: Normal complex activities in two further patients' fibroblasts.

steps/3.description: Reduced complex I activity was measured in cultured skin fibroblasts of one DDCH patient, and pleomorphic subsarcolemmal mitochondria were seen in another patient's muscle. Against this, respiratory-chain activities were normal in muscle of two patients and in fibroblasts of two brothers, and the mitochondrial network was normal in the founding patients' fibroblasts. The node is therefore a candidate mechanism, not an established one. The GO term is complex I assembly because the proposed route is BAP31-dependent import of the NDUFS4 subunit; the patient data measured complex I activity, not assembly.

evidence.snippet: White matter (WM) anomalies were the most frequent (7/11), and were described as reduced WM volume, myelination delay, hypomyelination, and WM hyperintensities.
evidence.explanation: Imaging evidence of deficient myelination in the largest series.

steps/4.description: Brain MRI shows delayed myelination, hypomyelination, reduced white-matter volume or white-matter hyperintensity in most males with loss-of-function variants. In one patient the white-matter changes resolved by age 12.

evidence.snippet: ANSD observed in our study is characterized by initial inner hair cell damage, followed by accelerated degeneration of cochlear outer hair cells.
evidence.explanation: Audiological course in the allelic nonsyndromic family; INDIRECT for DDCH.

steps/5.description: In the allelic auditory neuropathy family, hearing loss began with inner hair cell dysfunction and progressed to outer hair cell degeneration. The site of the hearing lesion in DDCH itself has not been studied; one DDCH patient had a normal inner-ear CT.

evidence.snippet: defines an XLID syndrome consisting of severe motor and intellectual disabilities, early dystonia, sensorineural deafness, and hypomyelinating white-matter changes associated with failure to thrive, microcephaly, and facial dysmorphism
evidence.explanation: The core neurological syndrome.

steps/6.description: Severe congenital dysfunction of the developing brain producing profound motor and intellectual disability, a hyperkinetic movement disorder, pyramidal signs, microcephaly and, in some patients, seizures and progressive cerebral atrophy. Which neural cell types are primarily affected is not known.

evidence.snippet: All patients presented with severe to profound DD, none achieved walking, all had absent or limited speech, and all but one had limited or no purposeful use of hands.
evidence.explanation: Developmental delay in all 12 males with loss-of-function variants.

steps/7.description: Severe to profound in males with loss-of-function variants, none of whom walked; mild to severe in males with missense variants.

evidence.snippet: All patients presented with severe to profound DD, none achieved walking
evidence.explanation: No male with a loss-of-function variant achieved walking.

evidence.snippet: Patients had severe intellectual disability (ID), dystonia, deafness, and central hypomyelination
evidence.explanation: Severe intellectual disability in the previously reported males.

evidence.snippet: severe motor and intellectual disabilities, early dystonia, sensorineural deafness, and hypomyelinating white-matter changes
evidence.explanation: Early-onset dystonia is a defining feature.

evidence.snippet: Neurological examination showed dystonic postures and/or choreic movements (12/12)
evidence.explanation: Dystonia and/or chorea in all 12 males with loss-of-function variants; the two movements are counted together, so no frequency is assigned to dystonia alone.

evidence.snippet: Neurological examination showed dystonic postures and/or choreic movements (12/12)
evidence.explanation: Choreic movements reported alongside dystonia.

evidence.snippet: DDCH syndrome, sensorineural hearing loss, generalized dystonia, and choreoathetosis
evidence.explanation: Choreoathetosis in an independent patient.

evidence.snippet: microcephaly (7/11), and increased muscle tone/pyramidal signs (6/11)
evidence.explanation: 6 of 11 males with loss-of-function variants (55%), the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Neurological examination showed dystonic postures and/or choreic movements (12/12), microcephaly (7/11)
evidence.explanation: 7 of 11 males with loss-of-function variants (64%), the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Seizures were seen in 3/12 patients (petit mal for one, not detailed in the 2 others).
evidence.explanation: 3 of 12 males with loss-of-function variants (25%), the OCCASIONAL band.

evidence.snippet: In the brain of the BAP31-deficient individuals, we observed white-matter changes reminiscent of those observed in hypomyelinating leukodystrophies
evidence.explanation: Hypomyelinating white-matter pattern on MRI.

evidence.snippet: A brain MRI revealed white matter atrophy, thinning of the corpus callosum, and delayed myelination.
evidence.explanation: Delayed myelination in an independent family.

steps/15.description: Hypomyelinating white-matter change is a defining feature. In the largest series 7 of 11 males had some white-matter anomaly, of which hypomyelination was one of several descriptions, so no frequency is assigned to hypomyelination specifically.

evidence.snippet: progressive brain atrophy especially in the white matter was apparent
evidence.explanation: Progressive atrophy on serial MRI.

evidence.snippet: Progressive aggravation of the phenotype with cerebral atrophy was observed in two individuals, who died at the end of adolescence.
evidence.explanation: Progressive cerebral atrophy in two of the founding patients.

evidence.snippet: Other reported anomalies were cortical atrophy (4/11), thin corpus callosum (3/9), atrophy of basal ganglia and thalami (2/11), and hypoplastic cerebellar vermis (2/11).
evidence.explanation: 4 of 11 males with loss-of-function variants (36%), the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Other reported anomalies were cortical atrophy (4/11), thin corpus callosum (3/9), atrophy of basal ganglia and thalami (2/11), and hypoplastic cerebellar vermis (2/11).
evidence.explanation: 3 of 9 assessed males (33%), the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Other reported anomalies were cortical atrophy (4/11), thin corpus callosum (3/9), atrophy of basal ganglia and thalami (2/11), and hypoplastic cerebellar vermis (2/11).
evidence.explanation: 2 of 11 males (18%), the OCCASIONAL band.

evidence.snippet: Moderate to profound SNHL was seen in 9/10 (with normal inner ear CT scan for one patient) and strabismus was frequent (6/11).
evidence.explanation: 9 of 10 assessed males (90%), the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: A hearing test showed bilateral profound sensorineural hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: Neonatal profound bilateral hearing loss in an independent patient.

evidence.snippet: We also report a heterozygous mother who has bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: Hearing loss in a heterozygous female.

steps/20.description: Moderate to profound, bilateral and usually congenital or early infantile; cochlear implantation has been used. Some carrier females also have sensorineural hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: Liver enzymes were increased in 8/10, either transiently (n = 4) or permanently (n = 4).
evidence.explanation: 8 of 10 assessed males (80%), the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Four affected individuals in our families harboring mutations in BCAP31 demonstrated transitory episodes of a 2- to 3-fold increase of liver transaminase levels during banal febrile illnesses.
evidence.explanation: Fever-associated transaminase elevation in the founding families.

steps/21.description: Transient or persistent, often rising two- to three-fold during ordinary febrile illness. Liver ultrasound was normal in the founding families; cholestasis and liver failure are features of the ABCD1-including deletions (CADDS) rather than of intragenic variants.

evidence.snippet: Analyses by using his cultured skin fibroblasts revealed that activities of respiratory chain complexes I, II, III, and IV relative to citrate synthase were 19.8%, 32.7%, 115.4%, and 39.9%, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Single-patient fibroblast measurement, complex I at 19.8% of control.

steps/22.description: Reported in cultured fibroblasts of a single patient; normal respiratory-chain activity was found in other patients' muscle and fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: In the primary fibroblasts of affected individuals, we found that BCAP31 deficiency altered ER morphology and caused a disorganization of the Golgi apparatus in a significant proportion of cells.
evidence.explanation: Patient fibroblasts lacking BAP31 show the ER and Golgi defect.

evidence.snippet: Disruption of the BAP31-Tom40 complex inhibits mitochondrial complex I activity and oxygen consumption by the decreased NDUFS4 localization to the mitochondria.
evidence.explanation: Cell-line experiments disrupting the BAP31-Tom40 complex, not patient cells, hence INDIRECT for this disease.

edges/2.description: BAP31 bridges the ER and mitochondria through Tom40 and promotes import of the complex I subunit NDUFS4, so its loss is expected to lower complex I activity. The disease-level data are mixed and are recorded on the target node.

evidence.snippet: It is very likely that the liver dysfunction reported in persons carrying large deletions involving BCAP31 and ABCD1 or SCL6A8 and BCAP31 can be attributed to BCAP31 loss.
evidence.explanation: Attribution of the liver phenotype to BCAP31 across deletion and intragenic cases.

edges/3.description: Liver enzyme elevation is attributed to BCAP31 loss because it occurs with intragenic variants and with every deletion that includes BCAP31; the hepatic mechanism is not known.

evidence.snippet: In the brain of the BAP31-deficient individuals, we observed white-matter changes reminiscent of those observed in hypomyelinating leukodystrophies
evidence.explanation: Links the trafficking defect to hypomyelination by inference from the MRI phenotype, not by measurement in glia.

edges/4.description: Proposed by the discovering authors from the white-matter phenotype and the known dependence of myelination on ER protein trafficking. No study has examined oligodendrocytes or myelin proteins in BAP31 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: The identification of loss-of-function mutations in BCAP31 provides the molecular basis of a Mendelian syndrome and links ER-to-Golgi exchange to severe congenital brain dysfunction and deafness.
evidence.explanation: The authors' link from the trafficking defect to the brain phenotype; the intermediate steps are not identified.

evidence.snippet: The identification of loss-of-function mutations in BCAP31 provides the molecular basis of a Mendelian syndrome and links ER-to-Golgi exchange to severe congenital brain dysfunction and deafness.
evidence.explanation: Deafness is named alongside the brain phenotype as a consequence of the same defect.

edges/19.description: The founding report attributes deafness to the same trafficking defect as the brain phenotype, without locating the lesion in the cochlea or the auditory pathway.

evidence.snippet: Functional studies of patient-derived LCLs revealed mitochondrial dysfunction, evidenced by increased ROS, reduced ATP levels, and decreased mitochondrial membrane potential compared with normal LCLs.
evidence.explanation: Mitochondrial dysfunction in cells from the allelic auditory neuropathy family.

edges/21.description: Proposed from a family with a BCAP31 in-frame insertion and nonsyndromic auditory neuropathy, whose lymphoblastoid cells showed mitochondrial dysfunction. It is an allelic phenotype, so its transfer to DDCH hearing loss is an inference. The cells were assayed for general mitochondrial dysfunction (ROS, ATP, membrane potential), not for complex I specifically, so drawing the edge from the complex I node is itself part of that inference.

evidence.snippet: These results indicate BCAP31 dysfunction as a potential cause of transient ANSD, progressing to sensorineural hearing loss through mitochondrial impairment.
evidence.explanation: The authors' proposed progression from auditory neuropathy to sensorineural hearing loss in the allelic family.

evidence.snippet: We identified loss-of-function mutations in BCAP31 in seven individuals from three families. These persons suffered from motor and intellectual disabilities, dystonia, sensorineural deafness, and white-matter changes, which together define an X-linked syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The founding gene-disease report.

evidence.snippet: Our study confirms the phenotype reported in males with intragenic LoF variants and shows that males with missense variants exhibit a milder phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Replication in 14 further families with intragenic variants, and the allelic severity difference.

evidence.snippet: Patients with deletions including BCAP31 and SLC6A8 have the same phenotype as BCAP31 patients.
evidence.explanation: BCAP31-SLC6A8 deletions fall within this entry.

evidence.snippet: Clinical exome sequencing in the trio identified a small intragenic deletion in exon 8 of BCAP31, c.709_721del (p.Val237Trpfs*69), originated de novo and not previously reported.
evidence.explanation: An independent de novo truncating allele with the DDCH phenotype.

genes/0.notes: BCAP31 (Xq28) lies between SLC6A8 (centromeric) and ABCD1 (telomeric). Reported disease alleles are splice, nonsense, frameshift and exonic deletions that abolish normal BAP31, plus a smaller set of missense variants with a milder phenotype. Deletions removing BCAP31 together with SLC6A8 give the same phenotype as intragenic BCAP31 variants and are included in this entry; deletions removing BCAP31 together with ABCD1 cause CADDS (see differential diagnoses). Missense variants have also been reported in adult-onset presentations outside the DDCH picture (ataxia with hearing loss, early-onset Parkinson disease with congenital deafness, nonsyndromic auditory neuropathy); those are allelic phenotypes, not features of this entry.

treatments/0.description: No disease-specific therapy exists. Care addresses feeding and growth, dystonia and other movement disorders, seizures, hearing, vision, and monitoring of liver enzymes during intercurrent febrile illness.

evidence.snippet: sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) requiring cochlear implantation
evidence.explanation: Cochlear implantation used in a DDCH patient; outcome not reported.

treatments/1.description: Cochlear implantation has been used for the sensorineural hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: We also describe two asymptomatic female carriers with somatic mosaicism which is particularly relevant for genetic counseling.
evidence.explanation: Maternal mosaicism affects recurrence-risk counseling.

treatments/2.description: Counseling for X-linked recessive inheritance, including the risk that carrier females are symptomatic and that apparently de novo cases may arise from maternal somatic mosaicism.

open_questions/0.rationale: The cellular lesion was characterised only in skin fibroblasts, where the Golgi is disorganised in about a third of cells and there is no UPR or apoptosis. The link to white matter rests on the MRI pattern and on the general dependence of myelination on secretory trafficking. No oligodendrocyte, neuronal or animal model of BAP31 deficiency addressing myelination was found in the sources cited here, and one patient's white-matter changes resolved by age 12, which does not fit a simple fixed myelin-synthesis defect.

open_questions/1.rationale: Complex I deficiency was measured in fibroblasts of one patient and fits BAP31's role in importing NDUFS4 at ER-mitochondria contacts, but normal respiratory-chain activities were reported in muscle of two patients and in fibroblasts of two brothers, and the mitochondrial network was normal in the founding patients' fibroblasts. The auditory-neuropathy data linking BCAP31 to mitochondrial dysfunction come from an allelic nonsyndromic family. The discrepancy could reflect tissue, assay or allele differences; a systematic comparison has not been reported.

evidence.snippet: Researchers have identified more than 230 different autosomal dominant Alzheimer disease (ADAD) mutations located in the genes for amyloid precursor protein (APP), presenilin 1 (PSEN1), and presenilin 2 (PSEN2)
evidence.explanation: Establishes the three-gene allelic architecture that constitutes the trigger of this chain.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in one of three genes (APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2) have been identified that cause alterations in Aβ processing
evidence.explanation: Links the germline variant directly to altered amyloid-beta processing, the next node.

steps/3.description: The proximal cause is a heterozygous germline pathogenic variant in one of three genes on the amyloid-beta biosynthetic axis: APP (the substrate, by missense variant near a secretase cleavage site or by whole-locus duplication), PSEN1, or PSEN2 (the catalytic subunit of the gamma-secretase that performs the final cleavage). More than 230 such variants are catalogued. Because the lesion is present from conception and acts constitutively, the entire downstream cascade is deterministic rather than probabilistic, and its timing is set largely by which variant is carried.

evidence.snippet: FAD mutations increase the release of amyloid β (Aβ)42 relative to Aβ40 by an unknown, possibly gain-of-toxic-function, mechanism.
evidence.explanation: Directly states the shift in the Abeta42:Abeta40 ratio produced by familial Alzheimer disease mutations.

evidence.snippet: Dominantly inherited Alzheimer’s disease (DIAD) is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in presenilin-1 (PSEN1), presenilin-2 (PSEN2), or the amyloid-beta precursor protein (APP) genes that alter APP processing, resulting in overproduction of aggregation prone amyloid β
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from variant to altered APP processing to overproduction of aggregation-prone amyloid-beta.

steps/4.description: The qualitative arm of the proximal lesion, and the mechanism of the point-mutation subtypes (PSEN1, PSEN2, and APP missense). Pathogenic variants shift the sequential, carboxypeptidase-like gamma-secretase cleavage of the APP C-terminal fragment so that longer, more aggregation-prone amyloid-beta species are released, raising the Abeta42:Abeta40 ratio. This node is the ADAD-specific substitution for the amyloidogenesis module's generic "amyloidogenic precursor protein" trigger: the precursor is amyloid-beta, and what destabilises it is not aging or somatic mutation but a constitutive germline change in how it is generated. A mechanistic caveat is carried by the qualitative_abeta_profile hypothesis: kinetic work shows familial Alzheimer variants change the qualitative spectrum of Abeta products through several distinct mechanisms, not only the Abeta42 quantity, and many PSEN variants paradoxically impair the enzyme. The parallel quantitative (gene-dosage) arm is modelled as the sibling node "Increased APP Substrate Dosage" rather than folded in here, because copy-number gain of APP does not alter gamma-secretase processing and does not by itself raise the Abeta42:Abeta40 ratio - it raises total substrate.

evidence.snippet: Duplication of the APP locus, resulting in accumulation of amyloid-beta peptides, causes ADEOAD with CAA.
evidence.explanation: States the gene-dosage mechanism explicitly: duplication of the locus, not an altered peptide or enzyme, produces amyloid-beta accumulation and disease.

steps/5.description: The quantitative (gene-dosage) arm of the proximal lesion, and the sibling of the gamma-secretase-processing node. Copy-number gain of the whole APP locus on chromosome 21 increases the amount of APP substrate presented to the normal secretase machinery, so more amyloid-beta is produced without any change in the enzyme or in the Abeta42:Abeta40 ratio. It is modelled as a distinct node precisely because it is the cleanest human dose-response argument for the amyloid hypothesis: no altered peptide chemistry is required, only more of the normal precursor. This node is arguably the more literal instance of the amyloidogenesis module's "amyloidogenic precursor protein" trigger, whose description names overproduction alongside mutation as a route to a metastable precursor. It converges with the qualitative arm on the shared downstream misfolding node, and its vascular emphasis is carried onward by the cerebral amyloid angiopathy node.

evidence.snippet: Beginning 25 years before expected symptom onset, Aβ42 concentrations in the CSF in mutation carriers appeared to decline, as compared with those in noncarriers.
evidence.explanation: The falling soluble CSF Abeta42 pool is the in vivo signature of amyloid-beta leaving solution, and is the earliest measurable event in the ADAD cascade.

steps/6.description: The excess longer amyloid-beta species depart their soluble monomeric conformation and self-associate into beta-sheet-rich, proteotoxic soluble oligomers that both seed further aggregation and directly impair synaptic function. In ADAD this step is read out in vivo as the earliest detectable biomarker change: CSF Abeta42 concentration begins to fall about 25 years before expected symptom onset as the peptide is sequestered out of the soluble pool.

evidence.snippet: As compared with noncarriers, mutation carriers had significant amyloid deposition in the precuneus 15 years before expected symptom onset
evidence.explanation: Times fibrillar amyloid deposition in living ADAD carriers and anchors it in the cascade.

evidence.snippet: There was no detectable amyloid deposition in noncarriers.
evidence.explanation: The absence of any deposition in non-carriers of the same pedigrees supports a deterministic genotype-to-fibril relationship.

steps/7.description: Oligomers nucleate and elongate into insoluble cross-beta amyloid fibrils that deposit as extracellular parenchymal plaques. This is the ADAD instance of the amyloidogenesis module's central effector. It is directly imaged in living carriers with Pittsburgh compound B PET, which becomes abnormal about 15 years before expected symptom onset, and characteristically shows early and prominent neostriatal signal - a feature more typical of ADAD than of sporadic disease. No non-carrier in the DIAN cohort had a positive scan, so the genotype-to-deposition link is essentially deterministic.

evidence.snippet: The amount of amyloid deposition in mutation carriers increased as a function of estimated years from expected symptom onset at least until clinical symptom onset.
evidence.explanation: Documents progressive, time-dependent accumulation of the tissue amyloid burden.

steps/8.description: Fibril deposition continues to accumulate as a growing cortical amyloid burden, expanding monotonically as the carrier approaches expected symptom onset. This is the ADAD instance of the amyloidogenesis module's tissue-accumulation effector: it converts the molecular fibril-formation event into an organ-level structural lesion and is the quantity that anti-amyloid antibody therapy is designed to reverse.

evidence.snippet: phosphorylation of tau at threonine 217 (pT217/T217) (which occurred at around −21 EYO) was followed by that of threonine 181 (pT181/T181) (−19 EYO), then t-tau increase (−17 EYO), then phosphorylation of tau at threonine 205 (pT205/T205) (−13 EYO)
evidence.explanation: Establishes the ordered sequence of site-specific soluble tau hyperphosphorylation in ADAD and times it two decades before symptoms.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that the events initially leading to increased tau phosphorylation in AD are probably related to aggregated Aβ pathology
evidence.explanation: Supports the causal edge from cortical amyloid accumulation to soluble tau hyperphosphorylation.

steps/9.description: The first tau event, roughly two decades before symptoms and separated from tangle formation by about 20 years. Cortical amyloid pathology triggers a stereotyped, ordered, site-specific rise in soluble tau phosphorylation occupancy measurable in CSF: threonine 217 first (about 21 years before expected onset, essentially in lockstep with rising amyloid PET signal), then threonine 181, then total tau, then threonine 205. This is the mechanistic bridge from the amyloid arm into the tau arm, and is why p-tau217 is now the leading amyloid-proximal fluid biomarker. It is modelled separately from tangle formation because the two events are ~20 years apart and, critically, move in OPPOSITE directions once tangles appear (see the downstream node).

evidence.snippet: First, we confirmed that tau-PET SUVR in mutation carriers only increased near the time of symptom onset
evidence.explanation: Times aggregated tangle pathology to near symptom onset, ~20 years after the upstream soluble hyperphosphorylation node.

evidence.snippet: Second, pT217/T217 and pT181/T181 began to decline significantly near the time of symptom onset, while phosphorylation at pT205/T205 slowed and t-tau levels continued to increase.
evidence.explanation: Documents the opposite direction of change (falling soluble p-tau as tangles form) that requires this to be a node distinct from the upstream hyperphosphorylation event.

steps/10.description: Aggregation of hyperphosphorylated tau into intraneuronal paired helical filaments and neurofibrillary tangles. In ADAD this is a LATE event: tau-PET signal in mutation carriers rises only near the time of symptom onset, roughly two decades after soluble p-tau hyperphosphorylation begins. At that point soluble pT217 and pT181 occupancy paradoxically FALL - plausibly through sequestration into the aggregates - while total tau keeps rising, so the soluble and aggregated tau species diverge. That opposite direction of change is the reason this is a separate node from the upstream hyperphosphorylation event, and it is what makes stage-blind interpretation of a p-tau result unsafe.

evidence.snippet: gantenerumab treatment significantly improved multiple CSF measures of synaptic degeneration, microglial activity, other inflammatory markers, and astrocyte activation markers
evidence.explanation: Shows that the microglial, astrocytic, and inflammatory markers are downstream of amyloid in ADAD and move when amyloid is removed.

steps/11.description: Plaque-associated microglia and reactive astrocytes mount a chronic innate immune response around amyloid deposits. In ADAD this arm is directly measurable and pharmacologically reversible: CSF markers of microglial activity, other inflammatory markers, and astrocyte activation all improved under gantenerumab treatment in DIAN-TU, showing this is a process downstream of amyloid rather than an independent one. It is modelled separately from synaptic loss, which is its consequence rather than the same event.

evidence.snippet: gantenerumab treatment significantly improved multiple CSF measures of synaptic degeneration
evidence.explanation: Documents synaptic degeneration as a measurable, amyloid-downstream, treatment-responsive process in ADAD.

steps/12.description: Loss of synapses in the neuropil surrounding plaques, driven both by proteotoxic soluble amyloid-beta oligomers and by microglial synaptic pruning. Synaptic loss is the structural correlate that best tracks cognitive impairment in Alzheimer disease, and it sits downstream of - not alongside - the microglial/inflammatory response. Like that response, CSF measures of synaptic degeneration improved under gantenerumab in DIAN-TU.

evidence.snippet: Brains from individuals with APP duplication showed abundant parenchymal and vascular deposits of amyloid-beta peptides.
evidence.explanation: Documents the vascular deposition arm alongside the parenchymal plaque arm in the gene-dosage subtype.

steps/13.description: A parallel vascular arm of the same deposition process: amyloid-beta, especially the shorter Abeta40 species, deposits in the walls of leptomeningeal and cortical arterioles. This is present to some degree in most ADAD but is a defining and severe feature of APP locus duplication, where it produces lobar intracerebral haemorrhage. Its clinical importance has grown because cerebral amyloid angiopathy is the substrate for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities during anti-amyloid antibody therapy.

evidence.snippet: Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities occurred in 53% (39/73) of participants: 47% (34/73) with microhaemorrhages, 30% (22/73) with oedema, and 6% (5/73) were associated with symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Documents haemorrhagic events (microhaemorrhage) and vasogenic oedema in ADAD carriers. Marked PARTIAL because these were observed under high-dose anti-amyloid antibody treatment, so the quote supports the vessel-wall vulnerability of this node but not the untreated haemorrhage rate.

steps/14.description: Amyloid infiltration of the arteriolar media and adventitia weakens the vessel wall, so cerebral amyloid angiopathy terminates in haemorrhagic events: lobar intracerebral haemorrhage and cortical microhaemorrhage. This is the clinical endpoint of the vascular arm, and it is also the substrate that makes anti-amyloid antibody therapy hazardous in this disease - amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (microhaemorrhage and vasogenic oedema) occurred in 53% of participants in the high-dose DIAN-TU gantenerumab extension. The evidence cited here is the trial's ARIA safety readout, which documents the haemorrhagic events themselves rather than the untreated natural history; the untreated-CAA haemorrhage claim in this node's description is not separately cited and should be treated as a described clinical association pending a properly quotable source.

evidence.snippet: Increased atrophy of bilateral hippocampi was detected in mutation carriers 15 years before expected symptom onset
evidence.explanation: Times the structural neurodegeneration node at about 15 years before expected symptom onset.

steps/15.description: Neuronal death producing measurable structural loss. Increased atrophy of the bilateral hippocampi is detectable on volumetric MRI about 15 years before expected symptom onset, with the precuneus and medial temporal structures affected earliest - matching the topography of early amyloid deposition. This is modelled separately from cerebral hypometabolism, which the same DIAN analysis times five years later.

evidence.snippet: A significant decrease in cerebral metabolism in the precuneus was detected in mutation carriers 10 years before expected symptom onset
evidence.explanation: Times cerebral hypometabolism at about 10 years before expected symptom onset, distinct from the 15-year atrophy timing of the upstream node.

steps/16.description: Regional failure of cerebral glucose utilisation, measured by FDG-PET, in territories losing synapses and neurons. In DIAN carriers a significant decrease in precuneus metabolism appears about 10 years before expected symptom onset - five years after hippocampal atrophy becomes detectable, which is why it is a distinct node rather than being bundled with atrophy.

evidence.snippet: Global cognitive impairment, as measured by the Mini-Mental State Examination and the Clinical Dementia Rating scale, was detected 5 years before expected symptom onset, and patients met diagnostic criteria for dementia at an average of 3 years after expected symptom onset.
evidence.explanation: Times the clinical consequence node relative to the rest of the cascade.

steps/17.description: The clinical end state, and the ADAD instance of the amyloidogenesis module's organ-dysfunction consequence, with the brain as the affected organ. Impaired episodic memory appears about 10 years before expected symptom onset, global cognitive impairment about 5 years before, and criteria for mild dementia are met about 3 years after expected onset, with progression to death over roughly a decade. Non-amnestic and neurological features (myoclonus, seizures, spastic paraparesis) are more common than in late-onset disease.

evidence.snippet: Genetic linkage studies have mapped a locus (AD3) associated with susceptibility to a very aggressive form of Alzheimer's disease to chromosome 14q24.3.
evidence.explanation: Maps and identifies the PSEN1 (AD3) locus underlying aggressive early-onset familial Alzheimer disease.

genes/0.notes: PSEN1 encodes presenilin 1, the catalytic aspartyl protease subunit of the gamma-secretase complex that performs the final intramembrane cleavage of the APP C-terminal fragment. Pathogenic missense variants reduce the processivity of successive carboxypeptidase-like cleavages, releasing longer Abeta species and raising the Abeta42:Abeta40 ratio. PSEN1 variants are the most common cause of ADAD and are associated with the earliest onset.

evidence.snippet: This suggests that some cases of AD could be caused by mutations in the APP gene.
evidence.explanation: Original demonstration of APP as a causal gene for familial Alzheimer disease.

evidence.snippet: Duplication of the APP locus, resulting in accumulation of amyloid-beta peptides, causes ADEOAD with CAA.
evidence.explanation: Establishes gene dosage of APP as sufficient to cause the disease, a dose-response argument for the amyloid mechanism.

genes/1.notes: APP encodes the amyloid precursor protein, the substrate from which amyloid-beta is liberated by sequential beta- and gamma-secretase cleavage. Pathogenic variants cluster around the cleavage sites flanking the amyloid-beta peptide and either shift cleavage toward Abeta42 or increase the aggregation propensity of the peptide. Duplication of the entire locus causes disease purely by increased gene dosage.

evidence.snippet: The presence of missense mutations in AD subjects in two highly similar genes strongly supports the hypothesis that mutations in both are pathogenic.
evidence.explanation: Establishes PSEN2 (STM2) as a second presenilin gene causal for familial Alzheimer disease.

genes/2.notes: PSEN2 encodes presenilin 2, the paralogous catalytic subunit of gamma-secretase that can substitute for presenilin 1. Pathogenic variants are the rarest cause of ADAD, with the N141I founder variant of the Volga German kindreds the best characterised. Onset is significantly later and more variable than for PSEN1 or APP.

evidence.snippet: The individual had two copies of the APOE3 Christchurch (R136S) mutation, unusually high brain amyloid levels and limited tau and neurodegenerative measurements.
evidence.explanation: Documents a protective APOE genotype uncoupling amyloid burden from tau, neurodegeneration, and clinical onset in an ADAD carrier.

genes/3.notes: APOE genotype is the dominant risk locus for sporadic late-onset Alzheimer disease but is NOT a major determinant of onset age in ADAD as a whole: in the largest meta-analysis, APOE genotype and sex did not significantly add to the variance in onset explained by mutation type and family history. The striking exception is the homozygous APOE3 Christchurch (R136S) variant, which delayed cognitive onset by about three decades in a PSEN1 E280A carrier despite very high brain amyloid - the single most informative human resilience observation in ADAD, and the basis for APOE-directed therapeutic strategies.

evidence.snippet: Gantenerumab significantly reduced amyloid plaques, cerebrospinal fluid total tau, and phospho-tau181 and attenuated increases of neurofilament light chain.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates target engagement and downstream biomarker effect in ADAD mutation carriers.

evidence.snippet: Gantenerumab and solanezumab did not slow cognitive decline in symptomatic DIAD.
evidence.explanation: Refutes a clinical (cognitive) benefit of gantenerumab in symptomatic ADAD in the double-blind period, despite biomarker engagement.

evidence.snippet: Partial or short-term amyloid removal did not show significant clinical effects. However, long-term full amyloid removal potentially delayed symptom onset and dementia progression.
evidence.explanation: Supports a possible clinical benefit of sustained complete amyloid removal in ADAD. Marked PARTIAL because the finding comes from an open-label extension with external controls, which the authors themselves flag as limiting.

evidence.snippet: Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities occurred in 53% (39/73) of participants: 47% (34/73) with microhaemorrhages, 30% (22/73) with oedema, and 6% (5/73) were associated with symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the principal safety liability of high-dose anti-amyloid antibody therapy in ADAD, relevant because cerebral amyloid angiopathy is part of the disease.

treatments/0.description: A fully human IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds aggregated amyloid-beta and promotes microglial plaque clearance.
