evidence.snippet: The anti-C5 monoclonal antibody eculizumab was the first treatment to improve hemolysis, thrombotic risk, and survival in PNH although at the price of a life-long intravenous fortnightly drug.
evidence.explanation: Establishes eculizumab as the first anti-C5 therapy improving hemolysis, thrombotic risk, and survival in PNH.

evidence.snippet: Eculizumab, the first approved C5 inhibitor, significantly reduced thrombotic risk and improved survival but did not eliminate anemia due to extravascular hemolysis.
evidence.explanation: Confirms eculizumab reduces thrombotic risk and improves survival, while noting residual extravascular hemolysis.

treatments/0.description: Humanized monoclonal antibody against complement component C5 that blocks cleavage to C5a and C5b, preventing membrane attack complex formation and terminal complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis. First disease-modifying therapy for PNH, reducing hemolysis, transfusion requirements, and thrombotic risk.

evidence.snippet: Ravulizumab, a longer half-life anti-C5 developed from eculizumab, administered every 8 weeks, improved patient convenience, and reduced pharmacokinetic breakthrough hemolysis (BTH) by establishing more stable anti-C5 concentrations.
evidence.explanation: Documents ravulizumab as a long-acting anti-C5 with every-8-week dosing and reduced breakthrough hemolysis.

treatments/1.description: Long-acting anti-C5 monoclonal antibody engineered from eculizumab with an every-8-week dosing interval, providing non-inferior control of intravascular hemolysis with reduced pharmacokinetic breakthrough hemolysis.

evidence.snippet: Upstream inhibition of complement cascade was also explored with the anti-C3 pegcetacoplan, and with the alternative pathway inhibitors iptacopan (anti-factor B) and danicopan (anti-factor D).
evidence.explanation: Documents pegcetacoplan as an anti-C3 proximal complement inhibitor for PNH.

evidence.snippet: New proximal complement inhibitors (CI) mainly targeting complement component C3 or factors of the amplification pathway such as pegcetacoplan, danicopan, and iptacopan became available and are meanwhile approved for marketing.
evidence.explanation: Confirms pegcetacoplan is an approved proximal complement inhibitor targeting C3.

treatments/2.description: Pegylated C3-targeted peptide inhibitor that acts proximally in the complement cascade, controlling both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis and improving hemoglobin in patients with residual anemia on C5 inhibitors.

evidence.snippet: Iptacopan, a first-in-class oral factor B inhibitor, has been shown to improve hemoglobin levels in these patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes iptacopan as a first-in-class oral factor B inhibitor that improves hemoglobin in PNH.

evidence.snippet: In the first trial, 51 of the 60 patients who received iptacopan had an increase in the hemoglobin level of at least 2 g per deciliter from baseline, and 42 had a hemoglobin level of at least 12 g per deciliter, each without transfusion; none of the 35 anti-C5-treated patients attained the end-point levels.
evidence.explanation: Phase 3 APPLY-PNH results quantify iptacopan's hemoglobin benefit over continued anti-C5 therapy.

treatments/3.description: First-in-class oral factor B inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway. In phase 3 trials, iptacopan monotherapy improved hemoglobin and reduced transfusion dependence in both anti-C5-experienced and complement-inhibitor-naive PNH patients with persistent anemia.

evidence.snippet: Upstream inhibition of complement cascade was also explored with the anti-C3 pegcetacoplan, and with the alternative pathway inhibitors iptacopan (anti-factor B) and danicopan (anti-factor D).
evidence.explanation: Documents danicopan as an alternative-pathway (factor D) inhibitor for PNH.

treatments/4.description: Oral factor D inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway, used as add-on therapy to a C5 inhibitor in patients with clinically significant C3-mediated extravascular hemolysis and residual anemia.

evidence.snippet: The biology of PNH has been progressively elucidated in the past few years, but therapeutic strategies remained unsatisfactory for decades, the only exception being stem cell transplantation, which is restricted to selected patients and retains significant morbidity and mortality.
evidence.explanation: Identifies stem cell transplantation as the only curative option, restricted to selected patients with significant morbidity and mortality.

treatments/5.description: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only established curative therapy for PNH but carries substantial treatment-related morbidity and mortality, and is generally reserved for severe bone marrow failure or clonal evolution rather than uncomplicated complement-responsive hemolysis.

evidence.explanation: This supports chronic dermatoses (including lichen sclerosus) as the inflammatory background for HPV-independent penile carcinogenesis.

evidence.explanation: This directly supports PeIN as an established precursor/risk lesion and classification component for penile cancer.

evidence.explanation: This supports E6/E7 oncoprotein action as the transforming mechanism in HPV-induced penile carcinogenesis.

evidence.snippet: Strong p16 positivity was a reliable surrogate marker for the detection of transcriptionally active high-risk HPV.

steps/5.description: In the HPV-associated pathway, persistent high-risk HPV infection of penile squamous epithelium expresses the E6 and E7 oncoproteins. E6 targets p53 for ubiquitin-mediated degradation and E7 inactivates the Rb tumor suppressor, abrogating cell-cycle checkpoints and producing compensatory p16INK4a overexpression. These viral oncoproteins substitute for the somatic driver mutations seen in HPV-independent tumors.

evidence.explanation: This directly supports TP53, CDKN2A, and HRAS mutations as near-exclusive drivers of the HPV-independent pathway.

evidence.snippet: genetic mutations in tumor suppressor genes drive HPV-independent penile carcinogenesis
evidence.explanation: This supports tumor suppressor gene loss as the central mechanism of the HPV-independent pathway.

steps/6.description: In the HPV-independent pathway, chronic inflammation (e.g., lichen sclerosus) is the background for accumulation of somatic mutations in tumor suppressor and cell-cycle genes. TP53, CDKN2A, and HRAS mutations occur almost exclusively in HPV-independent tumors, with frequent co-occurrence of TP53 and CDKN2A, driving checkpoint loss and proliferation.

evidence.snippet: Lymph node involvement is a common finding at first presentation and investigation of spread to deep nodes is important and can be done with the aid of PET-CT.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of occult inguinal lymph node metastasis in clinically node-negative invasive penile squamous cell carcinoma (PSCC) has remained a challenge, with substantial perioperative complications.
evidence.explanation: This supports occult inguinal lymph-node metastasis as a key feature of invasive penile cancer.

steps/7.description: Both carcinogenic pathways converge on malignant squamous cell proliferation with local invasion of the glans, coronal sulcus, or foreskin, followed by stepwise lymphatic dissemination to inguinal lymph nodes. Occult inguinal nodal metastasis in clinically node-negative disease is common, making nodal staging central to prognosis.

evidence.snippet: In two subtypes, PCH2 and PCH4, we identified mutations in three of the four different subunits of the tRNA-splicing endonuclease complex.

evidence.snippet: Human genome analyses now identified a CLP1 homozygous missense mutation (p.R140H) in five unrelated families, leading to a loss of CLP1 interaction with the tRNA splicing endonuclease (TSEN) complex, largely reduced pre-tRNA cleavage activity, and accumulation of linear tRNA introns.

steps/20.description: The tRNA splicing endonuclease (TSEN) complex, composed of TSEN2, TSEN15, TSEN34, and TSEN54, cleaves introns from pre-tRNA molecules at the canonical anticodon loop position. Mutations in TSEN54 (and other TSEN subunits) impair pre-tRNA processing, reducing the pool of mature, functional tRNAs available for translation. Developing pontocerebellar neurons have exceptionally high translational demands and are disproportionately vulnerable. This mechanism maps primarily to PCH2/PCH4 for TSEN genes and to PCH10 for CLP1. The TSEN complex also interacts with CLP1, an RNA kinase, reinforcing RNA-processing as the central pathogenic pathway.

evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia with spinal muscular atrophy, also known as PCH1, is a group of autosomal recessive disorders characterized by generalized muscle weakness and global developmental delay commonly resulting in early death.

evidence.snippet: Bi-allelic variants in exosome subunits EXOSC3, EXOSC8 and EXOSC9 have been reported to cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 1B, type 1C and type 1D, respectively, while those in EXOSC2 cause short stature, hearing loss, retinitis pigmentosa and distinctive facies.
evidence.explanation: Assigns all three structural exosome subunits bound on this node to their respective PCH1 subtypes.

evidence.snippet: The RNA exosome is a ubiquitously expressed complex of nine core proteins (EXOSC1-9) and associated nucleases responsible for RNA processing and degradation.
evidence.explanation: Source for the nine-subunit composition of the complex named in this node's description.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in EXOSC3, EXOSC8, EXOSC9, and the exosome cofactor RBM7 cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia and motor neuronopathy.
evidence.explanation: Groups the three subunits bound on this node as one exosome-level mechanism, which is what the node asserts.

evidence.snippet: Down-regulation of EXOSC8 and EXOSC9 in human cells leads to p53 protein stabilisation and G2/M cell cycle arrest.
evidence.explanation: Supports the p53 stabilisation step named in this node's description.

steps/21.description: Biallelic mutations in the structural subunits of the nine-subunit RNA exosome impair RNA processing and turnover and cause the PCH1 subtypes: EXOSC3 gives PCH1B, EXOSC8 gives PCH1C, and EXOSC9 gives PCH1D. This mechanism produces pontocerebellar hypoplasia with spinal muscular atrophy-like weakness and global developmental delay, but survival and clinical severity vary by genotype. In zebrafish and human cell models, loss of exosome subunits stabilises p53 and perturbs ribosome biogenesis, which has been proposed as the route from exosome deficiency to the neuronal loss seen in PCH1.

evidence.snippet: identification of an intronic mutation in RARS2, the gene encoding mitochondrial arginine-transfer RNA (tRNA) synthetase
evidence.explanation: First identification of RARS2 mutations causing PCH, establishing the mitochondrial tRNA synthetase deficiency mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The mutation was associated with the production of an abnormally short RARS2 transcript and a marked reduction of the mitochondrial tRNA(Arg) transcript in the patients' fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: Mechanistically links RARS2 mutation to reduced mitochondrial tRNA charging, impairing mitochondrial translation.

evidence.snippet: Blood and CSF lactate was abnormally elevated in all five patients at early stages
evidence.explanation: Elevated lactate is a biochemical signature of impaired mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation due to RARS2 deficiency in PCH6.

steps/22.description: Mutations in RARS2, encoding the mitochondrial arginyl-tRNA synthetase, reduce aminoacylation of mitochondrial tRNA-Arg. This impairs mitochondrial translation, decreases oxidative phosphorylation capacity, and leads to energy failure preferentially in high-metabolic-demand cells of the developing cerebellum and pons. Elevated CSF lactate and reduced respiratory chain complex activity are biochemical hallmarks.

evidence.snippet: identified a nonsense mutation in the vaccinia-related kinase 1 gene (VRK1) as a cause of SMA-PCH
evidence.explanation: Establishes VRK1 loss-of-function as the causative mutation in PCH1A, which combines pontocerebellar hypoplasia with anterior horn cell degeneration.

evidence.snippet: VRK1, one of three members of the mammalian VRK family, is a serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates p53 and CREB and is essential for nuclear envelope formation.
evidence.explanation: VRK1's role in nuclear envelope formation explains its neuronal vulnerability phenotype in PCH1A.

steps/23.description: In PCH1A, biallelic VRK1 loss-of-function mutations impair nuclear envelope formation and RNA processing in post-mitotic neurons. Motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord are additionally affected beyond pontocerebellar neurons, producing a spinal muscular atrophy-like clinical picture (hypotonia, muscle weakness, areflexia) superimposed on pontocerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: Over a dozen missense mutations in the TOE1 gene have been linked to Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia Type seven (PCH7), a rare but serious neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease that leads to early mortality.
evidence.explanation: Links TOE1 ribonuclease variants to PCH7, one of the two subtypes this node groups.

evidence.snippet: Patients harbored biallelic mutations in genes encoding the spliceosome components Peptidyl-Prolyl Isomerase Like-1 (PPIL1) or Pre-RNA Processing-17 (PRP17).
evidence.explanation: Identifies PPIL1 as a spliceosome component mutated in pontocerebellar hypoplasia with microcephaly.

evidence.snippet: Loss of either protein affected splicing integrity, predominantly affecting short and high GC-content introns and genes involved in brain disorders.
evidence.explanation: Supports impaired splicing integrity as the shared molecular consequence asserted by this node.

steps/24.description: Two PCH genes act on the maturation and function of small nuclear RNAs and the major spliceosome rather than on tRNA. TOE1 is a deadenylase that trims snRNA 3' ends, and PPIL1 is a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase component of the spliceosome. These are two steps in one pathway rather than two categories: the snRNAs TOE1 matures are components of the spliceosome PPIL1 belongs to, so biallelic loss of either gene converges on the same defect, loss of splicing integrity in developing neurons, giving PCH7 and PCH14 respectively.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that loss-of-function mutations in human CHMP1A cause reduced cerebellar size (pontocerebellar hypoplasia) and reduced cerebral cortical size (microcephaly).
evidence.explanation: Establishes CHMP1A loss of function as a cause of pontocerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: CHMP1A-mutant cells show impaired proliferation, with increased expression of INK4A, a negative regulator of stem cell proliferation.
evidence.explanation: Sources the impaired proliferation and INK4A derepression named in this node's description.

evidence.snippet: Chromatin immunoprecipitation suggests loss of the normal INK4A repression by BMI in these cells.
evidence.explanation: Sources the loss of BMI1 repression of INK4A named in this node's description.

evidence.snippet: We recently showed human loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in ESCRT-III member CHMP1A cause autosomal recessive microcephaly with pontocerebellar hypoplasia, but its mechanism was unclear.
evidence.explanation: Places CHMP1A in the ESCRT-III complex, the molecular identity this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: In Chmp1a null mice, this defect is associated with impaired sonic hedgehog (Shh) secretion and intraluminal vesicle (ILV) formation in multivesicular bodies (MVBs).
evidence.explanation: Sources the multivesicular body process bound on this node.

steps/25.description: CHMP1A is a subunit of the ESCRT-III membrane-remodelling complex. In null mice, loss of Chmp1a impairs intraluminal vesicle formation in multivesicular bodies and Sonic hedgehog secretion, and the cortical and cerebellar progenitors fail to proliferate; in patient cells the proliferation defect tracks increased INK4A expression and loss of its normal BMI1 repression. Biallelic loss of function gives PCH8. The proliferation arm rather than the trafficking arm is what the cited sources tie to reduced cerebellar size, so this node is kept separate from the TBC1D23 Golgi node.

evidence.snippet: TBC1D23, a Golgi-localized protein that is frequently mutated in the neurodevelopment disorder pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH), is specifically required for the LKB1 signaling at the Golgi.
evidence.explanation: Establishes TBC1D23 as a Golgi-localised protein mutated in PCH and names the signalling role stated in this node.

evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 11 (PCH11) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in TBC1D23.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the TBC1D23-PCH11 gene-disease assignment behind this node.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report biallelic TBC1D23 mutations in six individuals from four unrelated families manifesting a non-degenerative form of PCH.
evidence.explanation: Sources the non-degenerative character of PCH11 stated in this node.

evidence.snippet: TBC1D23 was previously identified as a bridging factor for endosome-derived vesicles and golgins at Trans-Golgi Network (TGN)
evidence.explanation: Sources the bridging role between endosome-derived vesicles and golgins stated in this node's description.

evidence.snippet: While pontine hypoplasia and pronounced microcephaly are in line with previous reports on PCH11, our observations of clearly postnatal atrophy of the cerebellum argues for a different pathomechanism than in the other forms of PCH and supports the hypothesis that TBC1D23 deficiency predominantly interferes with postnatal rather than with prenatal cerebellar development.
evidence.explanation: Sources the postnatal rather than prenatal timing of the cerebellar change in PCH11, which separates it from the other subtypes on this entry.

steps/26.description: TBC1D23 is a Golgi-localised adaptor that bridges endosome-derived vesicles to golgins during retrograde transport and is required for LKB1 signalling at the Golgi. Biallelic loss gives PCH11, which has been reported as a non-degenerative PCH subtype with postnatal rather than prenatal cerebellar change, setting it apart from the RNA-processing forms.

evidence.snippet: In siblings from two unrelated families who died soon after birth with a profound neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by pontocerebellar hypoplasia and apnoea, we discovered a missense mutation and an exonic deletion in the SLC25A46 gene encoding a mitochondrial protein recently implicated in optic atrophy spectrum disorder.
evidence.explanation: Reports the biallelic SLC25A46 lesions in lethal congenital pontocerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: This genotype-phenotype correlation underscores the importance of SLC25A46 and fine tuning of mitochondrial fission and fusion in pontocerebellar hypoplasia and central neurodevelopment in addition to optic and peripheral neuropathy across the life span.
evidence.explanation: Names mitochondrial fission and fusion as the process this node asserts is disrupted.

steps/27.description: SLC25A46 encodes a mitochondrial outer-membrane protein that tunes mitochondrial fission and fusion. Complete loss of function gives the lethal congenital PCH1E phenotype, while milder alleles of the same gene cause optic atrophy and hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy, so the severity of the PCH phenotype tracks the severity of the allele.

evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH) type 12 is a rare, perinatal lethal neurodegenerative genetic disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the COASY gene.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic COASY mutation as the cause of PCH12.

evidence.snippet: Recessive variants of this gene cause an exceptionally rare and devastating disease called COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration (CoPAN) while complete loss-of-function variants in COASY have been identified in fetuses/neonates with Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia type 12 (PCH 12).
evidence.explanation: Supports the allele-severity split between PCH12 and COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration stated in this node.

steps/28.description: COASY encodes CoA synthase, which carries out the last steps of de novo coenzyme A biosynthesis. Near-complete loss of function gives the perinatal lethal PCH12 phenotype, whereas hypomorphic COASY alleles cause COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration, a form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation.

evidence.snippet: We identified homozygous or compound heterozygous AMPD2 variants in eight PCH-affected individuals from six families.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic AMPD2 variants as a cause of pontocerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: The existence of various AMPD2 isoforms with different functions possibly explains the variability in phenotypes associated with AMPD2 variants: variants leaving some of the isoforms intact may cause SPG63, while those affecting all isoforms may result in the severe and early-onset PCH9.
evidence.explanation: Supports the isoform-dependent phenotype split stated in this node's description.

steps/29.description: AMPD2 encodes adenosine monophosphate deaminase 2, which converts AMP to IMP. Variants that disable all isoforms give the severe early-onset PCH9 phenotype, whereas variants that leave some isoforms intact have instead been reported in spastic paraplegia type 63.

evidence.snippet: Multiple subtypes of PCH have been identified, among which the rare subtype PCH type 16 is caused by MINPP1 genetic variants.
evidence.explanation: Establishes MINPP1 as the PCH16 gene.

evidence.snippet: These data suggest the involvement of IP6-mediated chelation on Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia disease pathology and thereby highlight the critical role of MINPP1 in the regulation of human brain development and homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: Supports inositol hexakisphosphate accumulation as the proposed mechanism stated in this node.

steps/30.description: MINPP1 is a multiple inositol polyphosphate phosphatase. Biallelic loss of function allows the chelator inositol hexakisphosphate to accumulate inside cells, which has been proposed as the route to the PCH16 phenotype.

evidence.snippet: We describe four families with children presenting with severe neonatal brainstem dysfunction and pronounced deficits in cognitive and motor development associated with four different bi-allelic mutations in PRDM13, including homozygous truncating variants in the most severely affected individuals.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic PRDM13 mutation as the cause of this PCH-like phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Brain MRI and fetopathological examination revealed a PCH-like phenotype, associated with major hypoplasia of inferior olive nuclei and dysplasia of the dentate nucleus.
evidence.explanation: Sources the inferior olive and dentate findings named in this node's description.

evidence.snippet: Notably, histopathological examinations highlighted a sparse and disorganized Purkinje cell layer in the cerebellum.
evidence.explanation: Sources the Purkinje cell layer finding named in this node's description.

steps/31.description: PRDM13 is a transcriptional repressor expressed in progenitors of the cerebellar ventricular zone, which give rise to the cerebellar GABAergic neurons including Purkinje cells. Biallelic PRDM13 loss produces a PCH-like phenotype with hypoplasia of the inferior olive, dysplasia of the dentate nucleus, and a sparse, disorganised Purkinje cell layer, so the lesion here is a failure of neuronal specification rather than of a housekeeping process.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that a homozygous, nonsense PCLO mutation underlies the autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, PCH3.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic PCLO loss of function as the cause of PCH3.

steps/32.description: PCLO encodes Piccolo, a scaffold protein of the presynaptic active zone. Biallelic nonsense PCLO variants underlie PCH3, historically described as cerebellar atrophy with progressive microcephaly, making PCH3 a synaptic rather than an RNA-processing or metabolic mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The common characteristics are cerebellar hypoplasia with variable atrophy of the cerebellum and the ventral pons.
evidence.explanation: Confirms cerebellar and pontine hypoplasia as the universal neuropathological endpoint across PCH subtypes.

evidence.snippet: We found a strong correlation (P < 0.0005) between TSEN54 mutations and a dragonfly-like cerebellar pattern on magnetic resonance imaging, in which the cerebellar hemispheres are flat and severely reduced in size and the vermis is relatively spared.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the characteristic dragonfly MRI pattern as a radiological correlate of the cerebellar degeneration in TSEN54-related PCH.

steps/33.description: Convergent downstream consequence of TSEN complex dysfunction, mitochondrial tRNA synthetase deficiency, and motor neuron degeneration. Pontocerebellar neurons fail to develop normally in utero (prenatal onset), followed by progressive postnatal degeneration. Neuropathology shows reduced cerebellar volume, simplified or absent foliation, and hypoplastic pons with loss of pontine nuclei. The cerebral cortex is relatively spared. MRI shows the characteristic dragonfly or butterfly sign of hypoplastic cerebellar hemispheres with preserved vermis in PCH2.

evidence.snippet: All subtypes share common characteristics, including hypoplasia/atrophy of cerebellum and pons, progressive microcephaly, and variable cerebral involvement.
evidence.explanation: Confirms cerebellar hypoplasia/atrophy as a shared characteristic of all PCH subtypes.

steps/34.description: Hypoplasia of the cerebellum is the cardinal structural finding, present in all PCH types. Prenatal onset with progressive postnatal atrophy. In PCH2, the characteristic "dragonfly" MRI pattern shows flat, severely reduced cerebellar hemispheres with relative sparing of the vermis.

evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasias (PCH) represent a group of neurodegenerative autosomal recessive disorders with prenatal onset, atrophy or hypoplasia of the cerebellum, hypoplasia of the ventral pons, microcephaly, variable neocortical atrophy and severe mental and motor impairments.
evidence.explanation: Establishes pontine hypoplasia as part of the core neuropathological phenotype defining PCH.

steps/35.description: Pontine hypoplasia accompanies cerebellar hypoplasia in most PCH types, reflecting degeneration of pontine nuclei and transverse pontine fibres.

evidence.snippet: All subtypes share common characteristics, including hypoplasia/atrophy of cerebellum and pons, progressive microcephaly, and variable cerebral involvement.
evidence.explanation: Establishes progressive microcephaly as a common feature across PCH subtypes.

evidence.snippet: The long-term follow-up revealed a virtual absence of psychomotor development, progressive microcephaly, and feeding difficulties.
evidence.explanation: Documents progressive microcephaly in PCH6 (RARS2) patients on long-term follow-up.

steps/36.description: Progressive postnatal microcephaly, most prominent in PCH2, reflecting ongoing neurodegeneration rather than a pure developmental failure. Head circumference is often normal or near-normal at birth and decreases progressively.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in TSEN54 are clinically associated with dyskinesia and/or dystonia and variable degrees of spasticity, in some cases with pure generalized spasticity.
evidence.explanation: Directly links TSEN54 mutations (PCH2) to dyskinesia and dystonia as characteristic clinical features.

steps/37.description: Hyperkinetic movement disorder with chorea and dystonia, characteristic of PCH2. Dyskinesia is associated with TSEN54 mutations and can be a prominent presenting feature in the first months of life.

evidence.snippet: Patients have severe cognitive and motor handicaps and seizures are often reported.
evidence.explanation: Confirms seizures as a frequently reported feature across PCH subtypes.

evidence.snippet: All patients rapidly developed a neonatal or early-infantile epileptic encephalopathy with intractable seizures.
evidence.explanation: Establishes early-onset intractable epilepsy as a defining feature of PCH6 (RARS2 mutations).

steps/38.description: Epileptic seizures occur across PCH subtypes, particularly PCH2 and PCH6. In PCH6, neonatal or early-infantile epileptic encephalopathy with intractable seizures is the presenting feature.

evidence.snippet: The long-term follow-up revealed a virtual absence of psychomotor development, progressive microcephaly, and feeding difficulties.
evidence.explanation: Documents feeding difficulties as part of the PCH6 clinical spectrum.

steps/39.description: Feeding difficulty is a common severe-care feature in PCH, reflecting profound neurodevelopmental impairment, hypotonia, dysphagia, and respiratory vulnerability. In RARS2-related PCH6 it accompanies progressive microcephaly and virtual absence of psychomotor development.

evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasias (PCH) represent a group of neurodegenerative autosomal recessive disorders with prenatal onset, atrophy or hypoplasia of the cerebellum, hypoplasia of the ventral pons, microcephaly, variable neocortical atrophy and severe mental and motor impairments.
evidence.explanation: Establishes severe mental impairments as part of the defining phenotype of PCH.

evidence.snippet: The long-term follow-up revealed a virtual absence of psychomotor development, progressive microcephaly, and feeding difficulties.
evidence.explanation: Documents virtual absence of psychomotor development (equivalent to profound intellectual disability) in PCH6.

steps/40.description: Profound intellectual disability is universal across PCH subtypes. Independent ambulation and meaningful speech are rarely if ever achieved. Cognitive development typically stalls in the first year of life.

evidence.snippet: The spinal muscular atrophies (SMAs) are a genetically and clinically heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by degeneration and loss of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord, leading to muscle weakness and atrophy.
evidence.explanation: VRK1 loss-of-function causes SMA-PCH (PCH1A) with degeneration of anterior horn cells, producing hypotonia and muscle weakness as core features.

steps/41.description: Neonatal and infantile hypotonia, often severe, contributing to feeding difficulties, respiratory compromise, and absence of motor milestones. In PCH1A, hypotonia is compounded by anterior horn cell degeneration.

evidence.snippet: Nonsense or splice site mutations in TSEN54 are associated with a more severe phenotype of more perinatal symptoms, ventilator dependency and early death.
evidence.explanation: Documents respiratory insufficiency severe enough to require ventilator support in PCH4 patients with null TSEN54 alleles.

steps/42.description: Respiratory insufficiency due to combined central and peripheral causes. In PCH1A, anterior horn cell loss causes ventilatory muscle weakness; in PCH4, neonatal respiratory failure is the immediate cause of death. In PCH2, severe cases with nonsense TSEN54 mutations may require ventilator dependency.

evidence.snippet: Blood and CSF lactate was abnormally elevated in all five patients at early stages
evidence.explanation: Supports elevated lactate as a frequent early biochemical feature in the original PCH6 cohort.

steps/43.description: Elevated blood or CSF lactate is a mitochondrial-disease clue in RARS2-related PCH6, although later reports indicate that lactate can be absent in some genetically confirmed patients.

evidence.snippet: Treatment is only symptomatic and prognosis is poor, as most patients die during infancy or childhood.
evidence.explanation: Supports poor survival as a major prognostic feature of PCH.

evidence.snippet: EXOSC3 mutations account for 30%-40% of patients with PCH1 with variability in survival and clinical severity that is correlated with the genotype.
evidence.explanation: Clarifies that survival is subtype- and genotype-dependent, especially within PCH1B.

steps/44.description: PCH has a poor prognosis overall, with death in infancy or childhood for many affected individuals. Survival varies by subtype and genotype; EXOSC3-related PCH1B can include longer survival, while severe TSEN54-related PCH4 is often neonatal lethal.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in TSEN54 are clinically associated with dyskinesia and/or dystonia and variable degrees of spasticity, in some cases with pure generalized spasticity.
evidence.explanation: Ties the TSEN54 lesion carried on this node directly to the dyskinesia phenotype.

edges/20.description: TSEN54-related disease is the PCH form in which dyskinesia and dystonia are the characteristic movement disorder.

evidence.snippet: Nonsense or splice site mutations in TSEN54 are associated with a more severe phenotype of more perinatal symptoms, ventilator dependency and early death.
evidence.explanation: Ties the severe TSEN54 alleles carried on this node to ventilator dependency.

edges/21.description: Severe TSEN54 genotypes carry perinatal respiratory failure and ventilator dependency.

evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasias (PCH) represent a group of neurodegenerative autosomal recessive disorders with prenatal onset, atrophy or hypoplasia of the cerebellum, hypoplasia of the ventral pons
evidence.explanation: Links TSEN-related PCH to prenatal pontocerebellar hypoplasia and atrophy, supporting the downstream edge.

edges/22.description: TSEN-complex defects converge on prenatal pontocerebellar maldevelopment with progressive atrophy.

evidence.snippet: Psychomotor retardation was profound in all patients but lifespan was variable, with 3 subjects surviving beyond the late teens.
evidence.explanation: Supports severe neurodevelopmental impact with variable survival in EXOSC3-related PCH1B.

edges/23.description: RNA exosome subunit loss converges on pontocerebellar hypoplasia and progressive neurodevelopmental impairment.

evidence.snippet: Blood and CSF lactate was abnormally elevated in all five patients at early stages
evidence.explanation: Reports the elevated lactate that this edge asserts follows from the mitochondrial translation defect.

edges/24.description: Impaired mitochondrial translation raises blood and CSF lactate, the biochemical signature that separates PCH6 from the RNA-processing subtypes.

evidence.snippet: In three patients follow-up neuroimaging revealed a progressive pontocerebellar and cerebral cortical atrophy.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports progression from RARS2-associated mitochondrial disease to pontocerebellar atrophy.

edges/25.description: RARS2-related mitochondrial translation defects are associated with progressive pontocerebellar and cortical atrophy.

evidence.snippet: The spinal muscular atrophies (SMAs) are a genetically and clinically heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by degeneration and loss of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord, leading to muscle weakness and atrophy.
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from anterior horn cell loss to muscle weakness that this edge asserts.

edges/26.description: Anterior horn cell loss produces the muscle weakness and hypotonia that define the SMA-like component of PCH1.

evidence.snippet: identified a nonsense mutation in the vaccinia-related kinase 1 gene (VRK1) as a cause of SMA-PCH
evidence.explanation: Establishes VRK1 loss as causal for the combined spinal muscular atrophy and pontocerebellar hypoplasia phenotype.

edges/27.description: VRK1-associated SMA-PCH combines anterior horn cell degeneration with pontocerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: Mouse knockouts of either gene were lethal in early embryogenesis, whereas PPIL1 patient mutation knockin mice showed neuron-specific apoptosis.
evidence.explanation: Shows that the splicing defect selectively kills neurons, the step linking this node to cerebellar degeneration.

edges/28.description: Failure of snRNA maturation and spliceosome function in developing hindbrain neurons converges on the shared pontocerebellar endpoint.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show Chmp1a is required for progenitor proliferation in mouse cortex and cerebellum and progenitor maintenance in human cerebral organoids.
evidence.explanation: Ties loss of CHMP1A to failure of cerebellar progenitor proliferation, the step this edge asserts.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that loss-of-function mutations in human CHMP1A cause reduced cerebellar size (pontocerebellar hypoplasia) and reduced cerebral cortical size (microcephaly).
evidence.explanation: Directly links CHMP1A loss of function to reduced cerebellar size.

edges/29.description: Failure of cortical and cerebellar progenitor proliferation converges on the shared pontocerebellar endpoint.

evidence.snippet: Altogether, this study provides a causative link between TBC1D23 mutations and PCH and suggests a less severe clinical course than other PCH subtypes.
evidence.explanation: Links TBC1D23 loss to the pontocerebellar phenotype and to its milder course.

evidence.snippet: While pontine hypoplasia and pronounced microcephaly are in line with previous reports on PCH11, our observations of clearly postnatal atrophy of the cerebellum argues for a different pathomechanism than in the other forms of PCH and supports the hypothesis that TBC1D23 deficiency predominantly interferes with postnatal rather than with prenatal cerebellar development.
evidence.explanation: Sources the postnatal timing this edge's description asserts.

edges/30.description: Loss of Golgi-directed retrograde trafficking converges on the shared pontocerebellar endpoint, though in this subtype the cerebellar change is reported as postnatal rather than prenatal.

evidence.snippet: This genotype-phenotype correlation underscores the importance of SLC25A46 and fine tuning of mitochondrial fission and fusion in pontocerebellar hypoplasia and central neurodevelopment in addition to optic and peripheral neuropathy across the life span.
evidence.explanation: Ties the mitochondrial dynamics defect to pontocerebellar hypoplasia and central neurodevelopment.

edges/31.description: Loss of mitochondrial membrane dynamics in developing hindbrain neurons converges on the shared pontocerebellar endpoint.

evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH) type 12 is a rare, perinatal lethal neurodegenerative genetic disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the COASY gene.
evidence.explanation: Links loss of CoA synthase directly to the pontocerebellar hypoplasia endpoint.

edges/32.description: Failure of coenzyme A supply in the developing hindbrain converges on the shared pontocerebellar endpoint.

evidence.snippet: We identified homozygous or compound heterozygous AMPD2 variants in eight PCH-affected individuals from six families.
evidence.explanation: Links biallelic AMPD2 loss to the pontocerebellar phenotype.

edges/33.description: Loss of AMP deaminase activity in developing hindbrain neurons converges on the shared pontocerebellar endpoint.

evidence.snippet: These data suggest the involvement of IP6-mediated chelation on Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia disease pathology and thereby highlight the critical role of MINPP1 in the regulation of human brain development and homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: Ties the inositol polyphosphate defect to pontocerebellar hypoplasia pathology.

edges/34.description: Accumulation of inositol hexakisphosphate in developing brain cells converges on the shared pontocerebellar endpoint.

evidence.snippet: snRNA-seq data mining and in situ hybridization in humans show that PRDM13 is expressed at early stages in the progenitors of the cerebellar ventricular zone, which gives rise to cerebellar GABAergic neurons, including Purkinje cells.
evidence.explanation: Places PRDM13 in the cerebellar progenitors whose failure produces the hypoplastic cerebellum.

edges/35.description: Failure to specify cerebellar GABAergic neurons converges on the shared pontocerebellar endpoint.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that a homozygous, nonsense PCLO mutation underlies the autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, PCH3.
evidence.explanation: Links loss of the active zone scaffold to the PCH3 neurodegenerative phenotype.

edges/36.description: Loss of presynaptic active zone scaffolding converges on the shared pontocerebellar endpoint.

evidence.snippet: All subtypes share common characteristics, including hypoplasia/atrophy of cerebellum and pons, progressive microcephaly, and variable cerebral involvement.
evidence.explanation: Names cerebellar hypoplasia as a characteristic shared across all PCH subtypes.

edges/37.description: Cerebellar hypoplasia with prenatal onset and progressive postnatal atrophy is the cardinal structural consequence of the converged mechanism.

evidence.snippet: All subtypes share common characteristics, including hypoplasia/atrophy of cerebellum and pons, progressive microcephaly, and variable cerebral involvement.
evidence.explanation: Names pontine hypoplasia or atrophy as a characteristic shared across all PCH subtypes.

edges/38.description: Loss of pontine nuclei and transverse fibres accompanies the cerebellar lesion in most subtypes.

evidence.snippet: All subtypes share common characteristics, including hypoplasia/atrophy of cerebellum and pons, progressive microcephaly, and variable cerebral involvement.
evidence.explanation: Names progressive microcephaly as a characteristic shared across all PCH subtypes.

edges/39.description: Continuing postnatal degeneration produces head growth that falls progressively away from the normal range.

evidence.snippet: Patients have severe cognitive and motor handicaps and seizures are often reported.
evidence.explanation: States that patients have severe cognitive handicaps.

edges/40.description: Failure of pontocerebellar development and ongoing degeneration leave profound cognitive impairment.

evidence.snippet: Patients have severe cognitive and motor handicaps and seizures are often reported.
evidence.explanation: States that seizures are often reported in PCH.

edges/41.description: Cortical and subcortical involvement accompanying the pontocerebellar lesion gives rise to seizures in a large fraction of patients.

evidence.snippet: Treatment is only symptomatic and prognosis is poor, as most patients die during infancy or childhood.
evidence.explanation: States the poor prognosis and early mortality of the group.

edges/42.description: Degeneration continues after birth and determines the poor prognosis of the group.

evidence.snippet: The long-term follow-up revealed a virtual absence of psychomotor development, progressive microcephaly, and feeding difficulties.
evidence.explanation: Reports the feeding difficulties that this edge asserts follow from the converged pontocerebellar lesion.

edges/43.description: Bulbar dysfunction from the pontocerebellar lesion impairs sucking and swallowing from the neonatal period onward.

evidence.snippet: In two subtypes, PCH2 and PCH4, we identified mutations in three of the four different subunits of the tRNA-splicing endonuclease complex.
evidence.explanation: Establishes TSEN complex subunit mutations (predominantly TSEN54) as causative for PCH2 and PCH4.

evidence.snippet: This mutation results in an amino acid substitution of alanine for serine at codon 307 (A307S), and it has previously been described in a Northern European subset of patients with PCH2
evidence.explanation: Sources the p.Ala307Ser founder allele and its Northern European ancestry association stated in these notes.

evidence.snippet: The PCH5 patient was found to be the result of compound heterozygosity for the common TSEN54 mutation (p.A307S) plus a novel splice site mutation.
evidence.explanation: Sources the PCH5 genotype named in these notes and the third TSEN54 subtype this record spans.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report three homozygous TSEN15 variants that cause a milder version of PCH2.
evidence.explanation: Sources the TSEN15 PCH2 subtype named in these notes.

genes/0.notes: Mutations in TSEN54, encoding the 54 kDa subunit of the TSEN complex, cause the most common forms of PCH (types 2 and 4). The founder missense allele c.919G>T (p.Ala307Ser) is present in the majority of PCH2 patients of European ancestry, often in homozygous form. Biallelic null or severe compound alleles cause the neonatal lethal PCH4 phenotype, and compound heterozygosity for p.Ala307Ser plus a splice-site allele has been reported in PCH5. Mutations in other TSEN subunits cause rarer PCH2 subtypes: TSEN2 gives PCH2B, TSEN34 gives PCH2C and TSEN15 gives PCH2F. PCH2D is caused by SEPSECS, not by a TSEN subunit. The scalar `subtype` slot is left unset on this record because TSEN54 spans the PCH2A, PCH4 and PCH5 rows in `has_subtypes` rather than a single one.

evidence.snippet: identified a nonsense mutation in the vaccinia-related kinase 1 gene (VRK1) as a cause of SMA-PCH
evidence.explanation: First identification of VRK1 as the causative gene for PCH1A (SMA-PCH) in human patients.

genes/1.notes: Homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in VRK1 (vaccinia-related kinase 1) cause PCH1A. VRK1 is a serine/threonine kinase essential for nuclear envelope formation that phosphorylates p53 and CREB. Its absence leads to combined pontocerebellar and anterior horn cell degeneration (SMA-PCH phenotype).

evidence.snippet: identification of an intronic mutation in RARS2, the gene encoding mitochondrial arginine-transfer RNA (tRNA) synthetase
evidence.explanation: First identification of RARS2 as the causative gene for PCH6 (mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase deficiency).

genes/2.notes: Biallelic mutations in RARS2, encoding the mitochondrial arginyl-tRNA synthetase, impair mitochondrial tRNA charging and oxidative phosphorylation, causing PCH6. CSF lactate is typically elevated. Patients may show elevated lactate in blood/CSF and reduced respiratory chain complex activity on muscle biopsy.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic mutations in EXOSC3 were detected in 10 of 27 families (37%).
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic EXOSC3 variants as causative for a substantial subset of PCH1/PCH1B.

genes/3.notes: Biallelic EXOSC3 mutations cause PCH1B, the most common genetically confirmed PCH1 subgroup in the referenced cohort. EXOSC3-related disease remains within the spinal muscular atrophy-like PCH1 spectrum but shows genotype-dependent severity and variable survival.

evidence.snippet: Thus, we have identified a defined clinical syndrome with progressive central and peripheral nervous system defects in 11 affected children from five families, all of whom carry a homozygous CLP1 R140H mutation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes homozygous CLP1 R140H as causal for a PCH10-related central and peripheral nervous system disorder.

genes/4.notes: Homozygous CLP1 pathogenic variants cause PCH10 through impaired interaction with the TSEN complex and defective pre-tRNA cleavage. The phenotype includes severe central nervous system involvement and peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: Bi-allelic variants in exosome subunits EXOSC3, EXOSC8 and EXOSC9 have been reported to cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 1B, type 1C and type 1D, respectively, while those in EXOSC2 cause short stature, hearing loss, retinitis pigmentosa and distinctive facies.
evidence.explanation: Assigns biallelic EXOSC8 variants to PCH1C.

evidence.snippet: mutations in the structural exosome genes EXOSC3 and EXOSC8 cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 1b (PCH1b) and type 1c (PCH1c), respectively, which are related autosomal recessive, neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence.explanation: Confirms EXOSC8 as the PCH1C gene and the autosomal recessive mode.

genes/5.notes: EXOSC8 encodes a structural subunit of the RNA exosome. Biallelic EXOSC8 variants cause PCH1C, which shares the PCH1 pattern of pontocerebellar hypoplasia with anterior horn cell degeneration.

evidence.snippet: Bi-allelic variants in exosome subunits EXOSC3, EXOSC8 and EXOSC9 have been reported to cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 1B, type 1C and type 1D, respectively, while those in EXOSC2 cause short stature, hearing loss, retinitis pigmentosa and distinctive facies.
evidence.explanation: Assigns biallelic EXOSC9 variants to PCH1D.

evidence.snippet: mutations in the structural exosome gene EXOSC9 cause a PCH-like disease with cerebellar atrophy and spinal motor neuronopathy.
evidence.explanation: Describes the EXOSC9 phenotype recorded in this entry.

genes/6.notes: EXOSC9 encodes a third structural subunit of the RNA exosome. Biallelic EXOSC9 variants cause PCH1D, in which cerebellar atrophy is accompanied by spinal motor neuronopathy.

evidence.snippet: In siblings from two unrelated families who died soon after birth with a profound neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by pontocerebellar hypoplasia and apnoea, we discovered a missense mutation and an exonic deletion in the SLC25A46 gene encoding a mitochondrial protein recently implicated in optic atrophy spectrum disorder.
evidence.explanation: Reports the biallelic SLC25A46 lesions underlying lethal congenital pontocerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: PCH1 is defined as PCH variant associated with anterior horn degeneration in the spinal cord with muscle weakness and hypotonia, and is associated with recessive variants in genes VRK1, EXOSC3, EXOSC8, EXOSC9 and SLC25A46.
evidence.explanation: Places SLC25A46 among the recessive PCH1 genes.

genes/7.notes: SLC25A46 encodes a mitochondrial outer-membrane protein regulating mitochondrial fission and fusion. Complete loss of function causes the lethal congenital PCH1E phenotype; milder alleles of the same gene cause optic atrophy and hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: Literature review has identified six PCH2B patients with missense, nonsense, frameshift, and splice site variants of the TSEN2 gene.
evidence.explanation: Assigns TSEN2 variants to PCH2B and indicates how few cases are reported.

evidence.snippet: Most patients with PCH2 have mutations in TSEN54, with occasional mutations found in TSEN34 or TSEN2, genes that encode subunits of tRNA splicing endonuclease.
evidence.explanation: Supports TSEN2 as an infrequent PCH2 gene relative to TSEN54.

genes/8.notes: TSEN2 encodes a catalytic subunit of the tRNA splicing endonuclease complex. Biallelic TSEN2 variants cause PCH2B, a far rarer PCH2 form than the TSEN54-associated PCH2A.

evidence.snippet: Most patients with PCH2 have mutations in TSEN54, with occasional mutations found in TSEN34 or TSEN2, genes that encode subunits of tRNA splicing endonuclease.
evidence.explanation: Assigns TSEN34 to PCH2 as an infrequent cause.

evidence.snippet: In two subtypes, PCH2 and PCH4, we identified mutations in three of the four different subunits of the tRNA-splicing endonuclease complex.
evidence.explanation: Original report identifying mutations in three TSEN subunits, including TSEN34, in PCH2 and PCH4.

genes/9.notes: TSEN34 encodes the second catalytic subunit of the tRNA splicing endonuclease complex. Biallelic TSEN34 variants cause PCH2C and, like TSEN2, account for only occasional PCH2 cases.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report three homozygous TSEN15 variants that cause a milder version of PCH2.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic TSEN15 variants as a cause of a milder PCH2 phenotype.

genes/10.notes: TSEN15 encodes the fourth subunit of the tRNA splicing endonuclease complex. Biallelic TSEN15 variants cause PCH2F, reported as a milder form of PCH2 than the TSEN54-associated disease.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that a homozygous, nonsense PCLO mutation underlies the autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, PCH3.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic PCLO loss of function as the cause of PCH3.

genes/11.notes: PCLO encodes Piccolo, a presynaptic active zone scaffold protein. A homozygous nonsense PCLO variant underlies PCH3, historically described as cerebellar atrophy with progressive microcephaly, making PCH3 the one synaptic rather than RNA-processing or metabolic PCH mechanism in this entry.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic TOE1 variants can cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 7 (PCH7), a condition characterized by pontocerebellar hypoplasia with genital abnormality.
evidence.explanation: States the TOE1-PCH7 assignment and the distinguishing genital feature.

evidence.snippet: We performed characterization of the thermal stability and activity of eleven PCH-linked TOE1 variants and found that eight variants have significant reduced protein thermal stability and that all but two variants impair TOE1's ribonuclease activity, particularly its exonuclease activity.
evidence.explanation: Shows that PCH-linked TOE1 variants reduce the protein's ribonuclease activity, supporting loss of function.

genes/12.notes: TOE1 encodes a deadenylase that trims the 3' ends of small nuclear RNAs. Biallelic TOE1 variants cause PCH7, distinguished from other PCH subtypes by genital abnormality, presenting as PCH with a 46,XY disorder of sex development in individuals with an XY karyotype.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that loss-of-function mutations in human CHMP1A cause reduced cerebellar size (pontocerebellar hypoplasia) and reduced cerebral cortical size (microcephaly).
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic CHMP1A loss of function as a cause of pontocerebellar hypoplasia with microcephaly.

genes/13.notes: CHMP1A encodes a subunit of the ESCRT-III membrane-remodelling complex. Biallelic loss of function causes PCH8, reported as reduced cerebellar size together with microcephaly. The gene is wired to its own ESCRT-III and progenitor-proliferation node rather than being grouped with TBC1D23, because no source cited here places CHMP1A in Golgi retrograde transport.

evidence.snippet: We identified homozygous or compound heterozygous AMPD2 variants in eight PCH-affected individuals from six families.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic AMPD2 variants as a cause of pontocerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: The existence of various AMPD2 isoforms with different functions possibly explains the variability in phenotypes associated with AMPD2 variants: variants leaving some of the isoforms intact may cause SPG63, while those affecting all isoforms may result in the severe and early-onset PCH9.
evidence.explanation: Supports the isoform-dependent split between AMPD2-related SPG63 and PCH9.

genes/14.notes: AMPD2 encodes adenosine monophosphate deaminase 2. Biallelic variants affecting all isoforms cause the severe early-onset PCH9 phenotype, while variants that leave some isoforms intact have been reported in spastic paraplegia type 63.

evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 11 (PCH11) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in TBC1D23.
evidence.explanation: States the TBC1D23-PCH11 gene-disease assignment.

evidence.snippet: TBC1D23, a Golgi-localized protein that is frequently mutated in the neurodevelopment disorder pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH), is specifically required for the LKB1 signaling at the Golgi.
evidence.explanation: Sources the Golgi localisation and LKB1 signalling role described here.

genes/15.notes: TBC1D23 encodes a Golgi-localised trafficking adaptor required for Golgi-based LKB1 signalling. Biallelic TBC1D23 variants cause PCH11, which has been reported as a non-degenerative PCH subtype.

evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH) type 12 is a rare, perinatal lethal neurodegenerative genetic disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the COASY gene.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic COASY mutation as the cause of PCH12.

evidence.snippet: Recessive variants of this gene cause an exceptionally rare and devastating disease called COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration (CoPAN) while complete loss-of-function variants in COASY have been identified in fetuses/neonates with Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia type 12 (PCH 12).
evidence.explanation: Supports the allele-severity split between PCH12 and COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration.

genes/16.notes: COASY encodes CoA synthase, which catalyses the final steps of de novo coenzyme A biosynthesis. Near-complete loss of function causes the perinatal lethal PCH12 phenotype, while hypomorphic alleles cause COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration.

evidence.snippet: Patients harbored biallelic mutations in genes encoding the spliceosome components Peptidyl-Prolyl Isomerase Like-1 (PPIL1) or Pre-RNA Processing-17 (PRP17).
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic PPIL1 variants as a cause of pontocerebellar hypoplasia with microcephaly.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic variants in PPIL1 have been recently found to cause a very rare type of pontocerebellar hypoplasia and congenital microcephaly in which simplified gyral pattern was not observed in all of the patients.
evidence.explanation: Independent series confirming the PPIL1 gene-disease assignment and describing its imaging variability.

genes/17.notes: PPIL1 encodes a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase component of the major spliceosome. Biallelic PPIL1 variants cause PCH14, reported as pontocerebellar hypoplasia with microcephaly.

evidence.snippet: Multiple subtypes of PCH have been identified, among which the rare subtype PCH type 16 is caused by MINPP1 genetic variants.
evidence.explanation: Establishes MINPP1 as the PCH16 gene.

evidence.snippet: These data suggest the involvement of IP6-mediated chelation on Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia disease pathology and thereby highlight the critical role of MINPP1 in the regulation of human brain development and homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: Supports inositol hexakisphosphate accumulation as the proposed consequence of MINPP1 loss.

genes/18.notes: MINPP1 encodes a multiple inositol polyphosphate phosphatase. Biallelic loss of function causes PCH16 and allows the chelator inositol hexakisphosphate to accumulate intracellularly.

evidence.snippet: We describe four families with children presenting with severe neonatal brainstem dysfunction and pronounced deficits in cognitive and motor development associated with four different bi-allelic mutations in PRDM13, including homozygous truncating variants in the most severely affected individuals.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic PRDM13 mutation as the cause of this PCH-like perinatal phenotype.

evidence.snippet: snRNA-seq data mining and in situ hybridization in humans show that PRDM13 is expressed at early stages in the progenitors of the cerebellar ventricular zone, which gives rise to cerebellar GABAergic neurons, including Purkinje cells.
evidence.explanation: Sources the cerebellar ventricular zone progenitor expression described here.

genes/19.notes: PRDM13 encodes a transcriptional repressor expressed in cerebellar ventricular zone progenitors. Biallelic PRDM13 variants cause PCH17, a fatal perinatal brainstem phenotype with cerebellar hypoplasia and disrupted Purkinje cell differentiation. A separate PRDM13 phenotype combines cerebellar dysfunction with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

evidence.snippet: Treatment is only symptomatic and prognosis is poor, as most patients die during infancy or childhood.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that only symptomatic treatment is available and prognosis is poor across PCH subtypes.

evidence.snippet: Children with PCH2 have generalized clonus, uncoordinated sucking and swallowing, impaired cognitive development, lack of voluntary motor development, cortical blindness, and an increased risk for rhabdomyolysis during severe infections.
evidence.explanation: Names the rhabdomyolysis risk during febrile illness that the hydration measure below is directed at.

evidence.snippet: Adequate hydration during prolonged periods of high fever may help avoid rhabdomyolysis.
evidence.explanation: The one specific preventive measure GeneReviews gives for TSEN54-related PCH, beyond general symptomatic care.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying therapy exists for any PCH subtype. Management is supportive: nutritional support via nasogastric tube or gastrostomy, respiratory support (including mechanical ventilation for severe cases), physiotherapy to manage spasticity and contractures, and palliative care. Genetic counselling for families is essential. One subtype-specific preventive measure is documented: children with TSEN54-related PCH2 carry an increased risk of rhabdomyolysis during severe infections, and GeneReviews recommends adequate hydration through prolonged high fever to reduce it.

evidence.snippet: The long-term follow-up revealed a virtual absence of psychomotor development, progressive microcephaly, and feeding difficulties.
evidence.explanation: Supports feeding support as a clinically relevant management domain, especially in severe PCH6.

evidence.snippet: Treatment is only symptomatic and prognosis is poor, as most patients die during infancy or childhood.
evidence.explanation: Supports supportive management for severe PCH manifestations.

treatments/1.description: Feeding therapy, aspiration-risk assessment, and enteral nutrition by nasogastric or gastrostomy tube are important for affected infants with dysphagia, hypotonia, failure to thrive, or severe neurodevelopmental impairment. This is supportive care and not disease-modifying treatment.

evidence.snippet: Nonsense or splice site mutations in TSEN54 are associated with a more severe phenotype of more perinatal symptoms, ventilator dependency and early death.
evidence.explanation: Supports respiratory support and palliative planning for severe TSEN54-related PCH4.

evidence.snippet: Major clinical features previously reported in PCH1, including intrauterine abnormalities, postnatal hypoventilation and feeding difficulties, joint contractures, and neonatal death, were rarely observed in mutation-positive infants but were typical among the mutation-negative subjects.
evidence.explanation: Supports respiratory and end-of-life planning for severe PCH1 presentations.

treatments/2.description: Respiratory monitoring, noninvasive or invasive ventilation when consistent with goals of care, and early palliative-care planning are relevant for severe PCH1A/PCH1B, PCH4, and other forms with hypoventilation, ventilator dependence, or life-limiting neurologic disease.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in TSEN54 are clinically associated with dyskinesia and/or dystonia and variable degrees of spasticity, in some cases with pure generalized spasticity.
evidence.explanation: Supports movement-disorder and spasticity-oriented supportive management in TSEN54-related PCH.

evidence.snippet: Patients have severe cognitive and motor handicaps and seizures are often reported.
evidence.explanation: Supports motor-disability-directed supportive therapy across PCH subtypes.

evidence.snippet: Contractures and scoliosis are managed by passive or active movement and bracing as needed.
evidence.explanation: Names the specific musculoskeletal measures GeneReviews recommends, which this treatment covers.

treatments/3.description: Physical therapy, positioning, contracture prevention, and symptom-directed movement-disorder management address hypotonia, spasticity, dystonia, dyskinesia, and progressive motor disability. These interventions are supportive and should be individualized by subtype and severity.

evidence.snippet: All patients rapidly developed a neonatal or early-infantile epileptic encephalopathy with intractable seizures.
evidence.explanation: Intractable seizures in PCH6 require anticonvulsant pharmacotherapy, consistent with antiepileptic drug use as a standard management approach.

treatments/4.description: Anticonvulsant medications for management of epileptic seizures in PCH2 and PCH6. No specific anticonvulsant is preferred; polytherapy is often required for refractory epilepsy in PCH6.

evidence.snippet: The genetic basis of different subtypes has been elucidated, which makes prenatal testing possible in families with mutations.
evidence.explanation: Supports counseling around molecular subtype, recurrence risk, and prenatal testing options.

treatments/5.description: Genetic counseling should address autosomal-recessive inheritance, recurrence risk, carrier testing, molecular confirmation of the familial subtype, and reproductive options including prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing when familial variants are known.

evidence.snippet: we identified the ciliary tip kinesins Kif7 and Kif17 as novel interaction partners of the small GTPase Arl3 and its regulatory GTPase activating protein (GAP) Retinitis Pigmentosa 2 (RP2). We show that Arl3 and RP2 mediate the localization of GFP-Kif17 to the cilia tip
evidence.explanation: Identifies RP2 as the GAP for Arl3 and establishes its role in ciliary-tip kinesin localization.

steps/1.description: RP2 functions as a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for the small GTPase ARL3 at the photoreceptor connecting cilium. RP2 and ARL3 regulate the trafficking of the ciliary-tip kinesins Kif7 and Kif17, which are required for normal intraflagellar transport and delivery of cargo to the cilium tip. Loss-of-function RP2 variants abolish or reduce this GAP/trafficking-regulatory activity.

evidence.snippet: siRNA-mediated loss of RP2 or Arl3 reduced the level of Kif7 at the cilia tip. This was further validated by reduced levels of Kif7 at cilia tips detected in fibroblasts and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) 3D optic cups derived from a patient carrying an RP2 nonsense mutation
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates reduced ciliary-tip kinesin localization in patient-derived RP2-null cells, directly linking RP2 loss to ciliary trafficking defects.

evidence.snippet: the treatment preserved cone viability, corrected mis-trafficking of M-cone opsin and restored cone PDE6 expression
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that AAV-RP2 gene replacement corrects opsin and PDE6 mistrafficking in Rp2-knockout mouse photoreceptors, confirming that loss of RP2 causes phototransduction-protein mistrafficking.

steps/2.description: Without functional RP2, ciliary-tip kinesin levels (Kif7) are reduced at the cilium tip, and lipidated phototransduction cargo normally released by ARL3-GTP at the connecting cilium is mistrafficked. In RP2-null patient cells and RP2-knockout mouse photoreceptors, this manifests as mislocalization of cone opsin and phosphodiesterase (PDE6) away from the outer segment.

evidence.snippet: the RP2 KO and RP2 patient-derived organoids showed a peak in rod photoreceptor cell death at day 150 (D150) with subsequent thinning of the organoid outer nuclear layer (ONL) by D180 of culture
evidence.explanation: Directly quantifies the kinetics of rod photoreceptor apoptosis in a human iPSC-derived RP2-deficient retinal organoid model.

steps/3.description: Progressive rod photoreceptor death follows chronic ciliary trafficking dysfunction, producing the early-onset, severe rod-cone dystrophy characteristic of RP2-related retinopathy. In human patients, rod photoreceptor cell models (patient-derived retinal organoids) show a peak of rod cell death by day 150 of culture, with subsequent thinning of the photoreceptor layer.

evidence.snippet: Full-field ERGs revealed rod-cone dystrophy in the vast majority, but with generalized (peripheral) cone system involvement of widely varying severity in the first 2 decades of life.
evidence.explanation: Documents early and widespread cone system involvement in a large natural history cohort of RP2-RP patients.

steps/4.description: Cone photoreceptors are affected both indirectly (loss of rod-derived trophic support) and directly (cone-intrinsic RP2-dependent ciliary trafficking dysfunction), producing generalized peripheral cone system involvement of widely varying severity within the first two decades of life and converting the initial rod-dominant disease into progressive central vision loss with complete loss of the foveal photoreceptor layer by the third decade in most patients.

edges/1.description: Loss of RP2 GAP activity and its role in ciliary-tip kinesin recruitment disrupts the trafficking checkpoint that normally delivers cargo to the connecting cilium and outer segment.

edges/2.description: Chronic mislocalization of ciliary and phototransduction proteins impairs photoreceptor outer segment maintenance, driving progressive rod photoreceptor degeneration.

edges/3.description: Progressive rod loss and direct cone-intrinsic trafficking defects together drive generalized peripheral cone system involvement, converting nyctalopia and peripheral field loss into central vision impairment; central/macular involvement occurs disproportionately early in RP2-RP.

evidence.snippet: Twenty-eight disease-causing variants were identified, with 20 not previously clinically characterized.
evidence.explanation: Documents the diversity of disease-causing RP2 variants in a large natural history cohort.

evidence.snippet: the tested RP2 mutants exhibited variable degrees of rescue of rod versus cone photoreceptor development as well as microphthalmia
evidence.explanation: Zebrafish rescue assay demonstrates that RP2 missense variants have variable, rather than uniform, pathogenic potential.

evidence.snippet: Preservation of cone function was achieved with a wide dose range over 18-month duration, as evidenced by photopic ERG and optomotor tests... the treatment preserved cone viability, corrected mis-trafficking of M-cone opsin and restored cone PDE6 expression.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates long-term functional and structural rescue with AAV-RP2 gene replacement in the RP2-knockout mouse model.

evidence.snippet: Adeno-associated virus-mediated gene augmentation with human RP2 rescued the degeneration phenotype of the RP2 KO organoids, to prevent ONL thinning and restore rhodopsin expression.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates AAV-RP2 rescue in a human iPSC-derived retinal organoid disease model, complementing the mouse gene-therapy data.

treatments/0.description: AAV-mediated RP2 gene augmentation has produced long-term (18-month) rescue of cone photoreceptor function and correction of opsin/PDE6 mistrafficking in Rp2-knockout mice, and has rescued the degeneration phenotype (preventing outer nuclear layer thinning, restoring rhodopsin expression) in patient-derived iPSC retinal organoids. As of the literature reviewed, no RP2-specific gene therapy has yet reached a registered human clinical trial (in contrast to RPGR, for which several trials are active).

evidence.snippet: Translational read-through inducing drugs (TRIDs), such as PTC124, were able to restore Kif7 levels at the ciliary tip of RP2 null cells.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that PTC124 restores ciliary-tip kinesin trafficking in RP2-null cells from a nonsense-variant patient.

treatments/1.description: For the subset of RP2-RP caused by nonsense (premature termination codon) variants, translational read-through inducing drugs (TRIDs) such as PTC124 have restored ciliary-tip kinesin (Kif7) trafficking in fibroblasts and iPSC-derived cells from a patient with an RP2 nonsense mutation, suggesting a potential genotype-specific small-molecule strategy. This remains a preclinical/investigational approach.

evidence.snippet: On the basis of the World Health Organization visual impairment criteria, 18 patients (34%) had low vision.
evidence.explanation: The substantial proportion of patients meeting low-vision criteria supports ongoing low-vision rehabilitative care.

treatments/2.description: Low vision aids, adaptive lighting, and orientation and mobility training are the mainstay of symptomatic management as visual field and acuity decline.

evidence.snippet: The phenotypic spectrum as described herein has prognostic and counselling implications for RP2 carriers and patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the direct genetic-counseling relevance of the variable carrier phenotype.

treatments/3.description: Genetic counseling addresses X-linked inheritance with variable penetrance, carrier testing and clinical evaluation for at-risk female relatives (since a substantial minority of carriers are symptomatic), and reproductive options, following molecular confirmation of the RP2 variant.

evidence.snippet: No patient with childhood-onset disease had an identifiable ellipsoid zone (EZ) after the age of 26 years at baseline or follow-up.
evidence.explanation: The near-uniform age of complete ellipsoid zone loss supports the value of regular structural monitoring.

treatments/4.description: Regular ophthalmologic follow-up with ERG, OCT (ellipsoid zone width, outer nuclear layer thickness), and BCVA monitors disease progression and identifies candidacy for future gene-therapy trials.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that this defect is a new type of congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG) of type IIf affecting the transport of CMP-sialic acid into the Golgi apparatus.
evidence.explanation: The original identification of the transporter defect as the disease lesion.

steps/1.description: Biallelic SLC35A1 variants leave the cell without a working Golgi CMP-sialic acid transporter. Truncating alleles abolish the protein; the reported missense alleles reduce transport rather than abolishing it, which is the likely reason their carriers present differently.

evidence.snippet: Slc35a1 encodes the cytidine-5'-monophosphate (CMP)-sialic acid transporter that transports CMP-sialic acid from the cytoplasm into the Golgi apparatus for sialylation.
evidence.explanation: States the transported species and its destination compartment, which is what this node claims is depleted. Marked BACKGROUND because the sentence opens the mouse study's abstract as a statement of what the gene encodes, not as one of its results. Graded OTHER rather than MODEL_ORGANISM for the same reason: no animal experiment established what the transporter carries, so MODEL_ORGANISM would assert that this mouse study measured it. IN_VITRO is not used either, because the cited paper does not say where the fact was established and this entry does not grade a source on unstated provenance.

steps/2.description: The Golgi lumen is deprived of CMP-Neu5Ac, the activated donor every sialyltransferase requires. Cytosolic sialic acid synthesis is unaffected, so the cell is not short of sialic acid; it is short of sialic acid in the compartment where it is used. That distinction is what makes dietary sialic acid an ineffective strategy here.

evidence.snippet: Patient primary fibroblasts and serum showed a considerable decrease in the amount of N- and O-glycans terminating in sialic acid.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of the hyposialylation in patient material, across both glycan classes.

evidence.snippet: We showed that SLC35A1 associates with ST3Gal4, the main α2,3-sialyltransferase acting on N-glycans. This phenomenon is compromised by the E196K (but not T156R) mutation in the SLC35A1 gene.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the second, allele-specific route to hyposialylation, and the contrast with the other missense allele that makes it allele-specific rather than general.

steps/3.description: Without the donor, sialyltransferases cannot cap glycans, and N-glycans, O-glycans and glycolipids across the cell are left without their terminal sialic acid. The p.Glu196Lys allele adds a second route to the same endpoint by decoupling the transporter from the sialyltransferase ST3Gal4.

evidence.snippet: In addition, an increased number of desialylated platelets was cleared by Küpffer cells in the liver of Plt Slc35a1–/– mice.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates hepatic clearance of desialylated platelets in the Slc35a1 conditional knockout, and names Kupffer cells as the clearing population. This is the animal evidence for the clearance arm of this node.

evidence.snippet: This leads to platelet clearance in the liver via hepatocyte Ashwell-Morell receptors, which is fundamentally different from the classical Fc-FcγR-dependent macrophage phagocytosis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the desialylation-to-hepatic-clearance mechanism, but in immune thrombocytopenia rather than in SLC35A1-CDG. Marked INDIRECT because applying it here requires the inference that platelets desialylated by a transporter defect are cleared the same way as platelets desialylated by antibody-triggered sialidase translocation.

steps/4.description: Loss of terminal sialic acid on platelet surface glycoproteins exposes the subterminal galactose that hepatic clearance receptors recognise, so circulating platelets are removed by the liver. In the conditional mouse the clearing cells are hepatic Kupffer cells. The hepatocyte Ashwell-Morell receptor route is established for desialylated platelets in immune thrombocytopenia and is the mechanism generally invoked here; it has not been shown directly in SLC35A1-CDG, so the evidence for that step is marked indirect.

evidence.snippet: megakaryocyte maturation was also impaired
evidence.explanation: The production arm of the thrombocytopenia mechanism, distinct from the clearance arm recorded on the neighbouring node.

steps/5.description: Hyposialylation also acts upstream of the circulating platelet, on its production. The conditional mouse shows both fewer bone marrow megakaryocytes and impaired maturation of the ones present, so the thrombocytopenia is a production defect as well as a clearance defect.

evidence.snippet: characterized by macrothrombocytopenia, neutropenia and complete lack of the sialyl-Lex antigen
evidence.explanation: Records the complete absence of the sialyl-Lewis-x antigen on polymorphonuclear cells. Marked BACKGROUND because the sentence is this 2016 paper's recapitulation of the authors' own 2005 clinical report, not a result of the splice-variant work it reports.

steps/6.description: Sialyl-Lewis-x is the selectin ligand that lets leukocytes roll on and adhere to activated endothelium, and its terminal sialic acid is not optional: without sialylation the ligand is not made. Its complete absence on polymorphonuclear cells was the finding that identified the index patient, and it makes the infection susceptibility an adhesion defect on top of the neutropenia rather than a consequence of low counts alone.

evidence.snippet: In the brain, two families of sialoglycans are of particular interest: gangliosides and polysialic acid.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the two brain sialoglycan families whose synthesis this node claims is deficient. Marked INDIRECT and REVIEW_SYNTHESIS: it is a review establishing what these glycans are, from which the deficiency in a sialylation-donor defect follows by inference rather than by measurement in this disease.

steps/7.description: The brain's two major sialoglycan families, gangliosides and polysialic acid on NCAM, both require the same Golgi donor. Their deficiency is the proposed basis of the neurological branch. This step is an inference from what these glycans are known to require and to do, not a measurement made in an SLC35A1-CDG brain, and no model reproducing the encephalopathy has been reported.

evidence.snippet: Mouse genetic studies and human disorders of ganglioside metabolism implicate gangliosides in axon-myelin interactions, axon stability, axon regeneration, and the modulation of nerve cell excitability.
