evidence.explanation: States what ganglioside deficiency does to neurons, from mouse genetics and other human ganglioside disorders. Marked INDIRECT because the inference to this disease's encephalopathy is a step the source does not take.

steps/8.description: Ganglioside deficiency is linked to disturbed axon-myelin interactions, axon stability and nerve cell excitability; polysialic acid deficiency to disturbed neurite outgrowth and synaptic connectivity. Together these are the proposed substrate of the developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures and encephalopathy seen in the neurological presentation.

evidence.snippet: Direct measurement of CMP-sialic acid transport into the Golgi showed a substantial decrease in overall rate of transport.
evidence.explanation: Measures the transport step itself in patient material, which is the edge from the genetic lesion to donor depletion rather than either node alone.

evidence.snippet: No complementation was obtained with either of the 2 patient alleles, whereas full restoration of the sialylated phenotype was obtained in the Lec2 cells transfected with the corresponding human wild-type transcript.
evidence.explanation: The complementation result that establishes causality: neither patient allele restores sialylation and the wild-type transcript does.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, later work from another laboratory determined one of the two variants identified by Martinez et al is very likely benign, since it was reported to be in the homozygous state in at least six unrelated healthy individuals
evidence.explanation: Graded REFUTE against the claim that the index patient's reported pair are both pathogenic. It does not dispute that the index patient had the disease, only the validity of one of the two alleles assigned to it.

evidence.snippet: Mutation analysis identified a homozygous c.303G > C (p.Gln101His) missense mutation that was heterozygous in both parents.
evidence.explanation: The second patient's genotype, homozygous missense with confirmed parental heterozygosity. This is the genotype that refutes any correlation between allele class and which clinical arm appears.

evidence.snippet: Our results suggest that three pockets in the central cavity of each transporter provide substrate specificity.
evidence.explanation: Gives the structural framework used to interpret where missense alleles sit and why they reduce rather than abolish transport.

genes/0.notes:
Encodes the only known Golgi CMP-sialic acid transporter, a multipass nucleotide-sugar transporter of the SLC35 family. Reported disease alleles across the three proven patients are the index patient's pair, homozygous p.Gln101His in the second, and p.Thr156Arg with p.Glu196Lys in the third. Structure-guided mutagenesis has mapped three substrate pockets in the central cavity, which is the framework in which missense alleles' effects on transport are interpreted.
One caveat on the index genotype: later work found that one of the two variants reported in 2005 is very likely benign, having been seen homozygous in at least six unrelated healthy individuals. The index patient's molecular diagnosis therefore rests on less than the original report implies, and this entry does not treat that genotype as an established truncating pair.

treatments/0.description: No targeted or curative therapy exists. Management is symptomatic: transfusion and bleeding precautions for thrombocytopenia, infection prophylaxis and treatment, anti-seizure medication, and developmental therapies.

evidence.snippet: sialidase inhibitors ameliorate anti-GPIbα-mediated thrombocytopenia in mice
evidence.explanation: The only evidence for this strategy, and it is in a different disease. Marked INDIRECT: transferring it to SLC35A1-CDG requires assuming a sialidase-inhibition benefit in a disorder where the sialylation never happened, which is a substantial inferential step and the reason this is curated as a candidate rather than a treatment.

treatments/1.description: A candidate strategy, not a treatment. Because the thrombocytopenia is driven in part by clearance of desialylated platelets, inhibiting the sialidase that strips the sialic acid is mechanistically rational. Sialidase inhibitors improved antibody-mediated thrombocytopenia in mice, but that was in immune thrombocytopenia, where the desialylation is enzymatic and reversible. In SLC35A1-CDG the platelets were never sialylated in the first place, so it is not obvious that blocking a sialidase would help. It has never been tested in this disorder.

open_questions/0.rationale: Across the three proven patients the arms combine differently: the second has both, the third has the neurological arm with explicitly no hematological abnormality, and the index patient has the hematologic arm with every neurological feature recorded as *not reported* rather than absent. So one of the three data points is an ascertainment gap rather than a negative finding, which is a distinction the published comparison table makes explicitly and which matters for any attempt to read a pattern off three patients. Genotype does not explain the variation: the patient with both arms is homozygous for a missense allele retaining 50% of transport activity, which is the mildest reported genotype and the broadest reported phenotype.

open_questions/1.rationale: The hematologic branch has a conditional mouse that reproduces it. The neurological branch has no model at all: the existing mouse deletes Slc35a1 only in megakaryocytes and platelets, so it cannot develop a brain phenotype. Everything downstream of the hyposialylation node on the neurological side rests on what gangliosides and polysialic acid are known to do in other settings, plus the observation that a patient with reduced Golgi sialic acid transport had an encephalopathy. That is a plausible chain, but no step of it has been measured in an SLC35A1-deficient nervous system. Recorded as a human-model mismatch rather than a plain knowledge gap because the model-system evidence that does exist covers the other branch, and its success there could be mistaken for support of the entry as a whole.

evidence.snippet: Sepsis - which is a severe life-threatening infection with organ dysfunction - initiates a complex interplay of host pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory processes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes infection as the initiating event of the host program modeled by the rest of this graph.

steps/0.description: A bacterial, viral, or fungal infection at any site - most often lung, abdomen, urinary tract, or bloodstream - releases pathogen-associated molecular patterns that engage host pattern-recognition receptors. Tissue injury at the site of infection adds damage-associated molecular patterns to the same sensing machinery. The identity of the pathogen is not what makes the syndrome; the host response to it is.

evidence.snippet: This recently implemented definition does not capture the heterogeneity or the underlying pathophysiology of the syndrome, which is characterized by concurrent unbalanced hyperinflammation and immune suppression.
evidence.explanation: Supports modeling the innate response as concurrently hyperinflammatory and immunosuppressive rather than as a single inflammatory phase.

evidence.snippet: NETosis during sepsis can be detrimental through various mechanisms, including induction of intravascular thrombosis and multiple organ failure
evidence.explanation: Supports curating neutrophil extracellular trap formation on this node: the same neutrophil effector that traps bacteria becomes injurious in sepsis, and the review names intravascular thrombosis and organ failure as its consequences, which are the two nodes downstream of this one.

steps/1.description: Innate immune cells mount a proinflammatory program with cytokine and chemokine release, complement activation, neutrophil recruitment, and reactive oxygen species production. In sepsis this response is not merely large but unbalanced: hyperinflammation and immune suppression run concurrently rather than sequentially, which is why the syndrome resists treatment framed as either simple inflammation or simple immunodeficiency.

evidence.snippet: Endothelial cells (ECs) are vascular, nonconventional immune cells that play a major role in the systemic response after bacterial infection to limit its dissemination.
evidence.explanation: Supports treating the endothelium as an active immune participant rather than a passive barrier in this node.

steps/2.description: The endothelium, acting as a nonconventional immune organ, switches to a proapoptotic, proinflammatory, proadhesive, and procoagulant phenotype. Shedding of the glycocalyx exposes adhesion molecules and procoagulant surface, increases permeability with interstitial fluid loss, and impairs vasomotor regulation.

evidence.snippet: The purpose of this review is to consider the state of oxidative stress, failure of the antioxidant systems and mitochondrial failure as the main physiopathological mechanisms leading to multiple organ dysfunction during sepsis.
evidence.explanation: States the review's framing of oxidative stress and mitochondrial failure as mechanisms of organ dysfunction, which is what this node captures.

steps/3.description: Irreversible oxidative stress injures mitochondria, so that cells cannot generate ATP even where oxygen is delivered. This cytopathic-hypoxia arm is curated as an alternative, complementary route to organ dysfunction rather than as a step in the microcirculatory chain.

evidence.snippet: Accordingly, the ISTH introduced SIC criteria in 2019 that are easy to use and require only platelet count, prothrombin time-international normalized ratio, and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment Score.
evidence.explanation: Supports the compensated sepsis-induced coagulopathy stage described in this node and names its operational measures.

evidence.snippet: Activated monocytes express tissue factor (TF) and phosphatidylserine (PS) on the surface, which initiate coagulation cascades.
evidence.explanation: Names tissue-factor-initiated coagulation as the entry into the cascade, which is the step the thrombogenesis module node this entry conforms to describes generically and which sepsis specializes to monocyte tissue factor.

evidence.snippet: Among the coagulation factors, thrombin is a critical mediator that regulates inflammation and coagulation
evidence.explanation: Identifies thrombin as the central mediator of this node, which is what makes it a conformer of the module's thrombin-driven fibrin formation node rather than only a generic coagulation abnormality.

steps/4.description: Coagulation activation with suppressed fibrinolysis produces widespread microvascular fibrin deposition and platelet consumption. This ranges from the compensated sepsis-induced coagulopathy stage, detectable with platelet count, prothrombin time-INR, and SOFA score, to overt disseminated intravascular coagulation as an end-stage consumptive state.

steps/5.description: Loss of capillary density, heterogeneous flow, and increased permeability uncouple regional perfusion from systemic hemodynamics. Tissue oxygen delivery falls even when cardiac output and arterial pressure are restored, which is the physiological reason macrocirculatory resuscitation alone does not reliably reverse organ dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: The pathophysiology of S-AKI remains incompletely understood, so most therapies remain reactive and nonspecific.
evidence.explanation: The source's explicit statement of incomplete mechanistic understanding is preserved rather than curated away.

steps/6.description: Acute kidney injury develops in roughly two thirds of patients with septic shock and is often present before medical attention is sought, making it an early sepsis-defining event rather than a late complication. It is curated as a distinct node because its mechanism is only partly the shared perfusion defect.

evidence.snippet: The immunosuppressive phase of sepsis is multifactorial and features defects in both innate and adaptive immunity, including apoptotic depletion of immune effector cells, increased numbers of regulatory T cells, decreased expression of positive co-stimulatory molecules, increased expression of negative co-stimulatory molecules, increased numbers of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and T cell exhaustion.
evidence.explanation: Supports both the lymphocyte-apoptosis annotation and the multifactorial immune-defect description of this node.

steps/7.description: Patients whose sepsis does not resolve enter a protracted immunosuppressed state marked by failure to clear the primary infection, acquisition of secondary infections, and reactivation of latent viruses. This arm accounts for much of the late mortality and is the rationale for immune-stimulating rather than anti-inflammatory therapy in selected patients.

evidence.snippet: Sepsis is now defined as infection with organ dysfunction. This definition codifies organ dysfunction using the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score.
evidence.explanation: States that organ dysfunction is definitional for sepsis and names the instrument used to operationalize it.

steps/8.description: Concurrent dysfunction across respiratory, renal, hepatic, coagulation, cardiovascular, and neurological systems, operationalized clinically as an increase in the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score. Organ dysfunction is not a complication of sepsis but the element that distinguishes sepsis from uncomplicated infection.

evidence.snippet: Sepsis should be defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
evidence.explanation: The consensus definition places the dysregulated host response, not the pathogen, causally between infection and organ dysfunction.

edges/0.description: Pattern recognition initiates the host response whose dysregulation, not the infection itself, defines sepsis.

evidence.snippet: During sepsis, ECs shift toward a proapoptotic, proinflammatory, proadhesive, and procoagulant phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Directly states the endothelial phenotype switch that this edge asserts occurs downstream of innate immune activation.

edges/1.description: Inflammatory mediators and activated leukocytes drive the endothelium into a proinflammatory, proadhesive, procoagulant state.

evidence.snippet: Patients with unresolved, prolonged sepsis enter a phase of immunosuppression that is characterized by a failure to eradicate the primary infection, the acquisition of lethal secondary infections and/or the reactivation of numerous latent viruses.
evidence.explanation: Supports the immunosuppressive arm as a downstream consequence of the same dysregulated host response.

edges/2.description: The anti-inflammatory arm of the same host program, running concurrently, produces a protracted immunosuppressed state in patients whose sepsis does not resolve.

evidence.snippet: One of the pivotal factors in these processes is the increase of reactive species accompanied by the failure of the antioxidant systems, leading to a state of irreversible oxidative stress and mitochondrial failure.
evidence.explanation: States the oxidative route from the inflammatory response to mitochondrial failure that this edge represents.

edges/3.description: Reactive species generated by the inflammatory response overwhelm antioxidant capacity and injure mitochondria.

evidence.snippet: The pathophysiology of sepsis-associated DIC is multifactorial, and in addition to coagulation activation with suppressed fibrinolysis, multiple inflammatory responses are initiated by activated leukocytes, platelets, and vascular endothelial cells as part of thromboinflammation.
evidence.explanation: Names endothelial cells among the drivers of the thromboinflammatory state this edge points to.

edges/4.description: The procoagulant endothelial surface, together with activated leukocytes and platelets, drives coagulation activation with suppressed fibrinolysis.

evidence.snippet: In addition, glycocalyx damage and vascular tone dysfunction impair microcirculatory blood flow, leading to organ injury and, potentially, life-threatening organ failure.
evidence.explanation: Directly asserts the glycocalyx-to-microcirculation causal step modeled by this edge.

edges/5.description: Glycocalyx damage and loss of vascular tone regulation directly impair microcirculatory blood flow.

evidence.snippet: However, DIC is not merely a decompensated coagulation disorder, but also includes early stages with systemic activation in coagulation.
evidence.explanation: Supports systemic coagulation activation as an early, ongoing process rather than only a terminal event. The abstract does not quantify the flow-obstruction contribution, so the microcirculatory consequence is inferred rather than stated here.

edges/6.description: Microvascular fibrin deposition obstructs capillary flow and compounds the perfusion defect caused by endothelial dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: In addition, glycocalyx damage and vascular tone dysfunction impair microcirculatory blood flow, leading to organ injury and, potentially, life-threatening organ failure.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly carries microcirculatory impairment through to organ injury and organ failure.

edges/7.description: Sustained hypoperfusion of multiple vascular beds produces the organ dysfunction that defines sepsis.

evidence.snippet: Possible pathogenic mechanisms to explain S-AKI include microcirculatory dysfunction, a dysregulated inflammatory response, and cellular metabolic reprogramming.
evidence.explanation: Names microcirculatory dysfunction as a pathogenic mechanism of sepsis-associated AKI; the source's own hedging is preserved in the node description.

edges/8.description: The kidney is among the earliest and most frequently injured organs, with microcirculatory dysfunction one of the proposed pathogenic routes.

evidence.snippet: The loss of the redox balance, together with a systemic inflammatory response during sepsis, can lead to progressive and irreversible mitochondrial failure, energy depletion, hypoxia, septic shock, severe sepsis, multiple organ dysfunction and death of the patient.
evidence.explanation: Directly asserts the mitochondrial-failure-to-multiple-organ-dysfunction step this edge represents.

edges/9.description: Energy depletion at the cellular level produces organ dysfunction independently of, and additively to, perfusion failure.

evidence.snippet: Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (S-AKI) is a common and life-threatening complication in hospitalized and critically ill patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes S-AKI as a common, life-threatening organ-level complication of sepsis.

edges/10.description: Renal dysfunction is one component of, and a major contributor to mortality within, the multiple organ dysfunction that defines sepsis.

evidence.snippet: we recommend administering antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 h of recognition
evidence.explanation: Recommendation 12 states the immediacy of antimicrobial administration directly, rather than leaving it to be inferred from sepsis being an emergency.

treatments/0.description: Prompt administration of appropriate antimicrobials is the intervention directed at the initiating infection. Guidelines recommend immediate administration for confirmed or very likely sepsis, and a rapid assessment of infectious versus non-infectious causes when sepsis is only possible and shock is absent.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Antimicrobial therapy reduces pathogen burden and therefore the PAMP load driving the host response, acting at the trigger node of the graph.

evidence.snippet: Source control may include drainage of an abscess, debriding infected necrotic tissue, removal of a potentially infected device
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the interventions this treatment covers, which is what the generic NCIT action term cannot express.

treatments/1.description: Drainage of an abscess, debridement of infected necrotic tissue, or removal of an infected device is the second intervention directed at the initiating infection. The guideline recommends rapidly identifying or excluding an anatomical focus that requires emergent source control, and implementing it as soon as medically and logistically practical.

evidence.snippet: Clinical experience suggests that without adequate source control, many severe presentations will not stabilise or improve despite rapid resuscitation and provision of appropriate antimicrobials.
evidence.explanation: States that antimicrobials and resuscitation do not substitute for source control, which is why this intervention is curated as acting on the trigger node in its own right rather than as part of antimicrobial therapy.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Removing or draining the focus eliminates the source of the pathogen- and damage-associated molecular patterns that drive the host response, acting on the same trigger node as antimicrobial therapy by a different route.

evidence.snippet: the use of crystalloids as first-line fluid for resuscitation in sepsis and septic shock
evidence.explanation: States the guideline's first-line fluid choice recorded in this treatment.

evidence.snippet: For patients with sepsis induced hypoperfusion or septic shock we suggest that at least 30 mL/kg of intravenous (IV) crystalloid fluid should be given within the first 3 h of resuscitation
evidence.explanation: Supplies the volume and timing. The guideline itself grades this a weak recommendation on low-quality evidence.

treatments/2.description: Intravenous crystalloid is the first-line resuscitation fluid for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, with at least 30 mL/kg suggested within the first three hours. This addresses the macrocirculatory deficit and does not by itself correct microcirculatory or bioenergetic failure.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Volume expansion targets the hypoperfusion node, though the guideline grades the specific volume recommendation weakly.

evidence.snippet: strong recommendation for norepinephrine as the first-line agent
evidence.explanation: States the guideline panel's first-line vasopressor recommendation recorded here.

treatments/3.description: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor for septic shock, restoring mean arterial pressure when fluid resuscitation alone is insufficient.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Vasopressor support restores perfusion pressure across vascular beds whose tone regulation has been lost.

evidence.snippet: For adults with septic shock on norepinephrine with inadequate MAP levels, we suggest adding vasopressin instead of escalating the dose of norepinephrine
evidence.explanation: Recommendation 38, which states the escalation step this treatment records. The guideline grades it weak on moderate-quality evidence.

evidence.snippet: Unlike most vasopressors, vasopressin is not titrated to response, but it is usually administered at a fixed dose of 0.03 units/min for the treatment of septic shock.
evidence.explanation: Supports the fixed-dose administration described here, which is what separates it from the titrated catecholamines.

treatments/4.description: For septic shock on norepinephrine with an inadequate mean arterial pressure, the guideline suggests adding vasopressin rather than escalating the norepinephrine dose. Unlike the catecholamines it is not titrated to response but given at a fixed dose, and it raises pressure through V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle rather than through adrenergic receptors.

evidence.snippet: binding of V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle resulting in increased arterial blood pressure
evidence.explanation: States the receptor mechanism by which this treatment acts on the perfusion node, and the one that distinguishes it from norepinephrine.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Vasopressin restores perfusion pressure by a non-adrenergic route, which is what makes it an addition to norepinephrine rather than a substitute for a higher dose of it.

evidence.snippet: The optimal dose, timing of initiation, and duration of corticosteroids remain uncertain; recent RCTs used 200 mg per day of IV hydrocortisone in divided doses
evidence.explanation: Supplies both the dose recorded in this treatment and the guideline's own statement that dose, timing, and duration are unsettled.

evidence.snippet: A meta-analysis conducted for this guideline revision (Supplementary Appendix 5) found an increase vasopressor-free days (MD 1.5 days; 95% CI 0.8- 3.11 days)
evidence.explanation: Gives the effect size the weak recommendation rests on. The guideline reports the same analysis finding increased neuromuscular weakness and no clear mortality effect, which is why the description does not claim a survival benefit.

evidence.snippet: a recent re-analysis of the aforementioned VANISH trial provided further evidence that corticosteroid exposure may be associated with increased mortality among adult septic shock endotype A patients
evidence.explanation: Supports the heterogeneity caveat recorded in this treatment's notes. The average effect the guideline's recommendation rests on need not be the effect in a given transcriptomic endotype.

treatments/5.description: For septic shock with an ongoing vasopressor requirement the guideline suggests IV corticosteroids, in practice hydrocortisone 200 mg/day in divided doses. This is the intervention aimed at the dysregulated inflammatory arm of the host response rather than at perfusion or at the pathogen. The evidence behind it is faster shock resolution and more vasopressor-free days, without a clear effect on mortality, and the optimal dose, timing, and duration remain unsettled.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: Glucocorticoid therapy is directed at the dysregulated inflammatory arm of the host response, and is the only intervention curated here that acts on that node. The cited evidence is clinical, being shock resolution and vasopressor-free days, and does not measure the activity of this node directly. The link therefore records where the drug is understood to act, not a demonstrated change in the node.

evidence.snippet: The pathophysiology of sepsis-associated DIC is multifactorial, and in addition to coagulation activation with suppressed fibrinolysis, multiple inflammatory responses are initiated by activated leukocytes, platelets, and vascular endothelial cells as part of thromboinflammation.
evidence.explanation: States the coupled coagulation-inflammation mechanism that this hypothesis group organizes the main causal graph around.

evidence.snippet: In addition, glycocalyx damage and vascular tone dysfunction impair microcirculatory blood flow, leading to organ injury and, potentially, life-threatening organ failure.
evidence.explanation: Links the endothelial arm of the model to microcirculatory failure and organ dysfunction.

hypotheses/0.description: Pathogen- and damage-associated molecular patterns drive dysregulated innate immune activation. Activated leukocytes, platelets, and endothelium engage in reciprocal amplification, degrading the endothelial glycocalyx, raising permeability, and activating coagulation while suppressing fibrinolysis. The resulting thromboinflammation obstructs and dysregulates the microcirculation, causing tissue hypoperfusion and organ dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: The loss of the redox balance, together with a systemic inflammatory response during sepsis, can lead to progressive and irreversible mitochondrial failure, energy depletion, hypoxia, septic shock, severe sepsis, multiple organ dysfunction and death of the patient.
evidence.explanation: States the redox/mitochondrial route to multiple organ dysfunction that defines this hypothesis group.

hypotheses/1.description: An alternative, non-exclusive account holds that organ dysfunction in sepsis is driven less by perfusion failure than by a cellular inability to use oxygen. Overwhelming reactive species production with failure of antioxidant systems produces mitochondrial injury, so that organs fail despite adequate delivery of oxygen. This is offered as a complementary rather than competing mechanism, and it predicts that restoring macrocirculatory flow alone will not reverse organ dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: To date, no clinical cohort study has directly established a causal link between GRP78 dysregulation and sepsis incidence or mortality in patients with cancer.
evidence.explanation: The review's own statement that the causal link is unestablished is the primary justification for curating this as a KNOWLEDGE_GAP rather than as a mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Patients with a history of cancer are at increased risk for acquiring and subsequently dying from sepsis, compared to the general population, although incidence and fatality rates are decreasing over time.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the excess sepsis risk in cancer is real, which is what makes the unexplained mechanistic residue worth tracking as a gap.

evidence.snippet: Surprisingly, cancer and sepsis share many immune defects, and the remarkable success of new immunotherapeutics in cancer has highlighted the potential for this new approach in sepsis.
evidence.explanation: Independent support that cancer and sepsis share immune-defect biology, which is the general premise the GRP78 hypothesis tries to make specific.

open_questions/0.rationale: Patients with a history of cancer carry a large excess risk of acquiring and dying from sepsis, and sepsis and cancer are independently known to share immune defects, which makes a cancer-specific susceptibility mechanism biologically plausible. A 2026 narrative review proposes GRP78/HSPA5 dysregulation as that mechanism, acting both as a pathogen entry cofactor and as a secreted immunosuppressive signal. The proposal is explicitly hypothesis-level: the review states that no clinical cohort study has established a causal link, and that its argument rests on in vitro work, animal models, and non-oncologic sepsis cohorts. It is therefore curated here as an open gap attached to the trigger and immunosuppression nodes, rather than as a curated causal edge, a GRP78 pathophysiology node, or a separate cancer-associated sepsis disease entry - any of which would assert more than the evidence supports.

evidence.snippet: Knowledge of the molecular processes associated with the development of oxidative stress should facilitate the development of effective therapies and better prognosis for patients with sepsis and organ dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: The review frames effective bioenergetically-targeted therapy as a future prospect, which is the unresolved half of this question. The sentence supports the gap by implication rather than stating it.

open_questions/1.rationale: Both routes to multiple organ dysfunction are curated here with supporting evidence, and they are not mutually exclusive. Neither source quantifies the relative contribution, and there is no validated bedside measure that separates a perfusion-limited from an oxygen-utilization-limited patient. This matters therapeutically: resuscitation strategies target the former, and would not be expected to reverse the latter.

evidence.snippet: All mutations resulted in reduced or absent SGPL1 protein and/or enzyme activity. Overexpression of cDNA representing SGPL1 mutations resulted in subcellular mislocalization of SGPL1.
evidence.explanation: Functional characterisation of the disease alleles as loss of function.

evidence.snippet: Sphingosine-1-phosphate lyase (SPL) is an intracellular enzyme that controls the final step in the sphingolipid degradative pathway, the only biochemical pathway for removal of sphingolipids.
evidence.explanation: Review establishing why loss of this single enzyme blocks all sphingolipid removal.

steps/1.description: Biallelic SGPL1 variants abolish or severely reduce sphingosine-1-phosphate lyase, the pyridoxal 5'-phosphate-dependent endoplasmic reticulum enzyme that irreversibly cleaves S1P into hexadecenal and phosphoethanolamine. Missense alleles reduce activity and can mislocalise the protein; truncating alleles abolish it. Because the lyase guards the only exit from sphingolipid metabolism, its loss blocks the entire degradative pathway.

evidence.snippet: Mass spectrometric analysis of patient dermal fibroblasts revealed significantly elevated levels of sphingosine-1-phosphate, sphingosine, ceramide species and sphingomyelin when compared to control.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the breadth of sphingolipid accumulation in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: Metabolic stable isotope labeling revealed that SPL deficiency does not invariably result in S1P accumulation. Instead, SPL-deficient cells maintain near-normal S1P levels through (a) feedback regulation of de novo sphingolipid synthesis via the ORMDL-ceramide axis and (b) increased diversion of excess ceramides into glycosphingolipids.
evidence.explanation: Qualifies the accumulation model: compensatory rerouting buffers S1P until the sphingolipid load exceeds it.

steps/2.description: Without the lyase, S1P, sphingosine, ceramides and sphingomyelin accumulate in plasma, urine and cells. S1P is a bioactive signalling lipid acting through five G-protein-coupled S1P receptors and intracellular targets, so the accumulation is not inert storage but excessive signalling. Metabolic labelling shows that cells partly buffer S1P by feedback-inhibiting de novo synthesis and diverting ceramide into glycosphingolipids; pathological intracellular S1P accumulation emerges when these compensations are overwhelmed, and Sgpl1-null kidneys show pronounced S1P enrichment and urinary excretion.

evidence.snippet: Immunofluorescence revealed SGPL1 expression in mouse podocytes and mesangial cells. Knockdown of Sgpl1 in rat mesangial cells inhibited cell migration, which was partially rescued by VPC23109, an S1P receptor antagonist.
evidence.explanation: Localises the enzyme to the glomerular cells and shows an S1P-receptor-dependent cellular defect.

evidence.snippet: Pharmacological ROCK inhibition with fasudil mitigated renal cytoskeletal defects in Sgpl1-/- and Sgpl1rosa+fl/fl mice and partially restored epithelial architecture.
evidence.explanation: Pharmacological rescue confirms Rho/ROCK as the mediator of the cytoskeletal lesion.

steps/3.description: SGPL1 is expressed in podocytes and mesangial cells. Excess S1P drives Rho/ROCK hyperactivation, disorganising the podocyte actin cytoskeleton; ultrastructure in the R222Q mouse shows foot process effacement and podocyte loss, and knockdown in mesangial cells impairs migration in an S1P-receptor-dependent manner. This is the disorder-specific initiating podocyte insult of the conserved nephrotic podocytopathy chain.

evidence.snippet: buildup of sphingolipid intermediates, including its bioactive substrate, sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), the latter causing lymphopenia, a hallmark of the disease
evidence.explanation: Attributes the lymphopenia to S1P accumulation.

evidence.snippet: S1P is an intracellular and extracellular signaling molecule involved in angiogenesis, vascular maturation, and immunity.
evidence.explanation: Background for the immune role of S1P signalling disrupted in the disease.

steps/4.description: Lymphocyte egress from thymus and lymph nodes follows an S1P gradient sensed by S1P receptor 1; loss of the lyase abolishes the gradient, trapping lymphocytes in lymphoid organs. T-cell lymphopenia is a near-universal feature, and although some T-cell function persists, patients have recurrent viral, fungal and bacterial infections and sepsis is a leading cause of death.

evidence.snippet: SGPL1_KO upregulated differentiation markers, while SGPL1_OE upregulated basal and proliferative markers. The advanced differentiation of SGPL1_KO was confirmed by 3D organotypic models that also presented with a thickened and retained stratum corneum and a breakdown of E-cadherin junctions.
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration of the keratinocyte differentiation and barrier defect in a human skin model.

steps/5.description: In SGPL1-knockout keratinocytes and organotypic skin equivalents, accumulated S1P, sphingosine and ceramide drive premature differentiation, a thickened retained stratum corneum, altered calcium-signalling gene expression and loss of E-cadherin junctions, reproducing the ichthyosis, acanthosis and hyperpigmentation seen in most patients with a reported skin phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Total mitochondrial volume was reduced in both S1P lyase deficient patient and HeLa cell lines. Mitochondrial dynamics and parameters of oxidative phosphorylation were altered when compared to matched controls, though differentially across the cell lines.
evidence.explanation: Primary measurement of the mitochondrial phenotype in patient-derived and engineered cells.

steps/6.description: Patient fibroblasts and SGPL1-knockout HeLa cells show reduced total mitochondrial volume and altered mitochondrial dynamics and oxidative phosphorylation parameters, consistent with sphingolipid-induced mitochondrial dysregulation. Its contribution to organ pathology and to phenotype severity is proposed but not yet established.

evidence.snippet: STAT3 pathway activation and elevated proinflammatory and profibrogenic cytokines observed in KO kidneys were attenuated by treatment.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the inflammatory and profibrotic signalling in the knockout kidney that underlies glomerulosclerosis.

evidence.snippet: Kidney biopsy showed focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in 2 patients and diffuse mesangial sclerosis in one patient. Steroids were given to 3 patients, but they did not respond. All 6 patients progressed to chronic kidney disease
evidence.explanation: Histology and steroid resistance in a clinical series.

steps/7.description: Podocyte injury breaks the size- and charge-selective filtration barrier, producing steroid-resistant nephrotic-range proteinuria. Kidney biopsies show focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (including the collapsing variant) or diffuse mesangial sclerosis, and Sgpl1-knockout kidneys show STAT3 activation with proinflammatory and profibrogenic cytokine elevation. Progression to end-stage kidney disease ranges from under a month to five years after onset of proteinuria.

evidence.snippet: Sgpl1-/- mice displayed disrupted adrenocortical zonation and defective expression of steroidogenic enzymes as well as renal histology in keeping with a glomerular phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Knockout adrenal histology establishing the tissue-level lesion.

evidence.snippet: Reduced cortisol output in response to progesterone stimulation was observed in two patient dermal fibroblast cell lines.
evidence.explanation: Patient-cell steroidogenic defect corroborating the adrenal phenotype.

steps/8.description: Sgpl1-null mice show disrupted adrenocortical zonation and defective expression of steroidogenic enzymes, and patient fibroblasts show reduced cortisol output after progesterone stimulation. In patients this manifests as glucocorticoid deficiency in early childhood, with mineralocorticoid deficiency in about a third, and prenatally detectable adrenal calcification in some. The intermediate steps by which sphingolipid accumulation disrupts adrenal development and steroidogenesis are not established.

evidence.snippet: In addition, the products of the SPL reaction have biological functions including regulation of autophagic flux, which is important in axonal and neuronal integrity.
evidence.explanation: Review of the proposed neuronal mechanisms, including the autophagy role of the lyase products.

evidence.snippet: Analysis reveals recurring patterns of features in affected patients, including isolated callosal dysgenesis and prominent involvement of the globus pallidus, thalamus, and dentate nucleus, with progressive atrophy and worsening of brain lesions.
evidence.explanation: Imaging evidence for the progressive deep grey nuclei and callosal lesions.

steps/9.description: Accumulated sphingolipids perturb membrane rafts and myelin, and loss of the lyase's products impairs autophagic flux important for axonal integrity. Clinically this produces a spectrum from callosal dysgenesis and microcephaly to progressive involvement of the globus pallidus, thalamus and dentate nucleus with atrophy, cranial nerve deficits, sensorineural hearing loss, peripheral motor and sensory neuropathy, seizures and developmental regression.

evidence.snippet: Kidney disorders (42, 80.8%) were mainly in the form of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS)
evidence.explanation: Systematic review frequency of kidney involvement, predominantly SRNS.

evidence.snippet: Sphingosine phosphate lyase insufficiency syndrome (SPLIS) is characterized by varying combinations of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (ranging from nonimmune fetal hydrops to adolescent onset)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews summary of the renal phenotype and its onset range.

steps/10.description: The most common presentation; onset ranges from congenital (including in utero) to adolescence, does not respond to corticosteroids, and progresses to kidney failure in a large proportion of patients.

evidence.snippet: Kidney biopsy showed focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in 2 patients and diffuse mesangial sclerosis in one patient.
evidence.explanation: Biopsy findings in a clinical series.

steps/11.description: The usual biopsy lesion, including the aggressive collapsing variant; diffuse mesangial sclerosis is also reported.

evidence.snippet: progressed to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in 19 (36.5%) patients at a median (IQR) age of 6 (1.4-42.6) months
evidence.explanation: Quantifies ESKD frequency and timing.

steps/12.description: Progression to end-stage kidney disease occurs in over a third of patients, at a median age of 6 months, and is a leading cause of death.

evidence.snippet: The most prevalent clinical feature was endocrinopathies, including primary adrenal insufficiency (PAI) (71.2%) and hypothyroidism (32.7%).
evidence.explanation: Systematic review frequency of PAI.

evidence.snippet: Glucocorticoid insufficiency in early childhood is the most common endocrine manifestation affecting 64% of the 50 patients reported with SPLIS, and a third of these individuals have additional mineralocorticoid deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Endocrine case series quantifying glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency.

evidence.snippet: The patient presented with hypoglycemia and seizures at age 2 years and was ultimately diagnosed with PAI (isolated glucocorticoid deficiency).
evidence.explanation: Isolated glucocorticoid deficiency as the presenting feature in an R222Q homozygote.

steps/13.description: Glucocorticoid insufficiency in early childhood is the most common endocrine manifestation; about a third of affected individuals also have mineralocorticoid deficiency. Adrenal insufficiency can be the sole presenting feature, particularly with the R222Q allele, and may present with hypoglycaemia and seizures.

evidence.snippet: We identified two unrelated consanguineous families with three children affected by the rare association of congenital nephrotic syndrome (CNS) diagnosed in the first days of life, of hypogonadism, and of prenatally detected adrenal calcifications, associated with congenital adrenal insufficiency in one case.
evidence.explanation: Original description of prenatal adrenal calcification in SGPL1 deficiency.

steps/14.description: Prenatally or neonatally detected adrenal calcifications are a distinctive feature that can be the first clinical indication of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: the latter causing lymphopenia, a hallmark of the disease
evidence.explanation: Identifies lymphopenia as a hallmark feature.

evidence.snippet: Patients with SPLIS exhibit lymphopenia, nephrosis, adrenal insufficiency, and/or neurological defects.
evidence.explanation: Lists lymphopenia among the core manifestations.

steps/15.description: T-cell lymphopenia is a hallmark, reflecting failure of S1P-gradient-dependent lymphocyte egress; some T-cell function usually persists.

evidence.snippet: Three patients had hypothyroidism, 2 had ichthyosis, 4 had immunodeficiency, 5 had neurological findings, and 2 had genitourinary system anomalies.
evidence.explanation: Frequency of immunodeficiency and other extrarenal features in a clinical series.

evidence.snippet: Twenty-six (49.1%) patients with available outcome were deceased at a median (IQR) age of 5 (1.5-30.5) months, mostly following ESKD (23%) or sepsis/septic shock (23%).
evidence.explanation: Sepsis as a leading cause of death reflects the clinical impact of the immunodeficiency.

steps/16.description: Immunodeficiency with recurrent infections is reported in a majority of well-characterised patients, and sepsis or septic shock accounts for about a quarter of deaths.

evidence.snippet: Where a skin phenotype is reported, 94% had abnormalities such as ichthyosis, acanthosis, and hyperpigmentation.
evidence.explanation: Frequency of skin abnormalities among patients with a reported skin phenotype.

evidence.snippet: In 7 families with SRNS and facultative ichthyosis, adrenal insufficiency, immunodeficiency, and neurological defects, we identified 9 different recessive mutations in SGPL1
evidence.explanation: Ichthyosis as a facultative feature in the discovery cohort.

steps/17.description: Ichthyosis, acanthosis and hyperpigmentation are reported in the large majority of patients in whom the skin was examined; hyperpigmentation may also reflect adrenal insufficiency.

evidence.snippet: neurologic abnormalities (cranial nerve deficits, developmental delay, regression/progression, and peripheral motor and sensory neuropathy)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews enumeration of the neurological features.

evidence.snippet: prominent involvement of the globus pallidus, thalamus, and dentate nucleus, with progressive atrophy and worsening of brain lesions
evidence.explanation: Progressive imaging changes underlying regression.

steps/18.description: Neurological involvement, present in about half of patients, ranges from developmental delay to progressive regression with deep grey nuclei atrophy.

evidence.snippet: The latter can include sensorineural hearing loss, cranial nerve defects, peripheral neuropathy, abnormal brain development, seizures and/or neurodegeneration.
evidence.explanation: Review listing cranial nerve defects among the neurological manifestations.

steps/19.description: Cranial nerve deficits, including ptosis, ophthalmoplegia and facial weakness, are a recognised neurological feature.

evidence.snippet: The latter can include sensorineural hearing loss, cranial nerve defects, peripheral neuropathy, abnormal brain development, seizures and/or neurodegeneration.
evidence.explanation: Review listing sensorineural hearing loss among the neurological manifestations.

evidence.snippet: neurologic abnormalities (cranial nerve deficits, developmental delay, regression/progression, and peripheral motor and sensory neuropathy)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists peripheral motor and sensory neuropathy.

steps/21.description: Peripheral motor and sensory neuropathy is part of the neurological spectrum.

evidence.snippet: The latter can include sensorineural hearing loss, cranial nerve defects, peripheral neuropathy, abnormal brain development, seizures and/or neurodegeneration.
evidence.explanation: Review listing seizures among the neurological manifestations.

evidence.snippet: MR imaging findings of abnormal deep gray nuclei, microcephaly, or callosal dysgenesis in an infant or young child exhibiting other typical clinical features of sphingosine-1-phosphate lyase insufficiency syndrome should trigger prompt genetic testing for SGPL1 mutations.
evidence.explanation: Neuroradiological series naming microcephaly among the recurring findings.

evidence.snippet: Analysis reveals recurring patterns of features in affected patients, including isolated callosal dysgenesis
evidence.explanation: Neuroradiological series identifying callosal dysgenesis as a recurring pattern.

steps/24.description: Isolated callosal dysgenesis is one of the recurring MRI patterns.

evidence.snippet: The levels of SGPL1 substrates, S1P, and sphingosine were markedly increased in the patients' blood and fibroblasts, as determined by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry.
evidence.explanation: Directly links loss of the enzyme to substrate accumulation in patients.

evidence.snippet: In vivo, Sgpl1-/- mice had pronounced urinary S1P excretion and renal S1P enrichment, accompanied by cytoskeletal disorganization and impaired epithelial morphogenesis. Mechanistically, we identify aberrant Rho/ROCK signaling as a key mediator of S1P-driven cytoskeletal dysregulation.
evidence.explanation: Links renal S1P accumulation to the cytoskeletal lesion via Rho/ROCK signalling.

evidence.snippet: Inactivating mutations of SGPL1-the gene encoding SPL-lead to a deficiency of its downstream products, and buildup of sphingolipid intermediates, including its bioactive substrate, sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), the latter causing lymphopenia, a hallmark of the disease.
evidence.explanation: States that S1P buildup is the cause of the lymphopenia.

evidence.snippet: Loss of SGPL1 caused an accumulation of S1P, sphingosine, and ceramides, while its overexpression caused a reduction of these species.
evidence.explanation: Keratinocyte knockout reproduces the sphingolipid accumulation upstream of the differentiation phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Accumulation of sphingolipid intermediates, as seen with loss of function mutations in SGPL1, has been implicated in mitochondrial dysregulation, including alterations in mitochondrial membrane potentials and initiation of mitochondrial apoptosis.
evidence.explanation: Frames sphingolipid accumulation as the trigger for the mitochondrial changes measured in the study.

evidence.snippet: SPL guards the only exit point for sphingolipid metabolism, and its inactivation leads to accumulation of various types of sphingolipids which have biophysical roles in plasma membrane rafts and myelin, and signaling roles in cell cycle progression, vesicular trafficking, cell migration, and programmed cell death.
evidence.explanation: Review connecting sphingolipid accumulation to membrane, myelin and neuronal signalling roles.

evidence.snippet: Ultrastructural analysis and super-resolution microscopy showed podocyte loss and foot process effacement. Transcriptional profiling revealed a pattern of cytokine upregulation and extracellular matrix remodeling.
evidence.explanation: Podocyte loss and effacement accompany proteinuria and glomerulosclerosis in the R222Q model.

evidence.snippet: Kidney disorders (42, 80.8%) were mainly in the form of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) and progressed to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in 19 (36.5%) patients at a median (IQR) age of 6 (1.4-42.6) months.
evidence.explanation: Documents progression from SRNS to kidney failure in over a third of patients.

evidence.snippet: In 7 families with SRNS and facultative ichthyosis, adrenal insufficiency, immunodeficiency, and neurological defects, we identified 9 different recessive mutations in SGPL1, which encodes sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) lyase. All mutations resulted in reduced or absent SGPL1 protein and/or enzyme activity.
evidence.explanation: One of the three simultaneous 2017 gene-discovery reports establishing SGPL1 as causative.

evidence.snippet: In this work, we have identified 4 different homozygous mutations, c.665G>A (p.R222Q), c.1633_1635delTTC (p.F545del), c.261+1G>A (p.S65Rfs*6), and c.7dupA (p.S3Kfs*11), in 5 families with the condition.
evidence.explanation: Independent simultaneous gene-discovery report in the adrenal-insufficiency cohort.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in SGPL1 (10q22.1; sphingosine-1-phosphate lyase 1) cause SPLIS. More than 45 disease-associated variants have been reported, including missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice-site and in-frame deletion alleles; all tested alleles reduce or abolish protein and/or enzyme activity, and several missense variants mislocalise the protein. The recurrent p.Arg222Gln (c.665G>A) allele accounts for roughly 20-30% of patients, is associated with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency and a milder course, and is pyridoxine-responsive in vitro and in some patients.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate the first potential targeted therapy for SPLIS and suggest that 30% of SPLIS patients might respond to cofactor supplementation.
evidence.explanation: First report of clinical and biochemical response to B6.

evidence.snippet: Neurological improvement, plasma S1P normalization, and increased SPL activity in patient-derived fibroblasts were observed after pyridoxine supplementation in a patient with R222Q-variant SPLIS.
evidence.explanation: Clinical response in an R222Q patient, corroborated by the R222Q mouse model.

evidence.snippet: Targeted therapy: Vitamin B6 supplementation.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management recommendation.

treatments/0.description: Targeted therapy for patients with pyridoxine-responsive alleles, notably R222Q: pyridoxal 5'-phosphate stabilises and augments the residual mutant enzyme, lowering sphingolipid biomarkers and improving neurological status in responders. It is recommended by GeneReviews and is limited to patients with a susceptible allele.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Cofactor supplementation partially restores activity of destabilised missense SGPL1 variants.

evidence.snippet: assess primary adrenal function every six to 12 months and before any major procedure
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews surveillance guidance underpinning replacement therapy.

evidence.snippet: While endocrinopathy in the syndrome generally presents in infancy, late-onset disease also occurs. Screening for these is therefore warranted both at diagnosis and through follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Rationale for ongoing endocrine screening and replacement.

treatments/1.description: Standard hormone replacement for primary adrenal insufficiency, with stress dosing; adrenal function should be reassessed every 6-12 months and before major procedures because adrenal insufficiency can emerge late.

evidence.snippet: annual free thyroxine and thyroid-stimulating hormone
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews surveillance recommendation for thyroid function.

treatments/2.description: Replacement for the primary hypothyroidism seen in about a third of patients; annual thyroid function testing is recommended.

evidence.snippet: Kidney transplantation significantly extended survival outcomes.
evidence.explanation: Natural history evidence for the survival benefit of transplantation.

evidence.snippet: All 6 patients progressed to chronic kidney disease; 5 required kidney replacement therapy (KRT) at a median age of 6 months. Deceased kidney transplantation was performed in one patient.
evidence.explanation: Clinical series documenting kidney replacement therapy and transplantation.

treatments/3.description: Dialysis and kidney transplantation for end-stage kidney disease; transplantation significantly extends survival and the nephropathy does not recur in the graft, because the enzyme defect is systemic but the glomerular lesion is intrinsic to the native podocytes.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Nephrotoxic medications; medications that require renal excretion (for individuals with renal insufficiency); live vaccines; exposure to infectious agents; transfusion products that have not been irradiated.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews list of agents and circumstances to avoid.

treatments/4.description: Because of T-cell lymphopenia, GeneReviews advises avoiding live vaccines, exposure to infectious agents and non-irradiated transfusion products, with immunological reassessment every 6-12 months; nephrotoxic drugs should also be avoided.

evidence.snippet: Treatment dramatically prolonged survival and prevented nephrosis, neurodevelopmental delay, anemia, and hypercholesterolemia.
evidence.explanation: Proof-of-concept efficacy in the knockout mouse.

evidence.snippet: Over time, treated mice developed nephrosis and glomerulosclerosis, which likely resulted in their demise. Our overall findings show that AAV-SPL 2.0 performs equal to or better than AAV-SPL. However, improved kidney targeting may be necessary to achieve maximally optimized gene therapy as a potentially lifesaving SPLIS treatment.
evidence.explanation: Second-generation vector results and the remaining kidney-targeting limitation.

treatments/5.description: Systemic AAV9-SGPL1 given to newborn Sgpl1-knockout mice dramatically prolonged survival and prevented nephrosis, neurodevelopmental delay, anaemia and hypercholesterolaemia; a CAG-promoter version (AAV-SPL 2.0) performs at least as well but treated mice eventually develop glomerulosclerosis, indicating that improved kidney targeting is needed. Proposed as a universal, genotype-independent therapy.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: Restores enzyme expression and activity, correcting the metabolic block at its source.

evidence.snippet: Pharmacological ROCK inhibition with fasudil mitigated renal cytoskeletal defects in Sgpl1-/- and Sgpl1rosa+fl/fl mice and partially restored epithelial architecture.
evidence.explanation: Preclinical efficacy of ROCK inhibition on the renal lesion.

treatments/6.description: Pharmacological Rho-kinase inhibition mitigated renal cytoskeletal defects and partially restored epithelial architecture in Sgpl1-deficient mice, identifying S1P-driven Rho/ROCK hyperactivation as a tractable downstream target independent of genotype.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: Blocks the Rho/ROCK signalling through which excess S1P disorganises the renal epithelial cytoskeleton.

evidence.snippet: It is appropriate to clarify the genetic status of apparently asymptomatic older and younger at-risk sibs of an affected individual in order to identify as early as possible those who would benefit from prompt initiation of treatment and awareness of agents/circumstances to avoid.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommendation on evaluation of relatives at risk.

treatments/7.description: Autosomal recessive counselling with a 25% recurrence risk; GeneReviews recommends clarifying the genetic status of at-risk sibs so that treatment and precautions can begin before symptoms.

evidence.snippet: Other manifestations of SPLIS include nephrotic syndrome, neuronal defects, and adrenal insufficiency, but their pathogenesis remains unknown.
evidence.explanation: Authors' explicit statement of the mechanistic gap.

open_questions/0.rationale: The lymphopenia is mechanistically explained by loss of the S1P egress gradient and the podocyte lesion by Rho/ROCK hyperactivation, but the adrenal and neurological pathogenesis remains unknown; recent data showing that S1P does not invariably accumulate in SPL-deficient cells make the tissue-specific trigger an open question.

evidence.snippet: SPLR222Q mice fed pyridoxine-enriched chow lacked obvious phenotypes.
evidence.explanation: Shows the hypomorphic model's phenotype is conditional on cofactor availability.

open_questions/1.rationale: The null mouse models the severe infantile end of the spectrum but cannot reproduce the milder hypomorphic disease; the pyridoxine-dependent R222Q knock-in, which is phenotypically silent on B6-enriched chow, is the first model of a hypomorphic allele and shows that diet can gate the phenotype, so extrapolation from the null to the common human genotype needs care.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Alcohol can exacerbate incoordination.
evidence.explanation: States the effect and its direction exactly as this entry records it.

evidence.snippet: We now report that a non-coding CTG expansion causes a novel form of spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA8). This expansion, located on chromosome 13q21, was isolated directly from the genomic DNA of an ataxia patient
evidence.explanation: The original identification of the causal expansion and its locus, from patient DNA rather than from a model system.

evidence.snippet: The neurological phenotype in SCA8 BAC expansion but not BAC control lines demonstrates the pathogenicity of the (CTG-CAG)n expansion.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the expansion itself is pathogenic rather than a linked marker, by contrasting expansion and control transgenic lines.

evidence.snippet: The (CTG·CAG)n repeat expansion is highly unstable and almost always changes in size on transmission: the repeat expansion is more likely to become larger when maternally transmitted and more likely to contract with paternal transmission.
evidence.explanation: Documents the transmission instability and its parent-of-origin bias, which this node records as a property of the lesion.

steps/4.description: The germline lesion is an unstable CTG-CAG repeat expansion on chromosome 13q21, in a region where ATXN8OS and the protein-coding ATXN8 overlap and are transcribed in opposite directions. The single expansion is therefore transcribed twice, in both senses, and everything downstream follows from that one fact: a CUG-repeat non-coding transcript from ATXN8OS and a CAG-repeat coding transcript from ATXN8. The repeat is highly unstable on transmission, tending to expand through the maternal line and contract through the paternal line, which is part of why the disease does not show the tidy repeat-size-to-onset relationship of the polyglutamine SCAs.

evidence.snippet: CUG(exp) transcripts accumulate as ribonuclear inclusions that co-localize with MBNL1 in selected neurons in the brain
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the foci and the co-localisation with MBNL1 that the sequestration claim rests on.

evidence.snippet: loss of Mbnl1 enhances motor deficits in SCA8 mice
evidence.explanation: Genetic interaction evidence that MBNL1 availability modifies the phenotype, which is what distinguishes sequestration from incidental co-localisation.

steps/5.description: The non-coding CUG-expansion transcript accumulates as ribonuclear inclusions in the nuclei of selected neurons and glia, where it binds and sequesters MBNL1. This is the same class of RNA gain-of-function lesion that drives myotonic dystrophy type 1, arriving here through a repeat that is short by the standards of that disease. The genetic evidence is the strong part: removing Mbnl1 makes SCA8 mice worse, which is what a sequestration model predicts and a bystander model does not.

evidence.snippet: SCA8 CUG(exp) transcripts trigger splicing changes and increased expression of the CUGBP1-MBNL1 regulated CNS target, GABA-A transporter 4 (GAT4/Gabt4)
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the expansion transcripts alter splicing of MBNL1 regulated CNS targets, which is the claim of this node.

steps/6.description: With MBNL1 sequestered, the alternative splicing it normally regulates shifts across its CNS target set. This is the molecular consequence of sequestration and is separated from what any individual mis-spliced target then does, because the splicing shift is general while only one target has been traced through to a physiological effect.

evidence.snippet: increased expression of the CUGBP1-MBNL1 regulated CNS target, GABA-A transporter 4 (GAT4/Gabt4)
evidence.explanation: Names the specific expression change this node records.

steps/7.description: Expression of the GABA-A transporter GAT4/Gabt4 rises. It is picked out from the wider splicing shift because it is the single target whose consequence has been measured rather than inferred, and because a transporter that clears GABA from the synaptic cleft has an obvious and testable physiological prediction.

evidence.snippet: the expression of noncoding (CUG)n expansion transcripts (ataxin 8 opposite strand, ATXN8OS) and the discovery of intranuclear polyglutamine inclusions suggests SCA8 pathogenesis involves toxic gain-of-function mechanisms at both the protein and RNA levels.
evidence.explanation: States that both arms operate, which is the reason this entry models them as parallel hypothesis groups rather than choosing between them.

steps/8.description: The CAG-direction transcript is translated conventionally from an AUG start into a nearly pure polyglutamine tract, which forms 1C2-positive intranuclear inclusions in cerebellar Purkinje cells and brainstem neurons. This was discovered after SCA8 had already been characterised as a non-coding expansion disease, and it is why SCA8 is now described as involving toxic gain of function at both the protein and the RNA level rather than at one of them.

evidence.snippet: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 8 (SCA8) is caused by a bidirectionally transcribed CTG·CAG expansion that results in the in vivo accumulation of CUG RNA foci, an ATG-initiated polyGln and a polyAla protein expressed by repeat-associated non-ATG (RAN) translation.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates all three products of the one expansion, which is the structure this pathograph is built around.

evidence.snippet: knockdown of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor eIF3F in cells reduces steady-state levels of SCA8 polySer and other RAN proteins
evidence.explanation: Identifies a modifier of RAN protein accumulation. Graded IN_VITRO because the knockdown was done in cells, unlike the mouse and autopsy findings in the same paper.

steps/9.description: The same expansion is translated from non-AUG start sites in more than one reading frame, producing homopolymeric proteins that no ordinary reading of the locus would predict: polyalanine, and later a polyserine product from the AGC frame. The polyserine burden increases with age and with disease severity. eIF3F was identified as a regulator of how much RAN protein accumulates, which is a rare handle on this class of mechanism.

evidence.snippet: We report a novel toxic SCA8 polySer protein which accumulates in white matter (WM) regions as aggregates that increase with age and disease severity.
evidence.explanation: States the aggregation, its white-matter localisation, and its increase with age and severity.

steps/10.description: PolySerine aggregates concentrate in white matter rather than in cerebellar grey matter, and the burden increases with age and with disease severity. This is the molecular event, kept separate from the tissue damage it is found alongside, because the relationship between them is co-localisation rather than a demonstrated causal step.

evidence.snippet: In vivo optical imaging studies in SCA8 mice confirm that Gabt4 upregulation is associated with the predicted loss of GABAergic inhibition within the granular cell layer.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the inhibitory deficit in vivo, which is what makes this a measured node rather than an inferred one.

steps/11.description: Inhibitory tone falls in the granular cell layer. This is where the molecular lesion becomes an electrophysiological one, and it was confirmed in vivo by optical imaging rather than predicted from the transporter's function alone.

evidence.snippet: Immunohistochemistry of human SCA 8 autopsy tissue (n = 4–7) shows accumulation of novel polySer RAN protein in cerebellar white matter, brainstem, and frontal cortex.
evidence.explanation: Human-only evidence that the polySerine protein is present in the white matter of SCA8 brains, with the number of cases stated. The spacing in "SCA 8" is an artifact of the cached PDF text and is preserved so the quote stays exact.

evidence.snippet: WM regions with polySer aggregates show demyelination and axonal degeneration in SCA8 human and mouse brains.
evidence.explanation: Reports the tissue damage co-located with the aggregates. Graded OTHER because this one sentence spans human autopsy and mouse findings and cannot be split textually; duplicating it under two evidence_source values would be the defect check-snippet-grading exists to catch, and choosing either one alone would misdescribe it.

steps/12.description: The white matter regions carrying polySerine aggregates show demyelination and axonal degeneration, in human as well as mouse SCA8 brains. This is the part of the mechanism that reaches outside the cerebellar cortex, and the most plausible structural basis for the pyramidal signs and cognitive features a purely Purkinje-cell account leaves unexplained.

evidence.snippet: On brain MRI, cerebellar atrophy affecting both the hemispheres and the vermis is usually found, with preservation of the brainstem and the cerebral hemispheres
evidence.explanation: Gives the imaging correlate of cerebellar degeneration and its distribution, which is what localises the lesion to this node.

evidence.snippet: (CTG)116 expansion, but not (CTG)11 control lines, develop a progressive neurological phenotype with in vivo imaging showing reduced cerebellar-cortical inhibition.
evidence.explanation: Ties the expansion directly to reduced cerebellar cortical inhibition in a controlled transgenic comparison.

steps/13.description: The convergence point. Purkinje cells are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, and their firing is degraded here from two directions at once: loss of granular-layer inhibition from the RNA arm, and intranuclear polyglutamine inclusions from the protein arm. Progressive loss of cerebellar output produces the ataxia, the scanning dysarthria and the oculomotor signs, and the cell loss is visible on MRI as global cerebellar atrophy sparing the brainstem.

evidence.snippet: SCA8 is a slowly progressive ataxia with onset typically in the third to fifth decade but with a range from before age one year to after age 60 years.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the defining phenotype and the extreme width of its onset range.

evidence.snippet: Life span is typically not shortened.
evidence.explanation: Supports the prognosis stated in the description, which distinguishes SCA8 from several other dominant ataxias.

steps/14.description: The defining feature. Gait instability is usually the presenting problem alongside dysarthria, and progression is slow enough to be measured in decades. Life span is typically not shortened, which is unusual among the dominant ataxias and shapes what management is for. Graded VERY_FREQUENT rather than OBLIGATE: non-ataxic presentations of a confirmed SCA8 expansion are documented, including dopamine-responsive parkinsonism, an ALS-like picture and isolated hemichorea, so the feature is not universal among affected carriers.

evidence.snippet: Common initial manifestations are scanning dysarthria with a characteristic drawn-out slowness of speech and gait instability.
evidence.explanation: Names scanning dysarthria as an initial manifestation, which is the claim about timing this phenotype records.

steps/15.description: Scanning dysarthria with a characteristic drawn-out slowness of speech is, with gait instability, one of the two common initial manifestations rather than a late complication.

evidence.snippet: eye movement abnormalities (nystagmus, abnormal pursuit and abnormal saccades, and, rarely, ophthalmoplegia)
evidence.explanation: Lists the oculomotor findings and their relative rarity within the group.

steps/16.description: One of a group of eye movement abnormalities that appear over the disease course, alongside abnormal pursuit and abnormal saccades, and rarely ophthalmoplegia.

evidence.snippet: Over the disease course other findings can include eye movement abnormalities (nystagmus, abnormal pursuit and abnormal saccades, and, rarely, ophthalmoplegia); upper motor neuron involvement; extrapyramidal signs; brain stem signs (dysphagia and poor cough reflex); sensory neuropathy; and cognitive impairment
evidence.explanation: Marked INDIRECT because the source says "upper motor neuron involvement" rather than spasticity specifically; spasticity is the usual manifestation of that, but it is an inference from this sentence.

steps/17.description: Upper motor neuron involvement is part of the recognised disease course. It is the phenotype the polySerine white-matter mechanism would predict, and one a purely cerebellar account does not.

evidence.snippet: On brain MRI, cerebellar atrophy affecting both the hemispheres and the vermis is usually found, with preservation of the brainstem and the cerebral hemispheres
evidence.explanation: Describes the atrophy pattern and the structures spared, which is the substance of this phenotype.

steps/18.description: Global cerebellar atrophy involving both hemispheres and the vermis, with the brainstem and cerebral hemispheres preserved. That sparing pattern is diagnostically useful, because several other dominant ataxias show pontine or supratentorial involvement as well.

edges/3.description: Transcription in the CUG direction produces the non-coding expansion RNA that forms nuclear foci.

edges/4.description: Transcription in the CAG direction produces a coding transcript that is conventionally translated into polyglutamine.

edges/5.description: The same expansion transcripts are additionally translated from non-AUG start sites in alternative reading frames.

edges/6.description: MBNL1 depletion alters splicing of its CNS targets, of which GAT4/Gabt4 is the demonstrated example.

edges/7.description: Increased expression of the GABA-A transporter GAT4 is the one demonstrated consequence of the splicing shift.

edges/8.description: Faster clearance of GABA from the synaptic cleft reduces inhibitory tone.

edges/9.description: Reduced inhibition in the granular cell layer degrades the timing of cerebellar cortical output.

edges/10.description: Intranuclear polyglutamine inclusions are found in the neurons whose function is lost, but the steps between inclusion and dysfunction are not established in SCA8 specifically.

edges/11.description: The polyserine product aggregates preferentially in white matter rather than in cerebellar grey matter.

edges/12.description: Marked indirect deliberately. The evidence is that aggregate and damage occupy the same regions; no intervention has removed polySer and rescued the white matter, so the steps between them are unknown.

edges/13.description: White matter degeneration involving corticospinal pathways is the proposed basis for the pyramidal features; the intervening steps are not established.

edges/14.description: Loss of cerebellar output is the immediate cause of the ataxia.

edges/15.description: The same loss of coordination applied to the speech apparatus.

edges/16.description: Cerebellar control of eye movement is degraded along with limb and speech coordination.

edges/17.description: Progressive cell loss at this node is what MRI measures as atrophy.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Alcohol can exacerbate incoordination.
evidence.explanation: Supports the exacerbating direction. INDIRECT because attributing it to this specific node is an inference from a clinical recommendation.

edges/18.description: Alcohol acts on cerebellar function that is already compromised. The link is marked indirect because the source states the clinical effect without identifying where in cerebellar circuitry alcohol acts in SCA8 specifically.

evidence.snippet: a heterozygous abnormal (CTG·CAG)n repeat expansion in the two overlapping genes ATXN8OS/ATXN8 identified by molecular genetic testing
evidence.explanation: Names the two overlapping genes carrying the diagnostic expansion.

genes/0.notes: Long non-coding RNA gene whose transcript carries the CTG expansion in the CUG direction. Its product is the toxic RNA species, so the gene is causative without encoding a protein.

evidence.snippet: encoded on a previously unidentified antiparallel transcript (ataxin 8, ATXN8) spanning the repeat in the CAG direction
evidence.explanation: Establishes ATXN8 as the antiparallel transcript over the same repeat, which is why it is a second causative gene rather than a second locus.

genes/1.notes: Protein-coding gene transcribed from the opposite strand across the same repeat, translated into the polyglutamine protein. Because ATXN8OS and ATXN8 share one physical expansion, they cannot be tested or inherited separately; this entry lists both because they carry different mechanisms, not different mutations.

evidence.snippet: SCA8 patients have expansions similar in size (107-127 CTG repeats) to those found among adult-onset DM patients.
evidence.explanation: Gives the measured repeat sizes in the original patients, from the report that identified the expansion.

genes/2.notes: Recorded as a property of the locus rather than as a separate gene entry. The original report sized patient expansions at 107-127 CTG repeats, comparable to adult-onset myotonic dystrophy. Wider ranges are quoted in review literature, but this entry records only the figure it can quote from a fetched primary source, because repeat size in SCA8 does not predict penetrance or onset age and an imprecise range invites over-reading.

evidence.snippet: loss of Mbnl1 enhances motor deficits in SCA8 mice
evidence.explanation: The modifier effect, stated as an experimental result in mice.

genes/3.notes: Not a disease gene. Listed as an experimentally demonstrated modifier: reducing Mbnl1 worsens the motor phenotype in SCA8 mice, which is the genetic evidence behind the RNA gain-of-function hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: Canes and walkers to help prevent falls; modification of the home (e.g., grab bars, raised toilet seats, ramps for motorized chairs) as needed
evidence.explanation: Lists the specific interventions recommended, which is what this treatment records.

treatments/0.description: Canes and walkers to prevent falls, plus home modification such as grab bars, raised toilet seats and ramps. There is no disease-modifying therapy, so management is entirely aimed at the consequences of cerebellar output loss.

evidence.snippet: Canes and walkers to help prevent falls
evidence.explanation: Supports the compensatory intent. Marked INDIRECT because the source states the intervention and its purpose, not a measured effect on ataxia.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: A symptomatic measure that compensates for lost coordination rather than acting anywhere in the mechanism. Targeted at the phenotype for that reason.

evidence.snippet: speech therapy and communication devices for those with dysarthria
evidence.explanation: Names the intervention and the phenotype it addresses.

treatments/1.description: For the scanning dysarthria, which is one of the two presenting features and a major determinant of employment and social participation.

evidence.snippet: speech therapy and communication devices for those with dysarthria
evidence.explanation: Supports the target. Marked INDIRECT because the recommendation is stated without an accompanying measured outcome.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Compensates for the speech deficit; communication devices substitute for speech outright rather than restoring it.

evidence.snippet: feeding evaluations to reduce risk of aspiration from dysphagia
evidence.explanation: Names the intervention and the specific risk it is meant to reduce.

treatments/2.description: Feeding evaluations to reduce aspiration risk from dysphagia, with dietary modification and, where needed, alternative feeding methods.

evidence.snippet: feeding evaluations to reduce risk of aspiration from dysphagia
