evidence.explanation: Supports the target; the outcome named is aspiration risk rather than the dysphagia itself, hence INDIRECT.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Manages the consequences of impaired swallowing rather than restoring brainstem function.

evidence.snippet: weighted eating utensils and dressing hooks to maintain some independence
evidence.explanation: Names the specific adaptive measures recommended and the goal they serve.

treatments/3.description: Weighted eating utensils and dressing hooks to preserve independence in daily tasks. Listed separately from mobility aids because it targets upper-limb dysmetria rather than gait, and because in a disease that does not shorten life the accumulated loss of everyday independence is most of the burden.

evidence.snippet: weighted eating utensils and dressing hooks to maintain some independence
evidence.explanation: Supports the compensatory intent. Marked INDIRECT because the source recommends the measures without reporting a measured effect.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Compensates for limb incoordination without acting on the mechanism.

evidence.snippet: physical activity to maintain muscular and cardiopulmonary conditioning
evidence.explanation: States the intervention and the specific goal, which is conditioning rather than coordination.

treatments/4.description: Maintaining muscular and cardiopulmonary conditioning. Worth listing on its own because it is prophylaxis against deconditioning rather than treatment of the ataxia, and because in a disease measured in decades the secondary effects of reduced activity have time to matter.

evidence.snippet: Sibs who inherit a (CTG·CAG)n repeat expansion may or may not develop clinical manifestations of SCA8.
evidence.explanation: States the irreducible uncertainty that makes counselling the substantive intervention it is here.

treatments/5.description: Unusually consequential in SCA8, because reduced penetrance and repeat instability mean that neither carrier status nor repeat size translates into a prediction. Counselling has to convey a risk that genuinely cannot be resolved by testing.

evidence.snippet: Here, we present three lines of evidence that RNA gain-of-function plays a significant role in SCA8
evidence.explanation: States the claim of this hypothesis group and that it rests on three separate lines of evidence rather than one observation.

hypotheses/0.description: The non-coding CUG-expansion transcript from ATXN8OS accumulates as ribonuclear foci that co-localise with MBNL1, depleting it from its normal splicing role. Supported by three independent lines of evidence in one study: foci that co-localise with MBNL1, a genetic interaction in which loss of Mbnl1 worsens motor deficits in SCA8 mice, and a specific downstream splicing and expression change (GAT4/Gabt4).

evidence.snippet: 1C2-positive intranuclear inclusions in cerebellar Purkinje and brainstem neurons in SCA8 expansion mice and human SCA8 autopsy tissue result from translation of a polyglutamine protein, encoded on a previously unidentified antiparallel transcript (ataxin 8, ATXN8) spanning the repeat in the CAG direction.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the polyglutamine protein, its origin on the antiparallel transcript, and its presence in human tissue as well as mice.

hypotheses/1.description: The CAG-direction transcript from ATXN8 is conventionally translated into a nearly pure polyglutamine protein that forms 1C2-positive intranuclear inclusions in Purkinje and brainstem neurons, in both transgenic mice and human autopsy tissue. This is the mechanism SCA8 was originally thought to lack, and its discovery is why SCA8 is now described as having toxicity at both the RNA and protein levels.

evidence.snippet: We report a novel toxic SCA8 polySer protein which accumulates in white matter (WM) regions as aggregates that increase with age and disease severity.
evidence.explanation: States the existence of the RAN polySer product and its relationship with age and severity, which is the substance of this hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: Although RAN proteins have been reported in a growing number of diseases, the mechanisms and role of RAN translation in disease are poorly understood.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own statement of how settled this mechanism is, quoted as the justification for grading this hypothesis EMERGING rather than CANONICAL.

hypotheses/2.description: The expansion is additionally translated without an AUG start codon in several reading frames, producing homopolymeric polyalanine and polyserine proteins. PolySer accumulates specifically in white matter, increases with age and disease severity, and co-localises with demyelination and axonal degeneration, a tissue distribution neither of the other two hypotheses predicts. Marked EMERGING rather than CANONICAL because the causal contribution of RAN products to the human phenotype rests on a smaller body of work than the RNA and polyglutamine arms.

open_questions/0.rationale: Reduced penetrance is not a footnote in SCA8; it is the reason a positive genetic test does not settle a diagnosis, and the reason counselling cannot give a family a usable risk figure. Repeat length, the obvious candidate explanation, does not do the work here that it does in the polyglutamine SCAs. Somatic instability, interruptions within the repeat tract, and modifiers of RAN translation such as eIF3F are all plausible, but nothing reviewed for this entry identifies the determinant.

open_questions/1.rationale: All three arms exist in human tissue, so this is not a case of a mechanism seen only in mice. But the causal weighting comes almost entirely from mouse and cell work: the Mbnl1 genetic interaction and the eIF3F knockdown are the two interventional results, and both are in model systems. In humans the evidence is co-localisation of aggregate with damage, which cannot separate cause from correlate. This is recorded as HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH rather than KNOWLEDGE_GAP because the evidence is not absent; it exists and is good, but its translational weight for the human disease is the open question.

evidence.snippet: Loss of heterozygosity of STK11, measured by the absence of LKB1 immunofluorescence, was observed in Sertoli cells of abnormal cords of testis samples from affected individuals.
evidence.explanation: Testicular biopsies from two boys with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome show loss of the second STK11 allele and absent LKB1 protein in Sertoli cells.

evidence.snippet: This was associated with loss of p21 expression and decreased phosphorylation of AMPK, known downstream targets of LKB1
evidence.explanation: Reduced AMPK phosphorylation in the same Sertoli cells is the functional readout of lost LKB1 kinase activity.

steps/5.description: In boys with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, the germline STK11 mutation is joined by loss of the second allele in Sertoli cells of the abnormal testicular cords, so those cells lack the LKB1 serine/threonine kinase. Loss of LKB1 reduces phosphorylation of its target AMPK, and AMPK no longer holds the CRTC transcriptional coactivators out of the nucleus.

evidence.snippet: A high-throughput sequencing of 520 cancer-related genes revealed FOXL2 C134W, CDKN2A E87Gfs*24, TP53 S183*, TERT c.-124C > T, and H3F3A K28R mutations in this case.
evidence.explanation: The FOXL2 C134W variant is present in an adult granulosa cell tumor of the testis.

evidence.snippet: is also found in the rare male version of GCTs and in some Sertoli-Leydig cell sex cord tumors
evidence.explanation: The introduction of this mechanistic study states that the variant occurs in male granulosa cell tumors, placing the testicular tumor under the same driver.

evidence.snippet: mutant FOXL2C134W acquires the ability to bind SMAD4, forming a FOXL2C134W/SMAD4/SMAD2/3 complex that binds a novel hybrid DNA motif AGHCAHAA, unique to the FOXL2C134W mutant.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the gained activity in granulosa cell lines; indirect for the testis because the work is on ovarian tumor biology.

evidence.snippet: The genes dysregulated in mouse AGCTs exhibited the hallmarks of cancer and were consistent with a gain-of-function of the mutated allele affecting TGFβ signaling.
evidence.explanation: A knock-in mouse carrying the variant develops ovarian adult granulosa cell tumors whose transcriptome reads as a gain of function of the mutant allele, supporting the modifier on this node.

steps/6.description: The recurrent somatic FOXL2 c.402C>G (p.C134W) variant of adult-type granulosa cell tumors, found also in the rare testicular adult granulosa cell tumor, changes what the FOXL2 transcription factor does rather than removing it. The mutant protein gains the ability to bind SMAD4 and, with SMAD2/3, occupies a hybrid DNA motif that wild-type FOXL2 does not bind, switching on genes for epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, stemness and oncogenesis.

steps/7.description: Testicular sex cord-stromal tumors arise from clonal proliferation of the non-germ-cell gonadal stromal lineages of the testis: steroidogenic Leydig cells of the interstitium, supporting Sertoli cells of the seminiferous tubules, and granulosa-type cells. This distinguishes them from germ cell tumors, which arise from the germ cell lineage.

evidence.snippet: β-catenin mutation in SCT results in nuclear β-catenin and cyclin-D1 expressions on immunohistochemical analysis.
evidence.explanation: Exon 3 CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutation in testicular Sertoli cell tumors produces nuclear beta-catenin and cyclin D1 expression, the molecular hallmark of constitutive canonical Wnt pathway activation.

steps/8.description: Recurrent activating (exon 3) mutations in CTNNB1 stabilize beta-catenin, leading to constitutive canonical Wnt signaling and nuclear beta-catenin accumulation in a subset of testicular Sertoli cell and Leydig cell tumors.

evidence.snippet: PRKAR1A alterations were present in all cases and appear to be the major driver in LCCSCTs.
evidence.explanation: Targeted sequencing of large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumors identified PRKAR1A alterations as the major molecular driver, supporting dysregulated cAMP/PKA signaling as the central mechanism in this Sertoli cell tumor variant.

evidence.snippet: A heterozygous missense somatic gsp mutation (R201C) was found in tumoral tissue, whereas no mutation was found in the surrounding normal tissue or in leukocyte DNA.
evidence.explanation: A tumour-restricted activating GNAS (gsp) mutation in a Leydig cell tumour, the Leydig-cell route into this node alongside PRKAR1A loss in Sertoli cell tumours.

steps/9.description: Activating GNAS mutations (constitutive Gs-alpha) and loss of the PKA regulatory subunit PRKAR1A (in Carney complex) both increase protein kinase A signaling, driving proliferation and steroidogenesis in Leydig and Sertoli cell tumors. PRKAR1A inactivation underlies large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumors in Carney complex.

evidence.snippet: overactivation of TGFBR1 in Sertoli cells would promote their transdifferentiation into granulosa-like cells and the formation of TGCTs.
evidence.explanation: A mouse model demonstrates that constitutive TGFBR1 activation in Sertoli cells drives their transdifferentiation into granulosa-like cells and testicular granulosa cell tumor formation, implicating TGF-beta signaling in SCST pathogenesis.

steps/10.description: In a genetically engineered mouse model, sustained Sertoli cell-specific activation of the TGF-beta receptor TGFBR1 is sufficient to reprogram Sertoli cells toward a granulosa-like fate and to drive testicular granulosa cell tumor formation. This provides a mechanistic link between TGF-beta signaling dysregulation and the granulosa-cell phenotype of a subset of testicular sex cord-stromal tumors.

evidence.snippet: Mean expression of aromatase and TGFbeta1 mRNAs in Tu was 6- and 2.3-fold higher than in ExTu, respectively (P<0.05).
evidence.explanation: In a large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor from a boy with bilateral gynecomastia, aromatase mRNA was six-fold higher in tumor nodules than in the adjacent normal-looking testis.

steps/11.description: Sertoli cell tumors arising in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and Carney complex, typically the large-cell calcifying type, overexpress aromatase and so convert androgen to estrogen within the testis. This is how prepubertal boys with these tumors develop gynecomastia and advanced bone age while their gonadotropins and testosterone stay prepubertal, and why aromatase inhibitors control those signs.

evidence.snippet: activating gsp mutation in Leydig cells may result in tumor development, leading to overexpression of the inhibin alpha subunit and hyperactivity of the testosterone biosynthetic pathway.
evidence.explanation: A somatic activating GNAS (gsp R201C) mutation in a Leydig cell tumor drove hyperactivity of the testosterone biosynthetic pathway, demonstrating autonomous tumoral steroidogenesis.

steps/12.description: Hormonally active Leydig cell tumors autonomously synthesize testosterone; peripheral and intratumoral aromatase converts androgens to estrogens. Excess sex steroids produce gynecomastia in adults and isosexual precocious puberty in prepubertal boys.

evidence.snippet: The more frequent hormonal manifestations of these tumors are high plasmatic and urinary estrogen levels, low serum testosterone, low testosterone/estradiol index, and FSH or LH low levels as well.
evidence.explanation: Summarises the endocrine picture of Leydig cell tumors as estrogen excess with suppressed FSH and LH, the two arms of this node.

evidence.snippet: Endocrine function tests showed decreased gonadotropin concentrations, and reduction of testosterone/estradiol ratio.
evidence.explanation: A man with bilateral gynecomastia and a Leydig cell tumor had a lowered testosterone-to-estradiol ratio with suppressed gonadotropins.

evidence.snippet: After surgery, the gynecomastia has completely disappeared and hormonal alterations returned to normal.
evidence.explanation: Removing the tumor reversed both the gynecomastia and the hormonal changes, tying them to the tumor's output.

evidence.snippet: The serum estradiol level was abnormally elevated reflecting the estrogen-secreting profile.
evidence.explanation: A benign Leydig cell tumor presenting with bilateral gynecomastia secreted estradiol.

steps/13.description: Tumor-derived estrogen excess produces gynecomastia and can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, reducing spermatogenesis and fertility.

evidence.snippet: The Testicular Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor (JGCT) is a rare testicular neoplasm that appears in the first months of life as a painless testicular mass.
evidence.explanation: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor, a testicular sex cord-stromal tumor, classically presents as a painless testicular mass.

steps/14.description: Painless unilateral testicular mass is the most common presentation of testicular sex cord-stromal tumors.

evidence.snippet: In adult patients, gynecomastia, oligozoospermia, erectile dysfunction, and other signs of feminization can be present
evidence.explanation: Adult Leydig cell tumors commonly present with gynecomastia and other signs of feminization due to tumoral sex steroid production.

steps/15.description: Gynecomastia results from tumor-derived estrogen excess and is a common presenting feature of hormonally active Leydig cell tumors in adults.

evidence.snippet: orchiectomy for boys with aggressive LCCSCT and gynecomastia to avoid premature epiphyseal fusion and induction of central precocious puberty
evidence.explanation: The Carney complex GeneReviews documents that aromatase-expressing large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumors in boys can induce gynecomastia and central precocious puberty, supporting the endocrine presentation of testicular Sertoli cell tumors.

steps/16.description: Sertoli cell tumors, particularly the large-cell calcifying variant in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and Carney complex, can present with precocious puberty.

edges/5.description: A subset of Sertoli and Leydig cell tumors are driven by CTNNB1 mutation.

edges/6.description: GNAS and PRKAR1A lesions activate cAMP/PKA signaling in tumor cells.

edges/7.description: In a subset of tumors, dysregulated TGF-beta signaling reprograms Sertoli cells toward a granulosa-like fate, contributing to granulosa-cell tumor formation.

edges/8.description: Tumor cells secrete sex steroids independent of normal regulation.

edges/9.description: Clonal expansion of the gonadal stromal cells forms the intratesticular mass through which most of these tumors present.

edges/10.description: Elevated cAMP/PKA signaling drives steroidogenic gene expression in Leydig cell tumors, promoting autonomous sex-steroid synthesis.

evidence.snippet: Loss of heterozygosity of the STK11 gene leads to an increase in aromatase expression associated with an increase in CRTC nuclear localization
evidence.explanation: States the step this edge asserts, from STK11 loss to aromatase overexpression, with CRTC nuclear localization as the intermediate.

edges/11.description: Without LKB1-dependent AMPK activity, CRTC coactivators accumulate in the nucleus and stimulate aromatase (CYP19A1) expression.

evidence.snippet: Gynaecomastia, although rarely related to testicular tumours, in boys with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) usually occurs due to large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumour (LCCSCT).
evidence.explanation: Attributes gynecomastia in boys with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome to the large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor.

evidence.snippet: In the last follow-up, 2 years after the start of therapy, he experienced a less tense Tanner-B2 and a decrease in HV
evidence.explanation: Breast development and height velocity fell on anastrozole, so the manifestations depend on aromatase activity; a therapeutic response is indirect support for the edge.

edges/12.description: Estrogen made by the tumor's aromatase drives breast growth and skeletal advancement; blocking aromatase reverses both.

evidence.snippet: orchiectomy for boys with aggressive LCCSCT and gynecomastia to avoid premature epiphyseal fusion and induction of central precocious puberty
evidence.explanation: The Carney complex GeneReviews recommends orchiectomy in boys with aggressive LCCSCT and gynecomastia specifically to prevent central precocious puberty, a consequence of the tumor's estrogen.

edges/13.description: Estrogen from an aromatase-expressing large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor advances skeletal maturation and can trigger central precocious puberty in boys.

edges/14.description: Excess estrogen drives gynecomastia and feminization.

evidence.snippet: Two months after surgery, the gynecomastia diminished gradually and estrogen levels returned to normal.
evidence.explanation: Gynecomastia and estrogen excess fell together after orchidectomy for a Leydig cell tumor, tying the breast growth to the tumor's estrogen.

edges/15.description: Tumor-derived estrogen stimulates male breast tissue growth; the gynecomastia regresses once the tumor is removed.

evidence.snippet: mutation analyses of the β-catenin gene (exon 3; CTNNB1) were performed.
evidence.explanation: Exon 3 CTNNB1 mutation analysis in testicular sex cord-stromal tumors identified recurrent beta-catenin mutations in Sertoli cell tumors.

evidence.snippet: A heterozygous missense somatic gsp mutation (R201C) was found in tumoral tissue, whereas no mutation was found in the surrounding normal tissue or in leukocyte DNA.
evidence.explanation: A somatic activating GNAS (gsp R201C) mutation was identified specifically in Leydig cell tumor tissue, implicating GNAS activation in tumorigenesis.

evidence.snippet: Such examples include Carney complex and large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor
evidence.explanation: Carney complex, caused by germline PRKAR1A inactivation, is a well-established predisposition syndrome for large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor.

genes/2.notes: RISK_FACTOR rather than CAUSATIVE for this entry: germline PRKAR1A inactivation (Carney complex) predisposes to one subtype, the large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor, and is neither necessary nor sufficient for testicular sex cord-stromal neoplasia as a whole. Sporadic large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumors also carry PRKAR1A alterations, hence the combined variant origin.

evidence.snippet: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and intratubular large cell hyalinizing Sertoli cell neoplasia
evidence.explanation: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, caused by germline STK11 inactivation, is associated with a distinctive intratubular large cell hyalinizing Sertoli cell neoplasia of the testis.

genes/3.notes: RISK_FACTOR for the same reason as PRKAR1A: germline STK11 inactivation (Peutz-Jeghers syndrome) predisposes to Sertoli cell tumors in a minority of the entry's cases. The tumor-level event is loss of the second allele in Sertoli cells (see LKB1 Loss in Sertoli Cells).

evidence.snippet: A high-throughput sequencing of 520 cancer-related genes revealed FOXL2 C134W, CDKN2A E87Gfs*24, TP53 S183*, TERT c.-124C > T, and H3F3A K28R mutations in this case.
evidence.explanation: Sequencing of an adult testicular granulosa cell tumor identified the FOXL2 C134W mutation, the hallmark driver of adult-type granulosa cell tumors.

evidence.snippet: orchiectomy for boys with aggressive LCCSCT and gynecomastia to avoid premature epiphyseal fusion and induction of central precocious puberty
evidence.explanation: Orchiectomy is indicated for aggressive Sertoli cell tumors with endocrine manifestations, supporting surgery as the mainstay of management.

treatments/0.description: Surgical removal of the tumor is the mainstay of treatment. Most sex cord-stromal tumors are benign and cured by radical inguinal orchiectomy or, for small benign lesions, testis-sparing (partial) orchiectomy.

evidence.snippet: RPLND remains an option to be performed immediately after orchiectomy, especially in patients who have tumors with malignant features and/or small-volume metastatic disease.
evidence.explanation: Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection is an option performed after orchiectomy for testicular sex cord-stromal tumors with malignant features or small-volume metastatic disease, directly supporting RPLND as a surgical management modality.

evidence.snippet: It has been demonstrated that certain histopathological risk factors can be useful in identifying those with malignant potential.
evidence.explanation: Histopathological risk factors identify sex cord-stromal tumors with malignant potential, guiding selection for patients who warrant more aggressive surgical management such as retroperitoneal lymph node dissection.

treatments/1.description: Considered for malignant sex cord-stromal tumors with features predictive of metastasis, since these tumors respond poorly to chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, sCD27 stimulated expression of CD40L on 10 of 10 BM MC samples and APRIL on 4 of 10 BM MC samples obtained from patients with WM as well as on LAD2 MCs.
evidence.explanation: This experiment supports a mechanistic microenvironment program in which WM-associated mast cells are induced to express trophic ligands.

evidence.snippet: Last, treatment of severe combined immunodeficiency-human (SCID-hu) mice with established WM using the SGN-70 antibody blocked disease progression in 12 of 12 mice, whereas disease progressed in all 5 untreated mice.
evidence.explanation: This xenograft result supports the biologic importance of the CD27-CD70 microenvironment axis in sustaining WM disease progression.

steps/2.description: Excess marrow mast cells provide trophic and survival signals to the lymphoplasmacytic clone, making the marrow microenvironment an active participant in WM pathogenesis.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that the L265P mutation is involved in the majority of Waldenström's macroglobulinemia.
evidence.explanation: This patient-series abstract supports MYD88 L265P as a major recurrent driver lesion in WM.

steps/3.description: MYD88 L265P is the dominant recurrent somatic lesion in WM and functions as an early oncogenic event in disease pathogenesis.

evidence.snippet: WM is an uncommon lymphoproliferative disorder characterized primarily by bone marrow infiltration and IgM monoclonal gammopathy.
evidence.explanation: The consensus definition identifies marrow infiltration as a primary clinicopathologic feature of WM.

evidence.snippet: Lymphoplasmacytic-lymphoplasmacytoid lymphoma (LPL)/Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia (WM) or immunocytoma (IMC) consists of diffuse proliferation of small mature B lymphocytes, plasmacytoid lymphocytes, and plasma-cells.
evidence.explanation: This abstract specifies the marrow-infiltrating tumor-cell composition that underlies the lymphoplasmacytic clone in WM.

steps/4.description: The disease-defining tissue state is infiltration of the bone marrow by a clonal lymphoplasmacytic population spanning mature B-cell, plasmacytoid, and plasma-cell differentiation states.

evidence.snippet: WM is an uncommon lymphoproliferative disorder characterized primarily by bone marrow infiltration and IgM monoclonal gammopathy.
evidence.explanation: The consensus definition supports monoclonal IgM production as a core downstream output of the malignant lymphoplasmacytic clone.

steps/5.description: The clonal lymphoplasmacytic population produces a monoclonal IgM paraprotein that accumulates in the circulation and mediates important downstream complications.

evidence.snippet: Peripheral neuropathy occurs in nearly half of patients with this condition, and hyperviscosity-related nervous system disorders are encountered in up to a third.
evidence.explanation: This review supports serum hyperviscosity as a common intermediate pathogenic process contributing to WM neurologic morbidity.

steps/6.description: High circulating IgM burden increases serum viscosity and contributes to neurologic morbidity in a substantial subset of patients.

evidence.snippet: By combined AS-PCR and Sanger sequencing, CXCR4(WHIM) mutations were identified in 44/102 (43%), 21/62 (34%), 2/12 (17%) and 1/20 (5%) untreated WM, previously treated WM, IgM MGUS and marginal zone lymphoma patients, respectively, but no chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, multiple myeloma, non-IgM MGUS patients or healthy donors.
evidence.explanation: This supports CXCR4 WHIM-like mutation as a recurrent, disease-enriched secondary genomic event in WM.

steps/7.description: A substantial subset of WM cases acquire subclonal WHIM-like CXCR4 mutations, adding heterogeneity to the MYD88-mutant clone and influencing treatment response.

evidence.snippet: WM is an uncommon lymphoproliferative disorder characterized primarily by bone marrow infiltration and IgM monoclonal gammopathy.
evidence.explanation: This consensus definition supports the causal pairing of marrow lymphoplasmacytic disease with its defining IgM paraprotein output.

edges/2.description: The marrow lymphoplasmacytic clone gives rise to the circulating IgM paraprotein.

evidence.snippet: Peripheral neuropathy occurs in nearly half of patients with this condition, and hyperviscosity-related nervous system disorders are encountered in up to a third.
evidence.explanation: This clinical review directly documents hyperviscosity-related neurologic complications in WM; coupled with the disease-defining IgM paraprotein, it supports serum hyperviscosity as a downstream pathogenic process.

edges/3.description: Heavy circulating IgM burden increases serum viscosity and contributes to neurologic complications.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that the L265P mutation is involved in the majority of Waldenström's macroglobulinemia.
evidence.explanation: This supports MYD88 L265P as a founding lesion contributing to the core marrow lymphoplasmacytic disease state.

edges/4.description: MYD88-mutant clones participate in the core lymphoplasmacytic marrow disease state.

evidence.snippet: The findings show that CXCR4(WHIM) mutations are more common in WM than previously revealed, and are primarily subclonal, supporting their acquisition after MYD88(L265P) in WM oncogenesis.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports CXCR4 mutation acquisition as a later subclonal branch layered onto the MYD88-mutant WM clone.

edges/5.description: Secondary CXCR4 mutations are commonly acquired after the MYD88 founder event.

evidence.snippet: Last, treatment of severe combined immunodeficiency-human (SCID-hu) mice with established WM using the SGN-70 antibody blocked disease progression in 12 of 12 mice, whereas disease progressed in all 5 untreated mice.
evidence.explanation: Interrupting the mast-cell linked CD27-CD70 signaling axis reduced WM progression in vivo, partially supporting this pathway as an upstream contributor to persistence of the lymphoplasmacytic clone.

edges/6.description: Microenvironmental mast-cell signals support persistence of the malignant lymphoplasmacytic clone.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that the L265P mutation is involved in the majority of Waldenström's macroglobulinemia.
evidence.explanation: This supports MYD88 L265P as the dominant recurrent somatic alteration in WM.

genes/0.notes: MYD88 L265P is the dominant recurrent somatic lesion in WM and is treated here as an upstream founder event in disease oncogenesis.

evidence.snippet: The findings show that CXCR4(WHIM) mutations are more common in WM than previously revealed, and are primarily subclonal, supporting their acquisition after MYD88(L265P) in WM oncogenesis.
evidence.explanation: This supports CXCR4 mutation as a recurrent secondary somatic event in WM.

genes/1.notes: WHIM-like CXCR4 mutations occur in a substantial subset of WM cases and are primarily subclonal, consistent with later acquisition after MYD88.

evidence.snippet: The panel reiterated that watchful waiting remains the gold standard for asymptomatic patients without critically elevated IgM or compromised hematopoietic function.
evidence.explanation: This consensus update supports watchful waiting as the standard management approach for asymptomatic WM.

treatments/0.description: Observation without immediate therapy is the standard disease-management strategy for asymptomatic WM without critically elevated IgM or compromised hematopoietic function.

evidence.snippet: For first-line treatment, chemoimmunotherapy (CIT) regimens such as dexamethasone, cyclophosphamide, rituximab (DRC), or bendamustine, rituximab (Benda-R) continue to play a central role in managing WM, as they are effective, of fixed duration, generally well-tolerated, and affordable.
evidence.explanation: The 2023 IWWM consensus panel identifies bendamustine-rituximab as a central fixed-duration first-line treatment option for symptomatic WM.

steps/2.description: The common gamma chain is the shared subunit of the IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21 receptors and signals through JAK3 and STAT5. How the signal is reduced depends on the allele. With p.Ile153Thr the chain is expressed at the cell surface at normal levels and downstream STAT5 phosphorylation is partially impaired; with p.Pro58Ser surface expression itself is reduced, because the mutant chain is mislocalised to the ER/Golgi interface; with p.Arg328Ter surface expression is normal, JAK3 binding is impaired, and STAT5 is still partially phosphorylated. What the alleles share is residual signalling, which is what separates this entity from X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, where the pathway is abolished.

genes/0.notes: The same gene as X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency; what differs is the allele. Four variants are curated here, all hypomorphic rather than null: c.812T>A p.Leu271Gln in exon 7, in the SH2-subdomain homology region of the cytoplasmic tail, in the index American family; c.458T>C p.Ile153Thr in a German family; c.172C>T p.Pro58Ser in a single boy; and the exon-8 nonsense variant p.Arg328Ter in two brothers. Other hypomorphic IL2RG alleles are reported in the literature but are not curated here. Note that the exon-7 substitution is reported by amino acid position and codon change (CTG to CAG) rather than by a coding-DNA identifier in the source, so the c. notation above is a reconstruction and should be treated as such. The hypomorphic classification is supported functionally for p.Ile153Thr, where surface CD132 expression is normal and STAT5 phosphorylation only partially impaired; for p.Leu271Gln it rests on the clinical and immunologic comparison with X-SCID rather than on a signalling assay. For p.Pro58Ser and p.Arg328Ter it is supported by signalling assays in patient cells.

steps/1.description: SMAX2-associated hemizygous variants cluster in exon 15 near the active adenylation domain, but they do not share one demonstrated biochemical defect. The recurrent synonymous c.1731C>T allele reduces UBA1 expression. In vitro, p.Met539Ile and p.Ser547Gly did not show statistically reduced adenylation, whereas p.Glu557Val showed a moderate reduction. The initiating lesion is therefore modeled as allele-specific UBA1 dysfunction rather than uniform adenylation failure or complete loss of UBA1 function.

evidence.snippet: UBA1 is the initial enzyme in the ubiquitination cascade and initiates the transfer of ubiquitin molecules to target proteins where they are degraded by the proteasome.

evidence.snippet: UBA1 is thus of fundamental importance to the modulation of ubiquitin homeostasis and to all downstream ubiquitylation-dependent cellular processes, including proteolysis through the ubiquitin-proteasome system and selective autophagy.

evidence.snippet: Our results demonstrate a surprising shift from the likelihood of these XL-SMA mutations playing a damaging role in Uba1's enzymatic activity with Ubiquitin, to other roles such as altering UBA1 mRNA splicing via the disruption of splicing factor binding sites, similar to a mechanism in traditional SMA, or disrupting binding to other important in vivo binding partners.

steps/2.description: UBA1 is the initiating enzyme of the ubiquitin cascade, but human SMAX2 tissue has not shown a uniform decrease in ubiquitination or proteasomal degradation. This node keeps those candidate cellular routes explicit without projecting the decreased ubiquitination seen after experimental knockdown onto human pathology.

evidence.snippet: Life span is significantly shortened because of progressive ventilatory insufficiency resulting from chest muscle involvement.

evidence.snippet: Here we report a male infant who presented from birth with predominantly truncal hypotonia following an antenatal history of reduced fetal movements.

edges/1.description: Different alleles may perturb splicing, binding partners, ubiquitin handling, or other UBA1-dependent processes through mechanisms not yet established in patient tissue.

edges/2.description: Human anterior-horn pathology is established, but the intervening allele-specific UBA1 mechanism is unknown.

edges/3.description: Human sensory involvement forms a separate branch from anterior-horn motor-neuron degeneration; its UBA1-dependent route is unknown.

edges/4.description: Cerebellar pathology was observed in one detailed human autopsy, but its relationship to specific UBA1 alleles is unresolved.

edges/5.description: Muscle-targeted knockdown supports a parallel model-only tissue-autonomous branch whose fidelity to human SMAX2 remains untested.

edges/6.description: Motor neuron loss denervates skeletal muscle, producing congenital hypotonia, areflexia, and profound weakness.

edges/7.description: In utero motor-system dysfunction can reduce fetal movement and thereby promote congenital joint contractures.

edges/8.description: The human neurophysiologic and postmortem sensory findings manifest clinically as sensory nervous system involvement.

edges/9.description: The observed cerebellar pathology is represented by the corresponding structural phenotype.

edges/10.description: Congenital lower-motor-unit dysfunction manifests as neonatal hypotonia.

edges/11.description: Lower-motor-unit dysfunction produces absent deep-tendon reflexes.

edges/12.description: Denervation and possible muscle-autonomous dysfunction produce generalized or distal weakness across the clinical spectrum.

edges/13.description: Facial muscle weakness produces the characteristic myopathic facial appearance.

edges/14.description: Phrenic and intercostal motor unit failure compromises ventilation.

edges/15.description: Bulbar and generalized weakness impair sucking and swallowing.

edges/16.description: Progressive neuromuscular weakness can produce secondary spinal curvature.

edges/17.description: Prenatal motor-system dysfunction manifests as reduced fetal movement.

edges/18.description: Fetal akinesia from motor neuron loss produces multiple congenital joint contractures.

edges/19.description: Fractures co-occur with congenital contractures, but the direct causal substrate is unknown.

edges/20.description: Muscle-intrinsic UBA1 reduction may contribute to weakness alongside denervation.

evidence.snippet: two missense mutations (c.1617 G-->T, p.Met539Ile; c.1639 A-->G, p.Ser547Gly) present each in one XL-SMA family, and one synonymous C-->T substitution (c.1731 C-->T, p.Asn577Asn) identified in another three unrelated families
evidence.explanation: Identifies the causative UBA1 (UBE1) variants segregating with XL-SMA.

evidence.snippet: XL-SMA is part of a growing list of neurodegenerative disorders associated with defects in the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway
evidence.explanation: Places XL-SMA among ubiquitin-proteasome pathway neurodegenerative disorders without proving one identical biochemical consequence for all variants.

evidence.snippet: Our data revealed that only one of the three XL-SMA missense variants impairs the Ubiquitin-adenylating ability of Uba1.
evidence.explanation: Establishes allele-specific rather than uniform adenylation impairment among the three tested missense variants.

genes/0.notes: UBA1 (ubiquitin-like modifier activating enzyme 1), the E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme, on Xp11.3. Hemizygous pathogenic variants cluster in exon 15 / the active adenylation domain (e.g. p.Met539Ile, p.Ser547Gly, the c.1731C>T synonymous variant reducing expression). The synonymous allele has direct expression evidence. Among tested missense alleles, p.Met539Ile and p.Ser547Gly retained adenylation activity in vitro while p.Glu557Val showed a moderate reduction, so neither a uniform adenylation defect nor complete loss-of-function is assigned across SMAX2 variants.

evidence.snippet: However, it remains unexplored how UBA1 impacts the muscle proteome, and whether muscle weakness can arise from reducing UBA1 function solely in skeletal muscle.
evidence.explanation: States the motivating tissue-mechanism question addressed in models but not yet resolved in human SMAX2.

evidence.snippet: Our data revealed that only one of the three XL-SMA missense variants impairs the Ubiquitin-adenylating ability of Uba1.
evidence.explanation: The allele-specific biochemical result establishes why generic UBA1 knockdown cannot be assumed to model every human SMAX2 allele.

open_questions/0.rationale: Muscle-targeted UBA1 knockdown in Drosophila and mice reduces ubiquitination and muscle function, but it does not model a specific human exon-15 allele. Human biochemical assays show heterogeneous effects across missense variants, and patient tissue establishes motor, sensory, and cerebellar pathology without demonstrating reduced ubiquitination. The model result is therefore evidence for a testable muscle-autonomous route, not proof of the human mechanism.

evidence.snippet: females who inherit the pathogenic variant will be heterozygotes and will usually not be affected.
evidence.explanation: The qualifier "usually" leaves female penetrance and modifiers unresolved.

open_questions/1.rationale: Reports are dominated by severely affected hemizygous male probands and multiplex families, while GeneReviews states that heterozygous females are usually unaffected and a recent case was de novo. This design cannot provide an unbiased female penetrance estimate, sex-specific rate, or genotype-specific natural history.
